News.title: Large fire at West Midlands beauty spot as people told to avoid area
News.content:
Large fire at West Midlands beauty spot as people told to avoid area

Eight fire crews were sent to the Barr Beacon nature reserve in Great Barr, Walsall, with other blazes also at Perry Hall Playing Fields and Kingfisher Park in Birmingham

View Image Another fire broke out at Perry Hall Playing Fields as families were told to leave the area

A large fire has broken out at another UK beauty spot as people have been told to avoid the area.

‌



Eight fire engines were sent to the Barr Beacon nature reserve in Great Barr, Walsall, to tackle the fire today. Police officers were blocking three entrances to the nature reserve this afternoon as smoke was billowing into the sky.

‌



A statement from West Midlands Fire Service this afternoon reads: "We have eight crews in attendance at Barr Beacon, Great Barr, where they've responded to a large grassland fire. Please avoid the area where possible."

‌



BirminghamLive reports Beacon Road was closed in both directions due to the fire, between B4151 Beacon Hill and Bridle Lane. Barr Beacon is described as "one of the highest points in the West Midlands", offering "spectacular views" over Birmingham.

This isn't the only grassland fire in the West Midlands today as the fire service also confirmed crews were in attendance at Perry Avenue. People were once again asked to avoid the area after the blaze broke out at Perry Hall Playing Fields, with six crews sent to the scene.

‌



Many families were present at the park at the time of the fire as the European Cycle Speedway 2026 tournament was held there. Drone footage showed a huge section of grass completely burnt as flames quickly spread through a large meadow area around 1pm.

A third fire is burning at Kingfisher Park in Hay Mills, east Birmingham, with large plumes of smoke and fierce flames visible. This incident is understood to have started around 4pm.

Many fires in the open have started across the UK in recent weeks as the country battles extended periods of scorching temperatures and low precipitations. Seven regions in England - half of the country - were placed in drought earlier this week by the Government, including London, East Anglia, Hertfordshire, and West Midlands.

Article continues below

The whole of Wales is also in drought.

News.title: 'We stretched our budget to buy dream home - only to discover the Japanese knotweed problem'
News.content:
'We stretched our budget to buy dream home - only to discover the Japanese knotweed problem'

Japanese knotweed spreads underground, so Nathan Hannaway and his family had no idea the garden of their fantastic new home was infested by the aggressive and invasive plant

View 5 Images Nathan Hannaway's dream home turned into a nightmare after the discovery (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

A couple who splashed out on an incredible five-bedroom Victorian home had to put their renovation plans on hold after discovering a hidden Japanese knotweed infestation - costing them a further £15,000.

‌



Nathan Hannaway and his partner spent £430,000 on the property in the affluent suburb but later found five shoots of the weed in the back garden.

‌



This invasive fast-growing weed takes over gardens and can be incredibly difficult to remove as it chokes other plants. It can block light, tears apart fences, sheds and brickwork and cause homeowners choas as it can easily remain undetected until it escalates into a more serious issue.

‌



It spreads through an underground network of roots and can wreak havoc on gardens, property values and house sales but some areas suffer more than others.

View 5 Images Nathan soon discovered his garden was overrun with Japanese knotweed (Image: Environet / SWNS)

Gardeners warned common plant can lift slabs, crush water pipes and wreck driveways READ MORE :

Nathan and his partner have had to spend £15,000 to remove the Japanese knotweed. They had moved from a two-bedroom house in Bury, Greater Manchester, to the address in Whitehall, near Blackburn, Lancashire, and hoped to transform its overgrown garden while creating more space to expand their family.

‌



But they became aware of the weed soon after moving in. Nathan, 33, said: "I was quoted £15,000 to remove it - I was shocked. What they found when they excavated was unbelievable. There was so much of it.

"When we heard it would be £15,000 to remove - that was a big chunk of our budget for the renovation. Everything I wanted to do with the garden is now on hold."

The father of two, who runs a wind-turbine testing company, had initially barely heard of it - so researched its red-speckled stems and walked along nearby riverbanks to see what it looked like. A survey by Environet found knotweed growing in three separate areas of his new home.

‌



View 5 Images The hidden infestation left the dad with a £15,000 bill (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

Nathan was not aware he and his family had moved to the UK's worst postcode for Japanese knotweed. New data shows Whitehall, the small neighbourhood in Darwen, Lancashire, with a population of 9,000, has the highest number of recorded infestations in the country.

A total of 92 incidences were logged in BB3 2, which sits in Blackburn with Darwen - itself named Britain's worst-affected borough with 2,135 cases, or 40 per square mile - in figures compiled by leading invasive-plant specialist Environet.

‌



View 5 Images The fast-growing plant spreads through an underground network of roots and can wreak havoc on gardens (Image: Environet / SWNS)

Nathan's neighbour Brian Hartley, 84, said he had seen knotweed appear in his garden during the 30 years he has lived there.

He said: "If you don't stay on top of it, it spreads like wildfire."

‌



Nearby at Blackburn Old Cemetery, fresh clumps have also been cordoned off to stop lawnmowers slicing the plant into fragments and spreading it across the grounds.

View 5 Images Britain's worst postcode for Japanese knotweed has been revealed (Image: Environet / SWNS)

Maurice Ffelan, 82, of the Friends of Blackburn Old Cemetery, said: "It's a bugger to get rid of. It can grow to 10ft tall."

‌



It can also grow up to 10cm a day in the summer heat, reaching up to three metres across a single season. Volunteers injects glyphosate weedkiller into mature stems in an attempt to kill the dense underground root system.

Maurice added: "The problem is if you start mowing it, you transfer little bits about and you don't notice until the next year when it suddenly starts popping up everywhere."

Guidance from Propertymark, the professional body for estate agents, says knotweed is material information which should be disclosed and warns it can reduce prices, delay transactions and cause sales to collapse.

‌



UK's knotweed hotspots

Blackburn with Darwen - 2,135 incidences; 40.36 per sq mile

Bristol - 1,323; 31.5 per sq mile

Bolton - 1,651; 30.59 per sq mile

‌



Brent - 464; 27.8 per sq mile

St Helens - 1,324; 25.15 per sq mile

Cardiff - 1,208; 20.94 per sq mile

‌



Newport - 1,752; 20.86 per sq mile

Haringey - 236; 20.65 per sq mile

Lambeth - 204; 19.39 per sq mile

Article continues below

Nottingham - 528; 18.23 per sq mile

News.title: 'Andy Burnham's levy on all estates would be the fairest option to ensure social care'
News.content:
The dead can’t take wealth with them, as my mam is fond of saying, so a levy on estates would be a fair way to fund Andy Burnham’s free social care revolution.

I tell my own brood they’d be extremely lucky to be charged inheritance tax because it would mean the three were sharing upwards of £500,000 and 95% leave less or absolutely nothing.

Slap on a 10% social care surcharge, a rate Burnham toyed with 16 years ago, and my lot would still be banking wads of moolah they never earned. Crucially, it would be a potentially far larger sum than me spending all my savings then flogging the Costa del Tyne house to fund exorbitantly expensive dotage help.

Reform critics waving skeletons with HMRC tax notices and Conservatives objecting to any tax to fund free care are proving empty vessels make most noise. For many, many families, pay-after-you-go would be cheaper and guarantee most of an estate survives to pass on instead of some old and frail losing virtually everything over £23,250 in England.

‌



Depleted savings and lost houses wouldn’t happen in Burnham’s new caring world yet there are alternatives to an inheritance levy. Remodelling private pension subsidies to boost tax relief from 20% to 25% for lower and middle earners and cutting it from 40% for higher earners could generate up to £20billion, one study says.

Equalising Capital Gains Tax with Income Tax could raise £12bn, says Wes Streeting. Then there is a £10bn 2% annual wealth tax on the 1,000 super-rich with upwards of £100m each, or the £24bn version championed by Patriotic Millionaires UK on those with more than £10m.

Creating a National Care Service alongside the NHS to deliver care free where needed would be a landmark achievement.

We’ll discover how radical this PM is against opponents who squeal against a death tax and produce no solutions to end folk going without care or losing savings and homes.

‌



View 5 Images Mr Burnham's vision has been branded a 'death tax'

Reform past its peak

Busy arguing with a bin in Clacton while his dodgy money troubles mount, King of Sleaze Nigel Farage glimpsed a grim future for himself, despite never setting foot in Greater Manchester.

The gloss is truly wiped from Farage, Reform down if not yet out, a party past its peak.

Andy Burnham’s resurrected Labour Party is leading in some opinion polls and the Greater Manchester Mayor contest showed why tactical voting and far-right enemy Restore may end Nauseous Nigel’s No10 dream.

‌



The most significant figure wasn’t Mayor Bev Craig’s 47.1%–21.0% first-round lead over Reform but the run-off 66.3%–33.7% lapping, as many Greens, Lib Dems and some moderate Tories voted Labour to stop Farage.

Come the next general election, when we put a single X on the ballot paper, tactical voting might be the widest ever (I’ve voted tactically in the past) with people more motivated by who they definitely don’t want rather than who they do.

That, plus racist Restore’s concerning 9% in polls, is why a slipping Farage could be spending more time with other people’s money.

View 5 Images Opinion polls make grim reading for Nigel Farage's party (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Badenoch running out of energy

Accused of peddling North Sea oil and gas lies as boiling Britain and Europe burn, Kemi Badenoch appears a fossil fool on the wrong side of net zero arguments.

Even traditional Tories, horrified at the world going up in flames, are turning against a leader purging her party of politicians embracing a cheaper, cleaner, more secure renewable future.

Tory energy spokeswoman Claire Coutinho admitted that increasing North Sea output won’t necessarily knock a penny off bills, while the Uplift transition group destroyed Badenoch’s highly misleading pollution arguments.

Two-thirds of Britons still back the goal to reach net zero by 2050 or earlier.

‌



So, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh wins the arguments, and it will be fossil fools like Badenoch and Reform who are burned.

View 5 Images Suella Braverman claimed the migrants whom reached Spain were heading for the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Braverman was scaremongering

Nearly all 60,000 who entered Spain’s enclave of Ceuta from Morocco and returned over the border didn’t stop twice-sacked Home Secretary Suella Braverman scaremongering.

The claim from a Reform Tory that “make no mistake, these men are on their way to the UK right now” was fundamentally dishonest.

‌



People can’t travel from Ceuta into mainland Spain without a passport or permission, while experience tells us only a tiny proportion may risk travelling across Europe to the Channel moat.

Her post reminds me of Farage’s 2016 Brexit “Breaking Point” poster of Syrian refugees on Slovenia’s border.

MP Jo Cox was killed by a far-right murderer on the same day.

Does Braverman care about the truth and consequences of her words? Or does she only crave power, unconcerned by consequences? The latter is suggested by her “invasion” rhetoric.

‌



View 5 Images Mr Burnham congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Greater Manchester Mayor (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News)

Going up

Bitter beaten rivals now pretending Labour new Mayor Bev Craig’s comfortable Greater Manchester conquest wasn’t remarkable can’t even kid themselves when a month ago Farage scented Reform victory. Long live the Queen of the North!

Going down

If the Tory Party infiltrated a double agent into Reform to destroy their Hard Right competitor from the inside he would look and sound very much like Robert “Honest Bob” Jenrick, a former EU champion and failed Immigration Minister as credible as a 19p coin.

News.title: 'Large' field fire next to M1 in Nottinghamshire halts traffic as people told to plan ahead
News.content:
'Large' field fire next to M1 in Nottinghamshire halts traffic as people told to plan ahead

Traffic is held on the M1 southbound between Hucknall and Nottingham as at least three fire engines and thick smoke can be seen

View 3 Images Traffic has been stopped on the M1 southbound (Image: HETC)

A large field fire has erupted next to one of the UK's busiest motorways, bringing traffic to a halt.

‌



The incident was reported around 6.45pm today, with the M1 in Nottinghamshire being closed southbound. The closure is located between junction 28 at Alfreton and junction 26 at Nottingham.

‌



Motorists have been told to plan ahead as thick smoke can be seen taking over the motorway, with at least three fire engines in attendance. A diversion route has been put in place.

‌



National Highways said: "The M1 in Nottinghamshire is closed southbound between J28 (Alfreton) and J26 (Nottingham) due to a fire in a field adjacent to the motorway. Nottinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service are working to extinguish the fire.

"National Highways Traffic Officers are providing assistance with traffic management on scene. If this closure impacts on your planned route, please allow extra journey time.

"Plan ahead, you may wish to re-route or even delay your journey." The agency described the blaze as "large" in a social media post.

‌



View 3 Images The smoke is blowing across the motorway (Image: HETC)

Diverted traffic is advised to follow the hollow square diversion symbol:

Exit the M1 southbound at J28

Join the A38 westbound and continue for just under 6 miles towards Ripley

At the A610 Hartshay Interchange at Ripley, turn left and take the A610

Continue south-easterly around Ripley, through Codnor and continue onward to then re-join the M1 at J26

‌



Traffic monitoring website Inrix added: "M1 Southbound blocked, stationary traffic due to serious fire and smoke blowing across the road from J28 A38 (Alfreton / Mansfield) to J26 A610 (Nottingham / Eastwood). Cameras show that there is a fire just off the motorway with smoke blowing across the road.

"Diversion - via the Hollow Square symbol via the A38 southbound into Ripley and along the A610 to Kimberley."

View 3 Images Dunwich Heath has completely burned down (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

Article continues below

The cause of the fire is not yet known. Multiple wildfires have started in recent weeks across the UK, including at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, Middlewick Ranges in Colchester and Cairngorms National Park in Scotland.

This comes amid extended periods of little precipitation, above-average temperatures and multiple heatwaves. Earlier this week, the Government announced half of England is now in drought.

The seven areas are East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire & the Isle of Wight, Devon & Cornwall, the West Midlands and Wessex. The whole of Wales is also in drought.

News.title: 'I patrol the Lake District — the way tourists behave every day disgusts me'
News.content:
'I patrol the Lake District — the way tourists behave every day disgusts me'

Millions visit the Lake District every year but those who help look after the national park in Cumbria say overtourism tensions are threatening to boil over

View 5 Images Local residents living in the Lake District National Park have complained about visitors' behaviour (Image: United Utilities)

Wild campers visiting the Lake District are ignoring the long-standing Countryside Code - with human excrement, fly-camping and irresponsible behaviour surging this summer, campaigners say.

‌



Those who manage the national park, which attracts millions of tourists every year, claim some guests are making life hell for locals. They say brainless parking, inconsiderate camping and mass littering is making a mockery of the "leave no trace" government guidelines to protect the environment. Paths blocked by campervans, discarded tampons and nappies and dogs let loose are just some of the other issues reported.

‌



Judith Derbyshire, a Westmorland and Furness councillor, has referenced a report made by patrol officers who are responsible for tackling anti-social behaviour. She says, as enforcement officers and volunteers battle to preserve the stunning national parks, problems are only increasing.

‌



Moment furious local sprays tourists' cars with muck near beauty spot Rydal Water READ MORE :

Drivers will add 41 minutes to a journey for better views, but lack ideas READ MORE :

View 5 Images Judith Derbyshire has called for more support for fed-up locals (Image: United Utilities)

Tourists risk huge fines in Lake District

She says the council has very few officers and a round-the-clock response service is a thing of the past. Local laws were tightened earlier this year in response to resident complaints.

Those causing environmental damage such as littering, starting fires, or the inappropriate use of motorhomes can now be fined up to £100 - but according to many locals, the rules are being flouted regularly.

‌



Ms Derbyshire, who is responsible for community safety, says since Covid there has been a huge increase in visitors with many arriving without plans for accommodation. That leads to "fly-camping" - taking spots away from designated camp sites.

5 View 5 Images Cars were sprayed with slurry after being illegally parked near Rydal Water (Image: Katy Parsons / SWNS) 5 View 5 Images An angry farmer took action with dozens of tourists' cars in the firing line (Image: Katy Parsons / SWNS)

‌



'You shouldn't be doing that'

Reading the report, she told the BBC: "Fifty-plus members of the public engaged with, 10 overnight campers spoken to, eight bags of rubbish collected and they had the joy of seeing one man using a bush as his toilet. I'm going to lower the standard of the conversation here but the issue is to do with human poo.

"Don't feel you can just come up, park up on a lay-by and then go and put a tent up down by the lake shore - you shouldn't be doing that.

"Putting it bluntly, we are going to have strong cutbacks from our funding as a local authority, we're not going to have the staff to be able to put that sort of thing in place."

‌



She says people can contact police if they see anyone behaving in a dangerous way - such as lighting a bonfire that could spread to a large area. Working together with residents and visitors is vital to getting the situation under control.

Ms Derbyshire added: "We want people to come to Lake District and it's good that there's a wider range of people coming here, it's just that we need to get them educated so they know what they can do and what they can't do."

View 5 Images Millions visit the Lake District every year, but not all of them abide by the Countryside Code (Image: Wasdale Action Group/A Wasdale Lad)

‌



'It really saddens me to see'

Earlier this summer, footage showed the moment dozens of cars were covered in slurry after they parked in a private field just yards away from Rydal Water, one of the country's prettiest beauty spots.

A large number of instances of littering, wildfires, and campers leaving equipment behind (known as fly camping) were logged in the Friends of the Lake District's annual survey.

One unhappy local wrote in this year's survey: "Some people have no social conscience and do not care about the impact of their behaviour on the environment or other people. We see litter on the fells, on lakesides and thrown out of cars onto grass verges. We even saw someone having a BBQ sat right next to a sign prohibiting it on Ullswater last year.

Article continues below

Another added: "I’m from the Lakes and have always appreciated the tourism and what it does for the area. However, I feel we have now got to the stage where tourism is over capacity and negatively impacting the area and the quality of life for residents and animals. Frequent traffic jams, poorly parked cars, and most upsetting of all, litter.

"Today we came across a discarded used nappy and a tampon. My children and I frequently go out with our litter pickers. It really saddens me to see the Lake District in environmental decline."

News.title: Man 'crushed' in horror accident as police probe death in industrial yard
News.content:
Man 'crushed' in horror accident as police probe death in industrial yard

Steven Dougall, of Falkirk, died in hospital after the industrial accident at the yard operated by his family's Horizon Reinforcing & Crane Hire Co. Ltd

View 2 Images Steven Dougall died in an industrial accident (Image: HANDOUT)

A 21-year-old man has died after allegedly being crushed while working at an industrial yard.

‌



Steven Dougall, of Falkirk, died in hospital after the incident on July 21 at the yard operated by Horizon Reinforcing & Crane Hire Co. Ltd - his family's business.

‌



Tributes have poured in for Steven who has been described as a "hardworking, kind-hearted young man" and a balloon release memorial has been held in Dollar Park.

‌



Police Scotland said the circumstances are not being treated as suspicious but it is investigating the incident along with the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).

View 2 Images Balloon's released in Stephen's memory (Image: HANDOUT)

A force spokeswoman said: “Around 9.55am on Tuesday, 21 July, 2026, we were called to a report of a man seriously injured at an industrial premises on Castle Drive in Falkirk.

‌



“Emergency services attended and a 21-year-old man was taken to Forth Valley Royal Hospital in Larbert by ambulance where he died a short time later. His family is aware.

“The death is not being treated as suspicious however enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances. The Health and Safety Executive has been made aware.” An HSE spokesman said: “We are aware and assisting Police Scotland with their enquiries.”

Over the last two weeks, tributes have flooded in for Steven with his family and the wider local community devastated by his sudden passing. Hundreds attended the release of balloons in his honour in Dollar Park last Tuesday, reported the Daily Record.

‌



An obituary posted online said: “The Falkirk community is mourning the heartbreaking loss of Steven Dougall, whose passing at the age of 21 has left his family, friends and loved ones devastated.

“Tributes shared in his memory reflect the profound impact he had on those around him and the deep sense of loss felt by everyone who knew him.

“Steven is being remembered as a hardworking, kind-hearted young man with ambitious goals and a bright future ahead of him… those closest to Steven remember him for his warm personality, infectious sense of humour, determination, and ability to create lasting memories with family and friends.”

Article continues below

It added his family has “requested privacy as they mourn their beloved son, grandson, cousin and friend”.

A keen amateur footballer, Steven’s life was also celebrated in a memorial match last week staged by Pantry FC, the local Monday league 6-a-side team he played for. The team posted: “Steven Dougall was the heart of Pantry and great friends with everyone involved, nobody was as competitive and infectious as him when it came to football in any form.

“The sudden loss of Steven has hurt everyone so deeply… We’d like to thank everyone who took part in this and especially all those who came to watch the game and support the boys in playing this match for Steven. It meant the world to those playing and to Steven’s family to see how many people turned out for him.”

News.title: Inside Britain’s cyber battlefield of the future as AI reshapes fighting
News.content:
Dawn had just broken over California’s Mojave desert but the heat was gathering and turning the distant mountains into a trembling blur.

Dust clung to boots, weapons and vehicles. The air smelled of diesel, scorched earth and hot metal. Then a British soldier stepped from a concealed position with a small controller in his hands.

Above him, almost invisible, an unmanned aircraft circled. On a screen below, enemy positions appeared as moving dots and live images. Coordinates were passed. Targets were confirmed. Seconds later, munitions fell behind hostile lines in ground too dangerous for any soldier to reach.

Sirens signalled a direct hit and casualties. Survivors dropped to their knees, tightening tourniquets around wounded comrades and carrying out emergency treatment in the dust.

‌



Before they had finished, driverless trucks and desert buggies were surging across the battlefield carrying water, ammunition, equipment and reinforcements.

No drivers. No pilots. No shouted orders carried down a trench.

View 6 Images A drone above the Mojave Desert, feeding live intelligence on enemy positions to troops below. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

The Mirror joined British and allied troops at the US Army’s National Training Centre at Fort Irwin to witness the wars to come – in which artificial intelligence will watch from above, sift intelligence, guide vehicles and determine where and when troops strike.

‌



The machines may not yet be in command, but they are becoming the eyes, ears and nervous system of the battlefield.

This was Project Convergence-Capstone 6 (PC-C6) involving the Five Eyes alliance of Britain, the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

In temperatures up to 49C, soldiers tested how they would fight an enemy armed with drones, cyber weapons, signal jammers and AI systems.

View 6 Images British soldiers take part in the vast Five Eyes exercise at Fort Irwin, testing how troops and artificial intelligence could fight side by side. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

‌



The familiar image of troops advancing behind tanks while commanders study paper maps is being overtaken by something faster, more connected and potentially more deadly.

A drone can spot a target beyond the horizon. AI can examine streams of video, intercepted signals and battlefield data in moments.

A commander can launch a strike before an enemy realises it has been found. The aim is to compress decisions that take hours into seconds.

Yet senior officers insist that the machines are not being allowed to choose who lives and dies.

‌



View 6 Images Colonel Jim Howard said AI would make soldiers faster, more effective and more lethal while keeping humans in control of battlefield decisions.

None of the gear being tested was fully autonomous, according to Colonel Jim Howard, commander of the British Army’s Experimentation and Trials Group. He told the Mirror: “You allow AI to do the science, and the human to do the art. You’re not looking at replacing people, you are augmenting and accelerating people, and giving them the tools to be faster and better, and more lethal.”

The machine finds patterns, processes data and points towards danger. The human makes the judgment and gives the order. But the balance is shifting.

A soldier may still pull the trigger, yet AI could increasingly determine what they see.

‌



Col. Howard said that if an enemy can be located and struck before British soldiers are exposed, fewer lives are placed in danger. But there is another threat.

Every drone, sensor, vehicle and communication system depends on software. An enemy that can hack or jam that network could blind an entire force, stop its vehicles or feed commanders false information.

A modern army could become almost powerless if their digital web is torn apart. British teams, therefore, attacked their own gear, trying to disrupt signals. Col. Howard said: “All capabilities went through electronic warfare attack and jamming, to see how resilient they are. Some are able to shrug it off – there’s some very clever tech.”

View 6 Images Vehicles race carrying supplies, equipment and reinforcements into areas considered too dangerous for human drivers. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

‌



At Fort Irwin, up to 60 pieces of gear were pushed through the dust and heat, including acoustic sensors, aerial drones and unmanned ground vehicles.

Col. Howard said: “There are technologies in that tent you could buy tomorrow. Others are more emergent and are going to require a bit more work,”

British troops were inserted into a US corps-level operation and required to connect their equipment with systems used by all five allied nations. Brigadier Karen Peek, the UK task force commander for PC-C6, said no country could face the emerging threat alone: “It is more complex than ever, and technology is evolving at a rapid rate. Making sure that we train as we would fight is really important.”

View 6 Images Mirror writer Jeremiah Hassel tries out the technology helping soldiers identify threats, process intelligence and direct operations on tomorrow’s battlefield. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

‌



Fighting an enemy they cannot see or hear, armies that cannot communicate or move quickly enough may be destroyed before they know what is happening.

Yet Brig. Peek said the most important achievement was not found inside any tech: “This exercise is about way more; it’s about people, and building that trust. The allies are learning, adapting, innovating, and we are much more ready now for future challenges.”

The soldiers remain at the centre of the fight. They still carry the weapons and make the final decisions. But all around them, largely unseen, AI is already beginning to dominate the battlefield.

News.title: One in 10 Brits haven't had a bath in over a decade as UK bathing habits shift
News.content:
One in 10 Brits haven't had a bath in over a decade as UK bathing habits shift

A new survey of 2,000 adults shows one in 10 Brits haven't taken a bath in more than a decade, with over half saying bathing has fallen out of fashion as shower vs bath preferences shift across the UK.

View 3 Images A fifth of people no longer have a bath in their home (Image: Getty Images)

One in 10 Brits haven't had a bath in over a decade, new research has revealed. A survey of 2,000 adults found 51% believe bathing has become outdated. Nearly half (48%) now favour a shower, while 18% of people don't even have a bath in their homes. Others (14%) made this change specifically to help cut their water usage.

‌



Recent studies, including the Shower Market Report , have recorded a rise in renovations being carried out to remove disused baths. A fifth of people have had a bath taken out of their homes in a bid to create a bigger shower space (43%), modernise their bathroom (42%), or convert to a walk-in shower (31%).

‌



View 3 Images Nearly half believe baths have gone out of fashion (Image: Getty Images)

‌



A spokesperson from leading smart Pay-As-You-Go energy supplier Utilita, which commissioned the research to support its award winning High5 tips series , including to keep showers to four minutes maximum, said: "Once a staple of the home, baths seem to have fallen out of favour for many across the UK.

"From homes getting smaller to costs getting higher, there are numerous reasons why this might be. But however you choose to clean and refresh, the most important thing is being conscious about your water usage, for the sake of both your pocket and the planet."

A fifth of those without a bath cite a lack of time to unwind, while 33% are too impatient for the time they take to run. Other reasons for the drop in popularity included not wanting to use excessive water for either cost-saving or environmental purposes, with 77% describing themselves as mindful of the amount of water they use.

‌



View 3 Images Three quarters are mindful of the amount of water they use (Image: Getty Images)

Nine in 10 (90%) take deliberate steps to cut their water consumption, such as only filling the kettle with the water they need (55%), collecting rain to water plants (29%), limiting hosepipe use (29%), and re-using grey water (13%).

More than a third (35%) have ditched baths for showers for precisely this reason. Three quarters (76%) also believe this makes a difference to lowering their water bills, with 77% saying the same about taking shorter showers.

‌



Three in 10 (32%) said knowing exactly how much money they could save or seeing real-time costs per minute (30%) would persuade them to cut down.

Utilita's spokesperson added: "Swapping baths for showers or reducing the time spent doing either can be a small, easy change that can have a lasting impact.

"It's great to see so many people are already doing this and have faith in the money they could save on their bills from this simple act.

Article continues below

"And no matter whether you prefer baths or showers, everyone can be a water-savvy person."

News.title: Burnham pledges to be 'relentless' in curbing small boat crossings
News.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged his government will be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

The prime minister said progress had been made and the government was "changing the whole approach", with enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs doubled on both sides of the Channel.

"People want to see this issue addressed," he said in Dover, adding: "We also need to build a system that offers safe routes for people as well, because that also takes away the selling point of the gangs."

The Conservatives said that Labour had not delivered on its promises on migration, while Reform UK said it would deploy the Royal Navy to ward off small boat crossing.

Political discussions around the UK's policies on illegal migration have resurfaced since tens of thousands of migrants swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday.

Burnham noted that 98% of the people who swam to the African territory had been returned to Morocco - which he said had dealt with the immediate issue.

But he added: "There's a broader issue about the Schengen area and our relationship with it, and of course, I would want to be in regular dialogue with the EU on those issues."

His comments came shortly after the Home Office announced that the number of National Crime Agency (NCA) officers tackling smuggling gangs facilitating small boat crossings had risen to almost 800 from 376 at the start of 2025.

Burnham said there had been a similar doubling of French officers.

Asked whether he wanted to change the tone of the debate around small boats, he said that he wanted to "deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue".

He added: "The public don't like the idea that the border looks like it's not controlled. We need to bring back that control. But also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it."

News.title: Man admits transporting Scottish woman's body in suitcase, Greek police say
News.content:
Greek police say a man has admitted transporting the body of a Scottish woman in a suitcase to an abandoned building.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, days after she was reported missing.

Local officers launched an investigation with cooperation from authorities in the US, the UK and Scotland, and now say they have arrested a 26-year-old man - the BBC understands he is from Afghanistan.

The force said he was brought to police headquarters on Thursday where he "confessed to his actions". He was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, robbery and weapons offences, but the exact charges have yet to be finalised under the Greek legal system.

News.title: Prolonged drought could cause shortage of some foods, farmers' union head says
News.content:
Bradshaw also suggested farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead.

"We have taken our food supply for granted for far too long," he added.

"Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well.

"It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products", Bradshaw told Radio 4's Broadcasting House.

In a message to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he said: "Let's draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK."

After a wet and mild start to the year, it has been exceptionally dry hot and dry with a succession of heatwaves across the UK.

The combination of low rainfall and prolonged heat has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers.

While droughts can occur naturally, climate change is making weather patterns more erratic, and heatwaves more frequent and intense.

Scientists say there is a greater risk of droughts happening as a result, and of them being more severe and longer-lasting when they do.

The Met Office reports that England saw just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it was 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

Heat health alerts are in place across most of England until at least 09:00 BST on Wednesday.

Amber alerts indicate a rise in deaths of vulnerable people and increased demand on health services are likely, while yellow alerts indicate these are possible.

News.title: Ariana Grande pulls out of musical for break from 'endless' scrutiny
News.content:
Ariana Grande is to withdraw from public appearances and will no longer star in an upcoming musical production in London when she ends her Eternal Sunshine tour.

A representative for the US singer, 33, told People magazine that she "will be taking a step back from visibility" when the tour ends next month after her appearances led to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny".

The company behind a revival of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George, due to play at the Barbican in 2027, confirmed that she would no longer be part of the production and had its "complete understanding and support".

Grande's physical appearance and health have been a topic of speculation in recent years.

This speculation has increased since the release of her latest album, Petal, two days ago and her appearance in promotional material for it.

Her representative stressed to People that Grande looked forward to finishing her tour "on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny".

They added: "She performs a very physical show, and there is a lot of athleticism involved. She performs healthily and successfully at a very high level night after night."

The Thank U, Next and 7 Rings singer was billed to appear alongside her Wicked co-star, British actor Jonathan Bailey, in the new production of Sondheim's critically acclaimed 1984 musical.

A representative for Empire Street Productions confirmed to the BBC that the musical would go ahead without Grande.

"Following this evening's announcement from Ariana Grande's team, we can confirm that she has decided to step back from Sunday in the Park with George," they said.

"We know this cannot have been an easy decision, and she makes it with our complete understanding and support. We wish her nothing but the best."

The BBC has approached Grande's representatives.

News.title: Massive Attack respond after Singapore ban over Palestine display
News.content:
Massive Attack have said they were "surprised and disappointed" by their treatment by Singaporean authorities after expressing pro-Palestine sentiments during a performance in the city-state.

The group wrote on Instagram on Sunday that its members were "detained by the police, isolated and separately questioned", with some subject to hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation.

The band's two members held up a Palestinian flag during its 29 July show there and shouted "free Palestine" alongside members of the audience.

Singapore, which has stringent rules on public speech and assembly, subsequently said it had indefinitely banned Massive Attack from returning to the country.

A police spokeswoman told the BBC on Friday that the two band members would not be allowed to re-enter Singapore and were barred from performing there.

Robert Del Naja and Grant Marshall were "given stern warnings" concerning alleged offences under two laws that restrict the public display of foreign flags and regulate political expressions at public events.

Massive Attack said that before the show and again at the end "large sections of the auditorium organically led chants of 'Free Palestine', presumably aware but undeterred that this spontaneous expression alone could violate their government's censorship laws".

The band did not address the ban directly, but described the situation as a "surreal experience" and said they "did not imagine that merely holding up the flag of a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries would violate any law".

They added that they were "proud to have made the impromptu expression" with fans in Singapore, who "clearly felt a moral imperative to show solidarity with the people of Palestine".

Massive Attack are known for openly expressing their political stance on a range of issues, including the war in Gaza.

Del Naja was arrested earlier this year on suspicion of showing support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action during a protest in London.

The 61-year-old sat among hundreds of fellow demonstrators with a sign that read "I Oppose Genocide, I Support Palestine Action".

Singapore has taken a strong stance on public statements on the Israel-Gaza war, with authorities in the multicultural country insisting this was necessary to preserve racial and social harmony.

The home affairs ministry put out a statement in 2023 advising against "the public display and wearing of articles" in relation to the Israel-Gaza war, including foreign national emblems.

Massive Attack are currently on a world tour, with performances next week in Australia following the end of its Asia leg.

The BBC has contacted the Singaporean police for comment.

News.title: Three in hospital after fire and crush at festival in London
News.content:
Three people were taken to hospital after a fire and crush at the entrance of a festival.

Organisers of Ghana Party in the Park, also known as Shattafest UK, at Copthall Playing Fields in Barnet, London, said the event was stopped following a "major incident" at about 18:00 BST on Saturday.

The Metropolitan Police said a fire had started near the gates, which meant they were closed temporarily.

A crowd built up, and there was a surge when the gates reopened, it said.

Organisers said the decision to end the festival was made on health and safety grounds.

They said in a statement the day had been "one of the most difficult" in the event's history and called what happened "deeply upsetting".

News.title: How ransom notes could help catch Nancy Guthrie's kidnapper
News.content:
On Friday, exactly six months after Nancy Guthrie was abducted, police released two ransom notes in the hope that they would help identify her kidnappers.

Guthrie, the mother of US news presenter Savannah Guthrie, was 84 when she went missing from her Arizona home in January.

Her disappearance sparked a months-long investigation which has turned up few apparent leads and fewer suspects.

So how could Nancy Guthrie's kidnapper, or kidnappers, be caught from these brief ransom notes?

The first of the notes, which are being treated as apparently credible, demanded millions of dollars in Bitcoin. The other claimed Guthrie died shortly after she was taken.

While the language in the notes might seem straightforward, police said the writer's "distinct linguistic characteristics" may be recognisable.

"There are a number of pieces of information in these notes that just might jar someone to say 'you know, I've heard that'," said Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos.

A forensic linguist told the BBC it's possible to glean crucial information about a person from just a few sentences.

"It's built upon the premise that we each carry an idiolect, or a word print, of our own that distinguishes our language from others," said William Eggington, a retired linguistics professor from Brigham Young University who is now a forensic consultant.

But, he said, investigators have to hold scientific scepticism when they analyse notes like this - especially when they have so few words to work with.

Furthermore, they have to account for the possibility that the person may be trying to disguise their natural writing voice.

News.title: Why I don't regret choosing a vasectomy in my 20s
News.content:
Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?

"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."

His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.

The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.

Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".

But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them.

"We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just toâ¦ make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision."

She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one.

The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.

Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.

News.title: Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche
News.content:
Prince William said he was "truly saddened to hear of the tragic death" of Purja, who he said "served with distinction" as a soldier before "becoming one of the greatest mountaineers".

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with.

"He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over."

Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme on Saturday that her organisation feared all members of the group were dead, and that Purja had led many expeditions she was on.

Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless".

Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit since Thursday's avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

News.title: Teenager dies after 'medical episode' at Kendal Calling festival in Cumbria
News.content:
A teenage girl died at the Kendal Calling festival in the early hours of the morning, police have said.

The 17-year-old suffered a medical episode at about 02:15 BST and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to Cumbria Police. The force asked people not to speculate about the circumstances of the incident.

It added officers were looking into the circumstances and wanted to speak to anyone who was in the area of the Calling Out tent and the Big Wheel around the time of the girl's death.

A spokesperson said: "Officers are particularly keen to speak with a group of women who alerted first responders to the girl after becoming concerned for her welfare."

They said the girl's family had been informed and were being supported by specialist officers.

The force asked people not to speculate, saying it could have a "significant impact" on the family and friends involved.

"We would ask that the investigation be allowed to take its course."

News.title: Ballot paper for Clacton by-election is longest in British electoral history
News.content:
The longest ballot paper in British political history is costing four times as much to print than regular ballot papers, the local council has said.

The list for the Clacton parliamentary by-election, which was prompted by the resignation of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, is 90cm (3ft) long.

When people unfold the paper, they will find it is longer than most adults' arms.

Tendring District Council chief executive Ian Davidson - who is the acting returning officer for the by-election in the Essex constituency - said organising the vote had been "manic".

People have already started returning postal votes to town hall and most registered voters will go to polling stations on 13 August.

Davidson said: "We've logistically been looking at the size of the ballot paper, how we fold it to get it into the envelope so we can send it out to our postal voters [and] how we manage the polling stations."

News.title: Four arrested over hate crime attack on ship crew
News.content:
Three men have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a Filipino crew member of a cargo ship was attacked in what police described as a hate crime.

Two other men, both also from the Philippines, were also assaulted during the attack involving a large group of people in Avonmouth, near Bristol, on Friday evening.

Police have arrested two men aged 19 and 45, as well as a 17-year-old boy, on suspicion of attempted murder and confirmed they had received reports of racist language being used during the incident.

They remain in custody, as well as a 38-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: Fires halt trains between London and Stansted Airport
News.content:
Trains between London and Stansted Airport have been stopped due to multiple trackside fires that have also affected some other routes.

Greater Anglia reported at 14:57 BST that a fire at Waltham Cross in Hertfordshire meant all trains had to be halted on one line. The London Fire Brigade (LFB) had requested this because the fires - including a large grass fire in Waltham Abbey - were close to the tracks, it said.

Rail services to and from Cambridge North, Meridian Water in Hertfordshire and Hertford East have also been affected.

Trains could be delayed, cancelled or diverted via Seven Sisters, a National Rail spokesperson said.

This included services to and from London Liverpool Street and Stratford.

National Rail said people needing to travel to Stansted Airport would have to take a train from London Kings Cross to Cambridge and then down to the airport, which they could do at no extra cost if they had already bought a ticket.

News.title: Gang of men hurl racist abuse at takeaway owner before violent attack
News.content:
A business owner has said that a group of men hurled racist abuse at him before punching him and smashing his head into a wall in the street in Falkirk.

Dr Zohaib Arshad said the group approached him on Grahams Road last month when he was visiting one of his takeaway shops and asked him when he was "leaving the country" before launching the unprovoked attack.

The 39-year-old, who practised as a vet in Pakistan, patched himself up with glue stitches rather than wait at A&E. He said his children are now fearful of being attacked in school.

BBC Scotland understands the police are treating the incident as a hate crime.

A spokesperson for the force said inquiries into the attack are ongoing.

Arshad stood as an Alba Party candidate for Falkirk at the 2024 General Election and is now a member of the SNP.

His political connections have resulted in the issue being brought to the attention of the Scottish Parliament, external - however he fears it would have gone unnoticed had he been any other member of the public.

News.title: Son of Wicker Man maker dies just weeks before his sequel to film premieres
News.content:
British filmmaker Justin Hardy, who directed a sequel to his late father Robin's 1973 cult horror classic The Wicker Man, has died aged 61.

His family said Hardy died on Friday night after suffering a heart attack, remembering him as "a man of family, of boundless creativity" and "so full of life right to the end".

A Bafta and Emmy nominated writer and director, Hardy was known for the documentary Children of the Wicker Man in 2024, made with his brother Dominic, which chronicled the legacy of their father's iconic film.

He had just completed production on Wrath of the Gods, the concluding chapter to the Wicker Man trilogy, which was due to premiere in London later this month.

Hardy also directed historical films and documentaries for the BBC, Channel 4 and CNN, including Princes In The Tower, Trafalgar Battle Surgeon, The Relief Of Belsen and Spanish Flu: The Forgotten Fallen.

His family said they were "devastated" by his death and "heartbroken" Hardy would not be able to see Wrath of the Gods open.

Dominic described his brother as having "an incredible appetite for life".

"We've lost him and we've lost that larger-than-life presence looking over us all," he said. "He really became a filmmaker his own right."

Dominic also praised Hardy's work on his last film as "incredibly beautiful", adding it was "a great satisfaction to him" to have made something new.

The Wicker Man, starring Edward Woodward and Christopher Lee, is the story of a police officer sent to a remote Scottish island community to investigate the disappearance of a local girl.

Wrath of the Gods was inspired by recently discovered scripts and storyboards by Hardy's late father Robin, marking the end of the trilogy that began with The Wicker Man and the 2011 follow-up The Wicker Tree.

Hardy, who also taught screenwriting at University College London, is survived by his wife Larissa, and their four children.

News.title: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row defends his work
News.content:
A Cambridge University professor has defended his academic work after finding himself at the centre of a plagiarism row.

The row erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Prof Jason Arday's work and questioned some of his stated achievements.

While some critics say the treatment of Arday, who is black, has been motivated by racism, others have said the claims of plagiarism were legitimate.

Arday admitted errors in his work, telling the Times, external in an interview on Saturday that he was accountable for those mistakes but that "what I am not is a liar".

He told the newspaper: "There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position."

He argued this was "racially motivated" and that he had become a "lightning rod" for criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information, and that similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the newspaper.

In 2023, the then 37-year-old sociologist became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge, telling the BBC at the time his work focused on neurodivergence and race in education.

He was diagnosed with autism and global development delay in his early years, to which his being unable to speak until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18 was attributed.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at Liverpool John Moores University and going on to teach at Roehampton, Durham and Glasgow.

News.title: Reform UK unveils plan for ‘largest military operation since WW2’ to stop small boats
News.content:

Reform UK has unveiled plans for what it describes as "the largest military operation in the English Channel since World War Two" to halt the arrival of small boats from France.

Under a government led by Nigel Farage, the party proposes deploying the Royal Navy to intercept all migrant vessels and return them to either France or Belgium, a strategy dubbed "Operation Fortress".

The party asserts that this ambitious plan aligns with international law, aiming not only to stop illegal crossings but also to serve as a humanitarian response. However, the Labour Party has dismissed the announcement as "reheated", arguing that "anger and easy answers won’t bring crossings down".

Zia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesman, articulated the party’s stark view, stating: "Britain is being invaded. Tory and Labour governments responded with a free ferry service and free hotels. Reform UK will respond by launching the largest military operation in the English Channel since World War Two."

He added: "Nigel Farage will order his Majesty’s Royal Navy to ensure that not a single unauthorised vessel crossing the English Channel makes it to the shores of the United Kingdom. Those who attempt it will be intercepted by our Armed Forces and returned to France."

Mr Yusuf claimed the move would render the border "impenetrable", ensuring "nobody" could reach UK shores via small boat.

To achieve this, Reform UK proposes establishing a joint military command, integrating units from the Royal Navy, Royal Marines, RAF, and British Army.

This would be complemented by a dedicated surveillance command to track incoming boats. The armed forces would be tasked with intercepting unauthorised vessels, detaining occupants, providing water, food, and medical assessments, before escorting them back on navy vessels.

The party also indicated it would pass emergency legislation "as necessary" to grant the joint command any additional required powers.

Reform UK cited the recent situation in the North African Spanish enclave of Ceuta, where approximately 60,000 migrants breached the border, as evidence of the "urgency" for its plan.

Most of those migrants had returned to Morocco by Sunday. The party framed its plan’s fundamental objective as humanitarian, claiming it would save lives in the Channel, where 162 people died between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage (Jordan Pettitt/PA) ( PA Wire )

A Labour Party spokesperson criticised Reform UK, stating: "Reform have reheated an old announcement in their latest desperate bid to distract from their growing sleaze scandals. Anger and easy answers won’t bring crossings down." The spokesperson added: "The serious action we’ve taken has started to have a real impact and has led to 46,000 attempted crossings stopped, and 70,000 people with no right to be here removed. We know there’s more to do on this complex issue."

The announcement comes as the English Channel recorded its busiest day for small boat crossings this year last Wednesday, with 752 migrants arriving in the UK. However, the overall number of arrivals for the year so far has seen a significant drop compared to previous periods. The provisional total stands at 14,526, marking a 43 per cent decrease from the 25,436 recorded by this time last year, and a 14 per cent reduction from the 16,903 during the same period in 2024.

In a separate development, Rupert Lowe, a former Reform UK MP who has since founded his own Restore party, extended an offer of collaboration to Mr Farage. In a video posted on X, Mr Lowe expressed willingness to set aside differences if Reform UK adopted some of Restore’s policies, including a ban on the burqa and Halal meat, and a referendum on the death penalty. He also stipulated that any future Cabinet under Mr Farage should exclude former Conservative ministers, such as Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

Mr Lowe stated: "I truly believe there could be sufficient common ground for our two movements to co-operate collectively (to) destroy the looming left-wing alliance that will finish off what hope remains for this country. We have recently shown how effectively co-operation can work locally on the Norfolk County Council, so why not at national level?" Mr Farage’s response on social media appeared lukewarm, suggesting there would "always be a home in Reform UK" for those rejecting the two main parties and seeking a "fundamentally different direction" for the country. He affirmed he was building a "broad coalition" but maintained that "only one party truly has the possibility of delivering change."

A suicide bomber has killed at least 14 people, including civilians and police officers, and wounded more than two dozen others, after targeting an anti-militant rally in northwestern Pakistan's Swat Valley on Sunday.

The attack took place in Kabal, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where demonstrators had gathered near a police station, chanting anti-militant slogans and demanding peace, according to district police chief Omar Khan.

Witnesses reported that speakers at the rally had stressed that ensuring security and eliminating militancy were the state’s responsibility. They also accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants, articulating residents' desire to live without fear after years of devastating violence in the region.

Bilal Faizi, a spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provincial emergency service, stated the attacker struck dozens of people chanting anti-militant slogans.

Police official Omar Khan specified that at least nine civilians and five officers were among the dead. Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the bombing, expressing deep sorrow and offering condolences to victims' families.

They also directed authorities to ensure the wounded received the best possible medical treatment, vowing Pakistan’s fight against terrorism would continue until eradicated. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also extended his condolences and prayers.

open image in gallery People carry a casket of a victim of suicide bombing, to transport after collecting from a hospital ( AP )

The Swat Valley, once a stronghold for Islamic militants who imposed a strict interpretation of Sharia law, were driven out by a major Pakistani military operation in 2007.

However, militants have resurfaced in recent months, fuelling fears that the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), are seeking to regain a foothold.

This resurgence has prompted residents to stage repeated anti-Taliban rallies protesting the militants’ presence.

While no group immediately claimed responsibility for the bombing, suspicion is likely to fall on the TTP. The group is distinct from, but allied with, Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers; many of its leaders and fighters have reportedly found sanctuary in Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan’s Taliban government of harbouring TTP militants, an allegation Kabul denies.

open image in gallery ( AP )

Pakistan has experienced a significant surge in militant attacks in recent years, with police and security forces frequently targeted. On Friday, Pakistan's military spokesman Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry revealed the country has recorded 3,145 "terrorism incidents" since January.

He stated 2,084 militants had been killed in the same period, while 819 Pakistanis, including soldiers, police officers, and civilians, had lost their lives.

Chaudhry further alleged Afghanistan-based militants had carried out 28 suicide attacks in Pakistan since January, claiming most were perpetrated by Afghan nationals or individuals associated with Afghanistan’s security forces. He asserted the TTP and other militant groups were conducting attacks inside Pakistan with the support of Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers, and affirmed Pakistan would continue to target the TTP and its support infrastructure. The attack underscores the volatile security situation and the ongoing struggle against militancy in the region.

Israeli airstrikes struck Gaza for a second consecutive day on Sunday, killing at least 18 Palestinians, medics reported. The renewed violence unfolded despite an announcement from U.S. President Donald Trump of a breakthrough in efforts to implement last year's ceasefire agreement.

From dawn, Israeli warplanes targeted Gaza City in the north, the central city of Deir al-Balah, and the southern area of Khan Younis, marking the highest daily death toll in weeks, according to Palestinian health officials.

President Trump's assertion on Thursday, claiming Palestinian Hamas militants and other armed groups had agreed to disarm, had previously raised hopes of a turning point in efforts to end the conflict.

On Sunday, Israel's Energy Minister Eli Cohen, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's security cabinet, stated the government would offer Hamas an opportunity to disarm, though he expressed "very sceptical" doubts about its likelihood.

Speaking to Israel's Army Radio, Mr Cohen asserted there was no agreement to cease attacks on Gaza, suggesting Israel, which already controls 70 per cent of the enclave, might need to assume full control if Hamas failed to disarm.

"In the deal we signed with the United States, our stance is that Hamas must be dismantled. This is the first thing that must happen," he added.

Later that day, a spokesperson for Mr Netanyahu's office informed Reuters that Israel had conveyed its concerns to the US regarding the disarmament plan.

"The most important concern for Israel is that nothing can happen before Hamas completely and truly disarms ...," said Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister's office.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

In Deir al-Balah, strikes claimed at least four lives, according to Palestinian health officials. A separate assault in Mawasi, near Khan Younis, wounded five and ignited several tents, the civil emergency service reported.

Palestinian officials also reported the deaths of a couple and their nine-year-old son in a strike on a Mawasi home.

In Gaza City, medics confirmed another couple and their child perished in an apartment strike, while two further individuals died in a tent near the Egyptian representative mission's office.

Later on Sunday, two more fatalities were reported in the city's eastern Zeitoun neighbourhood. Near Jabalia in northern Gaza, Palestinian officials confirmed one death.

The Israeli military stated that a strike on an apartment in Deir al-Balah had targeted two commanders of Hamas' elite "Nukhba" force.

Strikes in Gaza City and Jabalia also aimed at "military operatives", the military added, though it was still reviewing the situation. A subsequent Israeli airstrike on a car in Gaza City killed at least three Palestinians near Saraya Square, medics reported.

President Trump's 'Board of Peace', the US-led body overseeing the ceasefire, had on Friday published a 15-point roadmap detailing the final steps for implementing the agreement.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's lead envoy for Gaza, noted that the widespread strikes occurred despite efforts by the board and mediators to secure agreement among Palestinian factions on the roadmap for President Trump's plan.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

In a post on X, he affirmed he was collaborating with parties, mediators, and regional partners to "de-escalate and create the space for the full implementation of the President's plan". "Achieving a lasting peace is hard but achievable if everyone makes their best efforts," Mr Mladenov stated.

Since a ceasefire was agreed in October, at least 1,230 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes, according to Gaza health authorities. Hamas does not release figures on its combat fatalities. Over the same period, four Israeli soldiers have been killed, Israeli tallies indicate.

Hamas has maintained that Israel must cease its attacks in Gaza and withdraw its troops, in line with other key terms of the ceasefire deal, before it will agree to surrender weapons to a newly designated Palestinian body tasked with governing Gaza. A senior Hamas official stated on Sunday that the group had shown "considerable flexibility", yet accused Israel of attempting to impose a de facto situation on the ground through intensified strikes.

"This escalation, coinciding with progress on the political track, clearly demonstrates that the occupation government is seeking to undermine efforts aimed at ending the war and to impose facts on the ground by force," Basem Naim said in a statement.

Mohammed Dahlan, a former senior Fatah official based in the United Arab Emirates, claimed in a Facebook post that Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and a senior adviser involved in the US initiative, had informed him he was collaborating with the Israeli side to halt attacks on Gaza. Mr Dahlan added that contacts with the US were ongoing to ensure the agreement's full implementation, stressing that its success now hinged on Israel completely ending its daily attacks on Gaza.

Reuters has sought comment from the US State Department regarding Mr Dahlan's remarks, with no immediate response from Israel.

A Democratic senator and veteran once again took aim at the Trump administration over the Iran war on Sunday, claiming that the president’s chosen diplomats Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are not up to the task.

Sen. Mark Kelly was on CBS’s Face the Nation as he implored the president to put more experienced diplomatic representatives in charge and ditch his “real estate buddy” Witkoff, as well as his son-in-law.

Both men have helmed negotiations between the U.S. and Iran for months as the Trump administration has struggled to get out of a war it promised would only last for a few weeks.

"I would suggest to him, though, that the solution is not to do the same thing that he's been doing — not to have his real estate buddy and his son-in-law in charge of a negotiation,” said Kelly.

Instead, he said, Trump should “put some people in here that know how to do this, how to talk to the Iranians, and put a coalition together, bring our allies back together.”

open image in gallery Sen. Mark Kelly urged Donald Trump to ditch his two top negotiators on Sunday ( Getty )

Kelly endured a public spat with the Department of Defense and an attempt to change his rank by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth last year over his criticism of the agency, which a judge said was illegal and reversed.

But he’s been a chief critic of the administration’s foreign policy since the end of February, when Trump launched a war with Iran and vowed to dismantle Iran’s nuclear program. Kelly and others questioned the need, after strikes on Iranian targets last summer supposedly “obliterated” the targets, which were three Iranian nuclear development facilities.

open image in gallery Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have led Donald Trump’s negotiating team in talks with Iran ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery The burial of Iran's slain Supreme Leader attracted massive crowds earlier this month ( Reuters )

Now, with the nuclear program firmly in the background, the Trump administration has turned to attempting to find a way back to the status quo. The president spent weeks securing a deal announced in June, which re-opened the Strait of Hormuz to global shipping traffic but did little else in the short term. That deal, and the U.S.-Iran ceasefire, have since collapsed.

White House officials have been struggling to force Iran to re-open the strait or secure unrestricted safe passage for shipping traffic for months, to no avail.

In recent days the president has suggested that he has little interest in negotiation, and claimed that Iran frequently goes back on its word. What that means for the war, the Strait of Hormuz, and the global oil markets currently in turmoil due to all of the above, is still unclear. This past week, at a Cabinet meeting, he threatened to bomb another area of an Iranian nuclear site struck by the U.S. last year where satellite imagery has shown workers digging in an area called “Pickaxe Mountain”.

Gas prices in the United States are now well north of $4 a gallon on average, putting a major dent in the summer travel season for millions of Americans while also driving up costs on nearly every sector of the goods economy. Grocery prices remain high and Republicans have largely failed to make their case that the president and their party are laser-focused on affordability and bringing down consumer spending pressures, as Trump’s approval rating has sunk to some of its lowest recorded levels.

Democrats do not poll any better than Trump on the issue of Iran, though, as the party has been split in its response with some hawkish members including those tied to the party establishment cheering the initial strikes.

On Saturday, Trump was once again touting the prospect of another possible ceasefire deal on Truth Social, claiming that he’d called off a wave of U.S. strikes to allow negotiations to continue.

“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump seemingly urged all parties involved on Saturday.

Witkoff and Kushner were also tasked with bringing an end to the Ukraine-Russia war, something Trump repeatedly promised would be resolved on the first day of his second term, January 20, 2025. While they failed to make any significant progress before shifting their focus to Iran, it has been reported that they may visit Kyiv this month. It would be their first visit to Ukraine.
