World.title: Japan Lower House to install security cameras in Diet building
World.content:
The House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, will install security cameras in the Diet building starting in fiscal 2027.

The plan has been considered partly in response to an incident in which a government employee secretly filmed a woman in a Diet building restroom in 2021.

The planned move to expand camera coverage beyond the areas around the gates and fences raises concerns about increased surveillance, as negotiations between the ruling and opposition parties over the handling of important bills are often conducted behind closed doors in the Diet building.

In June, a Lower House Steering Committee panel unanimously approved the plan to install security cameras in the main part of the building and an annex as well as at the entrance to and in the corridors of another annex.

Waiting rooms allocated to each Diet group will not be monitored. The number of security cameras and the necessary costs will be determined later. When the matter was considered in 2015, the total cost was estimated at ¥180 million for 66 cameras.

In the Parliament building, lawmakers and government officials often become active during plenary sessions and budget committee meetings, or when tensions between the ruling and opposition parties escalate. However, outside of these times, it is not uncommon for the premises to be quiet even while the Diet is in session.

Meanwhile, when the ruling and opposition parties need to revise bills or discuss deliberation schedules, related lawmakers sometimes engage in private talks in the Parliament building.

A veteran member of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, who is well-versed in Diet affairs, expressed concern that lawmakers and others “would not be able to move discreetly.”

At the panel meeting in June, Yasuhiro Nakagawa, acting Diet affairs chief of the opposition Centrist Reform Alliance, emphasized the importance of “guaranteeing freedom of political activities.”

There has been no movement in the House of Councilors, the upper chamber, regarding the installation of security cameras.

World.title: Etc.books: A lone bookstore in Tokyo pushes against sexism
World.content:
Editor Akiko Matsuo remembers the first time she organized a protest. It was 2018, after Tokyo Medical University was found to have manipulated entrance exam scores to reduce the number of women admitted.

“That’s when I realized that when you raise your voice, people hear you,” Matsuo says while sitting in the book-filled office space at Etc.books, the feminist publishing house she founded that same year and whose bookstore has since become a gathering place for readers and activists.

Named for those who appear as “etc.” or footnotes in society, Etc.books (stylized in all lowercase) expanded into a bookshop in Tokyo’s Shindaita neighborhood in 2021. Today, its shelves hold some 3,000 titles, from children’s picture books and cookbooks to philosophy. Most are in Japanese, though English, Korean and other languages are represented. Despite their varied genres, each reflects the store’s commitment to feminist values.

World.title: 1 in 4 people in Japan believes AI could replace friends and family: poll
World.content:
One in four people in Japan believes that more advanced artificial intelligence will replace their friends and families in the future, a Jiji survey on communications has found.

The proportion of those who expressed this belief stood at 24.9%, while 65.1% said they did not think AI would replace their friends and families.

Of the respondents aged between 18 and 29, 32.5% said that advanced AI would replace their friends and families in the future. The proportion stood at 30.1% among respondents in their 30s, 29.2% among those in their 40s and 31.4% among those in their 50s.

In the survey, 30.8% of the overall respondents said they use generative AI, such as ChatGPT, while 67.8% said they do not.

The usage rate came to 53.3% among those aged between 18 and 29, 56.2% among those in their 30s, 47.4% among those in their 40s, 27.4% among those in their 50s and 21.9% among those in their 60s.

Asked what they use generative AI for, with multiple answers allowed, 64.7%, the largest group, said they use it for work, followed by 35.3% who cited cleaning, cooking and other household chores and 27.1% who said they use it to ask questions about current affairs. Also, 21.7% said they chat with AI about their favorite music, characters and celebrities, and 12.8% said that they use AI to express worries and complaints about love and work.

The interview-based survey was conducted on 2,000 people age 18 or older nationwide for four days from June 12. Valid responses were given by 57.1%.

World.title: This children’s cafeteria in Shikoku serves up free meals and global perspectives
World.content:
From a kitchen high in an office building in Matsuyama, Ehime Prefecture, a team of cooks races to prepare a meal ahead of another busy Saturday dinner service.

Some stir stews and soups simmering in large pots on the stove, others cut and season chicken in large steel bowls, and even more slice and dice onions, potatoes and garlic.

Preparations begin around noon and stretch into the evening. As the clock approaches 5 p.m., guests begin to trickle in.

World.title: Extra budget may be compiled for Kumamoto quake
World.content:
Some officials of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s administration have floated the idea of compiling a second supplementary budget for fiscal 2026 in response to extensive damage caused by a massive earthquake that hit Kumamoto Prefecture Tuesday last week.

The focus is on the decision of the prime minister, who prioritizes the regular budget and calls for an end to the government’s reliance on supplementary budgets.

With the funding source for the planned consumption tax cut on food from next April still unclear, moving forward with additional fiscal spending could undermine market confidence, analysts said.

World.title: Europe’s key rivers are drying up as extreme heat impact widens
World.content:
Europe’s biggest rivers, vital arteries for the region’s heavy industries, are drying up after the region was seared by a series of heat waves.

As water levels in the Rhine and Danube fall toward record lows, that’s starting to disrupt the transport of chemicals, oil products and other goods, while boosting freight costs. Soaring temperatures are also curbing power generation at riverside reactors from France to Hungary, pushing up energy prices and straining Eastern European economies.

Following the wildfires that ravaged France and Spain, it’s another sign of how climate change is taking its toll on the fastest-warming continent. The river disruptions are becoming a test of how quickly the region can adapt infrastructure built around 20th-century conditions to a climate where extreme low water is likely to be increasingly common.

World.title: Shigure may look a bit unusual, but he’s a very special cat
World.content:
Don’t allow this fellow’s somewhat unusual appearance to put you off. This is Shigure and he’s a very special cat.

About 2 years old, Shigure is new to ARK. After the death of his owner, he arrived with two other cats, Kosame and Ajisai, the latter is believed to be his sibling.

All three are visually impaired, but that doesn’t stop any of them from enjoying life.

Shigure is the adventurer. He’s fearless but also extremely funny and friendly. Despite his poor vision, Shigure loves playing with his toys. In fact, anything moving is likely to be treated as a toy and he’ll pounce on it straight away, including food.

His fondness for play has been a large factor in helping him achieve his impressive weight of over 5 kilograms!

We’re hoping he’ll catch the eye of someone who will see past his slightly unusual appearance and want to care for a bold, brave boy brimming with confidence and curiosity.

World.title: Hong Kong, CSRC deepen financial ties ahead of first yuan bond futures launch
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has met the head of mainland China’s securities regulator to discuss deepening links between the two financial markets ahead of the launch of the city’s first yuan-denominated bond futures.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Sunday evening that he met China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) chairman Wu Qing at Government House in Central to exchange views on deepening mutual access between the financial markets in Hong Kong and the mainland.

The high-level meeting with the CSRC delegation took place ahead of the debut on Monday of China’s first yuan-denominated five-year bond futures on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Lee said the launch of the first of its kind of product in the city would provide an “effective” offshore risk management tool and help attract international investors to the mainland bond market and to hold Chinese treasury bonds on a long-term basis.

“This is a key step in enhancing the RMB [renminbi] product ecosystem, and further consolidates Hong Kong’s status as the world’s offshore RMB business hub,” he said.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, the Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, Joseph Chan Ho-lim, the chairman of Securities and Futures Commission of Hong Kong, Kelvin Wong Tin-yau, and SFC CEO Julia Leung Fung-yee were present at the meeting.

World.title: Jardine Foundation to end scholarships for Oxford, Cambridge undergrads
World.content:
An educational trust established by Hong Kong-based conglomerate Jardine Matheson will end its prestigious undergraduate scholarship programme for Oxford and Cambridge universities after a strategic review, redirecting the funds to institutions in Asia.

According to the Jardine Foundation’s website, students starting their studies later this year will be the final cohort of undergraduate “Oxbridge” scholars to be covered by the programme.

The move marks the end of an undergraduate scholarship programme that has lasted for 44 years.

“The Jardine Foundation remains committed to providing access to higher education by talented students across the Asian communities in which Jardines operates,” it said.

“Following a strategic review, the foundation will be increasing its focus and investment in Asia, expanding opportunities for local students to study at leading universities in the region.”

The foundation added that it would continue to support the current Jardine scholars at the two universities and the 2026 awardees, as well as its existing Oxford and Cambridge postgraduate scholarship programmes.

World.title: Spend HK$10,000 a month on your pets? Why not, say cat lovers at Hong Kong expo
World.content:
With 14 cats and a dog at home, Hong Kong couple Mr and Mrs Cheung spend more than HK$10,000 (US$1,275) a month on their beloved pets.

“Pets are meant to be spoiled rotten,” said Mrs Cheung, a pet groomer in her thirties who visited the cat expo in Wan Chai on Sunday with her husband and four Maine Coon cats. The cats were dressed up and carried in a HK$4,000 stroller made in Japan.

She said the four cats enjoyed going out, but were “a bit emotional today” because of the attention they received from eventgoers.

Halfway through their visit, the couple had already spent about HK$2,000 on cat food and snacks from Hong Kong and Taiwan brands.

“We do not have a budget in mind; we will buy anything that is right for us,” Mr Cheung said.

He said they used to buy cat food from Taiwan and ship it to Hong Kong because of the premium quality, so they were happy to see more Taiwanese brands at this year’s event.

World.title: Rains fail to deter Chiikawa fans and big spenders after roundabout cancellation
World.content:
The return of an exhibition featuring popular Japanese manga series Chiikawa to Hong Kong drew crowds and big spenders on a rainy Sunday afternoon, even though the organiser cancelled a much-anticipated roundabout for safety reasons.

While some fans expressed disappointment over the halted rides at the K11 Musea promenade on the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront, others welcomed the alternative arrangement, which allowed them to take photos with several characters on the stationary roundabout.

Some spent thousands of Hong Kong dollars on merchandise.

“It is a bit disappointing, as my son was looking forward to hopping on the roundabout,” said Joey Chan, a corporate secretary in her thirties. She was visiting with her son and her husband, who is also a corporate secretary.

The show, Chiikawa Artiverse, organised by local design studio AllRightsReserved, is in its second year and will run until September 6.

A premium exhibition ticket, which includes the roundabout experience, costs HK$590 (US$75), while a general ticket costs HK$200, with fewer freebies.

World.title: How retirees can win against rising healthcare cost in Hong Kong
World.content:
Retiree Philip Kong says he realised Hong Kong’s healthcare system needed a wake-up call when he discovered that receiving treatment for his prostate condition in neighbouring Shenzhen could potentially cut his medical bill by nearly 90 per cent.

The 75-year-old was diagnosed with an enlarged prostate earlier this year and set to pay HK$210,000 (US$26,780) for a scheduled surgery at Hong Kong Sanatorium and Hospital – until a family friend, who is a urologist, suggested another option.

The alternative? The University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen Hospital – a 2,000-bed clinical, teaching and research facility in Futian that opened in 2012 – offered a full examination, including blood and urine tests, for about HK$300 and an extra HK$20,000 for the standard inpatient procedure.

In the end, Kong opted not to go for the larger discount and paid for the “deluxe” HK$60,000 package. It included a private room with a sea view and meant the operation was performed by three “professor-grade” specialists.

“It is a fraction of the cost, and treats you like a king,” Kong said after making an initial trip to the hospital to explore his options.

Philip Kong was diagnosed with an enlarged prostate earlier this year and was set to pay HK$210,000 for surgery at the Hong Kong Sanatorium and Hospital. Photo: Jonathan Wong

While Kong, who has lived and worked in Hong Kong as a businessman all his life, is enrolled in the Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme, the episode has still left him shaken.

World.title: Mainland transit gives Hongkongers option for Europe trips amid Middle East war
World.content:
Transiting through mainland China for long-haul destinations from Hong Kong has become an alternative to stopping off in the Middle East amid safety concerns brought about by the US-Israel war on Iran, the city’s travel agents have said.

Alex Lee Chun-ting, general manager of Miramar Travel, told the South China Morning Post that the war in the Middle East had initially reduced interest in long-haul tours to Europe in summer, but he now expected a 3 per cent increase year on year.

Lee said safety concerns over flying through the Middle East and pricier airfares had made residents hesitant to travel, with many forgoing routes via the Gulf region and opting for direct long-haul flights, pushing up demand and prices.

“[Some mainland airlines] noticed this trend, too, and offered us group discounts for tours departing from Hong Kong, with stopovers in Shanghai or Beijing before heading to Europe,” Lee said, adding that this had absorbed some of the demand for Middle Eastern airlines.

Lee acknowledged that the alternative mainland route was unexpected and had emerged because of the war, as Hong Kong travellers increasingly became open to services from across the border due to improvements in airlines and airports.

For those headed to London – one of the most popular destinations for Hongkongers – Lee observed that economy flights transiting through the mainland were on average HK$1,000 to HK$2,000 (US$127 to US$255) cheaper than direct services from Hong Kong for the peak summer travel season, exclusive of fuel surcharges and taxes.

Carmen Chan Hiu-nam, Goldjoy Holidays’ chief operating officer, said about 50 per cent of its European tour customers opted to press on with their trips transiting via the mainland in March and April – a figure she considered low.

World.title: Kowloon Walled City action film sequel’s gritty, nostalgic set draws residents
World.content:
Tucked in a corner of a hi-tech industrial estate in Yuen Long, a cluster of cluttered flats has been designed to evoke a gritty Hong Kong slum. It is the main set for the sequel to the nostalgic blockbuster film Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.

The set, constructed on an empty factory site at Yuen Long InnoPark, recreates the iconic Kowloon Walled City, featuring details such as a banner hanging outside the building that reads: “Pleading to give our home a way to survive”.

Set in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the sequel, Twilight of the Warriors: The Final Chapter, captures the era leading up to the demolition of the historic enclave. The film is directed by Soi Cheang and stars returning actors Raymond Lam Fung, Terrance Lau Chun-him, Louis Koo Tin-lok and German Cheung Man-kit, alongside new addition Daniel Wu.

The original film, released in 2024, was a revenge drama that centred on brotherhood among the triad gangs that ruled the crime-ridden estate during the 1980s.

The sprawling and detailed film set for Twilight of the Warriors: The Final Chapter. Photo: Dickson Lee

Ben Kock, who works in the industrial area and frequently jogs past the site during his lunch breaks, has had a front-row seat to its transformation, though he did not initially realise it was the set for the film sequel.

World.title: Rosewood Hotel Group to press on with clubhouse takeover as opposition escalates
World.content:
Rosewood Hotel Group in Hong Kong will press ahead with a controversial plan to change the operator at a clubhouse in Central on August 8, despite escalating opposition from a group of members, the South China Morning Post has learned.

Sources said the hotelier’s Carlyle & Co private club would take over the operation of the Town Club in Central from the Hong Kong Golf & Tennis Academy (HKGTA) as planned.

However, a group of HKGTA patrons is still pursuing ways to oppose the takeover, including writing to the Legislative Council Secretariat after filing complaints with the Consumer Council and the Customs and Excise Department under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance.

“The transitional changes will proceed as planned on 8 August,” an insider familiar with the situation said.

Rosewood had delayed the change of operator by two months from June.

In what Rosewood called a rebranding of the Town Club, the planned takeover of operations emerged several months ago and angered a group of HKGTA members especially those with perpetual memberships.

They had paid as much as HK$2.68 million (US$342,086) for a perpetual membership and said they had learned through news reports that Carlyle & Co would take over the operation of the Town Club in early June.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018842/Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.title: Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018842/Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.content:
In an eastern Chinese village, harvesting cicada nymphs for consumption has evolved from a seasonal tradition into a lucrative side business for farmers, fueled by a local official’s livestreaming business. But critics are questioning whether the trade is flourishing at the expense of local ecosystems.

This summer, Liu Lei, a village official of Dongjiezhuang Village in the eastern Shandong province, began selling wild cicada nymphs through livestreaming, sourcing the insects from locals. In the past week, he has come under fire online, with social media users citing environmental concerns.

Known in Chinese as zhiliaohou, or “cicada monkeys,” nymphs — immature, wingless cicadas who emerge after three to five years feeding on plant matter underground — have long been considered a summer delicacy in northern and eastern China. Historical texts, including the sixth-century agricultural encyclopedia “Qimin Yaoshu,” describe consumption of the insects in the region.

Liu, one of a growing number of village official influencers, markets local specialties and agricultural products such as honey and peaches on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, to boost the local economy.

Liu’s videos show villagers — largely seniors — going out each night at dusk, armed with flashlights and plastic bags, to search for the insects in the nearby forest. They then sell their collections to Liu at a designated point in the village for extra income. Each cicada sells for around 1 yuan ($0.14).

One 60-year-old local said he had caught more than 200 cicada nymphs in a single night. “I usually don’t eat them myself. One cicada nymph is priced higher than an ear of corn,” he said.

Liu’s actions have triggered debate online. While some support him for bringing in income for farmers, others argue that livestreaming has transformed a long-standing tradition into a commercial rush. Experts also warn that large-scale collection could threaten biodiversity and disrupt local food chains.

In an interview with local media, Liu said villagers have harvested cicada nymphs for decades without damaging the environment. “We have a tradition of only collecting nymphs that have just emerged from the soil,” he said. “Once they’ve molted into adult cicadas, no one catches them because they are no longer edible.”

Although Cryptotympana atrata, the preferred cicada species being collected, is not nationally protected, entomologists warn that large-scale population decimation could still affect local ecosystems.

Zhao Li, curator of the Insect Museum of West China in Chengdu, capital of the southwestern Sichuan province, told local media that cicadas help recycle nutrients in forests and provide food for birds and other wildlife. Their shed exoskeletons, Zhao added, are also widely used in traditional Chinese medicine.

Authorities have attempted to curb the collection of cicadas in some regions. In 2024, forestry officials in Tongchuan, a city in the northwestern Shaanxi province, warned against unauthorized harvesting of cicadas in forests and protected areas, stating that large-scale collection could damage vegetation, increase wildfire risks, and violate forestry regulations.

Specifically addressing the Dongjiezhuang Village case in a video posted to Douyin, Li Mingli, chairman of agricultural brand consulting firm Beijing Fangyuan, noted that, “Livestream traffic can amplify demand far beyond what unwritten local customs can regulate.”

Li suggested that instead of harvesting wild cicadas, the village could build a cicada farm, providing locals with a more stable source of income while reducing pressure on wild populations. He added that local authorities could also introduce collection quotas and rotate harvesting areas.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018839/China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.title: China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018839/China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.content:
ZHEJIANG, East China — Wang Hui, a 68-year-old from Beijing, used to avoid intense exercise whenever possible. The retiree’s fitness regime mostly consisted of the odd brisk walk, and maybe a few leg raises at home.

But that suddenly changed a few months ago, when her daughter informed her she’d signed Wang up for a Hyrox race.

The fitness craze, which originated in Germany a few years ago, is not for the faint of heart: participants must complete eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by a set of strength exercises ranging from lunges to pushing a heavy sled.

Curious and keen to connect with her daughter — a long-time fitness enthusiast — Wang threw herself into training, building up from 1-kilometer jogs to 8-kilometer runs in just two months.

Then, one day in July, Wang found herself walking alongside her daughter into a cavernous expo center in the eastern city of Hangzhou packed with more than 6,000 competitors and 7,000 cheering spectators.

As she stood under the pulsing strobe lights, ears throbbing from the pumping bass, Wang could not have felt more out of her comfort zone. But she suspects that was her daughter’s intention all along.

“My daughter keeps surprising me,” she told Sixth Tone after completing the event in July. “She shows me, ‘I can still do this,’ ‘I can still do that.’”

Wang is far from alone. As Hyrox explodes in popularity across China, the races have unexpectedly begun to attract an ever greater number of retirees — many of them competing in their first event well after turning 70.

For some, the races represent a fresh challenge or an excuse to get fit. For others, like Wang, they offer a chance to reconnect with adult children for whom Hyrox has become a new obsession.

Even by global standards, Hyrox has taken off in China at astonishing speed. The first official Chinese Hyrox race took place as recently as 2024, with 1,700 fitness enthusiasts competing in a hall in Beijing.

Now, events are held all over the country, with early-bird registration often selling out within minutes despite costing up to 800 yuan ($125) for an individual entry fee — more than three times the entry fee for a typical marathon in China. At a recent race in Shanghai, over 10,000 people took part.

As elsewhere, Hyrox fans in China tend to be young, middle-class, and super-fit. Local races are filled with ripped 20- and 30-somethings working in competitive industries such as finance and artificial intelligence.

On Chinese social media, Hyrox’s appeal to such high-fliers has become a running joke. Users often quip that the sport taps into a deep Chinese love for hard work and standardized tests. Some even liken Hyrox training to preparing for the gaokao, China’s grueling college entrance exams.

But the sport also has a more inclusive side. At some events, participants can sign up in teams of two or more — allowing them to divide the workload — and the lack of cut-off time means slower competitors can complete the race.

That has opened the door to a growing number of elderly contenders. Online, there has been a wave of social media posts in recent months from Chinese millennials sharing their experiences of entering Hyrox races alongside their aging parents, many of them attracting thousands of likes.

Wang’s daughter, Xie Shanshan, is part of that trend. Now in her 40s, she took up running years ago while living and working in Beijing — competing in several half-marathons — before pivoting to Hyrox as the sport began to gain traction.

For Xie, the hope was that competing in the team event with her mother would give them a shared experience. But she also aimed to give Wang — who has been retired for years — a healthy jolt.

And she appears to have succeeded. After the initial shock wore off, Wang fully committed to the training and finished the Hangzhou race, with Xie reminding her to pace herself.

“We didn’t go at 100% effort,” Wang said. “My daughter kept saying, ‘Steady, steady, it’s about the taking part, not speed.’”

When asked whether it’s a good idea for seniors to participate in such high-intensity sports, Wang said it was easy to fall into a rut after retirement, spending all day scrolling social media or watching TV.

“But if you can step out and join social activities with younger people, your thinking and values get reenergized,” she said. “The real appeal lies in connecting with the younger generation, adding vitality to life, and broadening horizons.”

Other child-parent teams competing in Hangzhou shared similar experiences. Yu Lian, a 45-year-old CrossFit enthusiast, had been training for nearly a decade and had already run solo in two Hyrox races.

But after seeing online that some of her favorite fitness influencers had brought their parents along to Hyrox events, she decided to ask her 74-year-old father to join her at her next race.

According to Yu, he immediately replied: “Just tell me what to do, and I’ll do it. I walk so much every day. I’m already the number one in our neighborhood!”

Though Yu had emphasized “safety first,” her father took the training unexpectedly seriously. For nearly two months, he took brisk walks outside several times a week, and ended up losing 5 kilograms.

On race day, it was a similar story. Yu’s plan was to do all the strength exercises herself, while her father walked alongside her. But he ended up getting far more involved than she had expected.

After each kilometer run, she found him already waiting for her at the work station, arm outstretched, ready to pull her forward. In the final event — the “wall ball,” where competitors have to throw a heavy medicine ball against a wall — her father, fueled by the crowd’s energy, grabbed a ball and nailed the target on the second attempt.

For Yu, the race came to feel like an important bonding experience. Growing up, her relationship with her father had always been reserved — love was expressed through deeds, not words, she recalled.

The term “parent-child bonding” usually conjures up images of young families with small children, but Yu said she felt that older generations — those in their 40s and 70s — needed it just as much.

“Interactions between adult children and aging parents are often limited,” Yu said. “Participation in the race is a meaningful way to foster various types of connection.”

Yet, for all its emotional benefits, Hyrox can be a dangerous activity — especially for a beginner in their 60s or 70s. Li Cong, a functional training, pilates, and sports rehabilitation instructor in Shanghai, warned the sport presented a high injury risk.

“After running, the small stabilizing muscles around our joints fatigue,” she said. “When we then do weighted sled pushes or kettlebell exercises, the lower back and knees are forced to compensate and bear all the weight. When your form breaks down under fatigue, the injury rate is much higher than if you trained running and strength separately.”

Sun Yang, a senior rehabilitation therapist in the sports medicine department at Shanghai’s Huashan Hospital, echoed those concerns. A Hyrox devotee herself, she approaches training with caution.

“I stop and rest for a few days if I feel any discomfort,” Sun said. “I don’t allow myself to continue exercising while overtired or in pain.”

Wang Zheng — no relation to Wang Hui — thought long and hard before inviting his mother to form a Hyrox team with him.

As a 32-year-old fitness professional, Wang Zheng had already competed in 22 Hyrox events, and he was keen to bring his mother, Ma Jing, into his world. But he also knew that the traditional, hardcore format wasn’t a fit for everyone.

Luckily, the mixed-doubles category offered a solution. “In mixed doubles, I can take on 90% of the workload, and there is no cut-off time at the venue. That meant I could finally bring my mom along to play,” he said.

Ma, a 65-year-old retiree living in eastern China’s Shandong province, was initially apprehensive when her son suggested entering a race together. “I was actually a bit scared, afraid of embarrassing him,” she recalled.

But her fear soon gave way to a deeper motivation. “I don’t want to be a burden to my son as I get older, and the first step is to stay healthy,” Ma said. “So I thought, let me challenge myself.”

The training ended up having a profound impact on Ma. She moved in with her son in the southern city of Shenzhen months before the race so that they could prepare together, and watching his tough routine gave her a new understanding of his commitment.

His dedication also inspired Ma to take her own training seriously. In November, the pair completed the race in Shanghai in 100 minutes, with Ma’s performance surpassing her son’s expectations. The atmosphere even motivated her to take on several exercises that she had never tried before.

Now, flush with her triumph, she has decided to push on with her training. She runs 5 to 10 kilometers a day, hits the gym for strength training 20 days a month, and is lining up her next races.

“Since I’ve decided to compete, I have to show up in my best form,” she said.

More importantly, Ma said Hyrox had helped shatter her self-doubt. “I used to think I wasn’t ready, but actually, we don’t need to prepare for everything. Just participating is a reward in itself.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran.

(Header image: Elderly participants in Hyrox races. Xie Anran/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829/The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.title: The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829/The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.content:
This is the second article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED). Read Part 1.

China is the origin of tea, and its global vocabulary remains deeply rooted in Chinese. The English word “tea” derives from the Minnan (Hokkien) dialect, reflecting maritime trade routes that carried the leaf from the coastal ports of China’s eastern Fujian province to Europe. Meanwhile, “char” (or “cha”), originating from Mandarin or Cantonese, persists in British slang as a colloquial term for a cup of tea. More recently, the Indian-derived “chai” — a popular blend of black tea, milk, sugar or honey, and spices — has gained traction in Western coffee shops. Yet the foundational lexicon of tea in English remains unmistakably Chinese.

While China produces a wide array of premium teas, English dictionaries have historically been highly selective in what they adopt. Among the commonly accepted lists of China’s most celebrated teas, only Wuyi rock tea (Bohea) and Keemun black tea (Keemun) traditionally made the cut, both transliterated from regional names. However, a closer reading of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) reveals a more expansive linguistic landscape: nearly 30 Chinese tea terms have been formally incorporated into English. Some are widely used, while others survive as lexical relics. This lexicon includes foundational terms such as green tea, white tea, oolong, and congou; premium black teas like pekoe, souchong, and Lapsang souchong; historic green teas including Hyson and Singlo; post-fermented varieties such as Pu-erh; and descriptive terms such as pearl tea (gunpowder tea) and imperial tea.

Within this OED-derived lexicon of Chinese tea terms in English, one striking anomaly stands out: the theatrical caricature of “Widow Twankey.” The linguistic transformation began in Tunxi, a historic tea hub in the eastern Anhui province. The city’s name was phonetically adapted into “Twankay” to denote large quantities of green tea exported from the region during the 18th century. As this tea became associated with lower grades in Western markets because of its older, coarser, and more ragged leaves, “Twankay” was later repurposed by playwrights into the comedic character “Widow Twankey,” and eventually entered British slang as a term for cheap gin.

In 1861, playwright H.J. Byron named Aladdin’s mother “Widow Twankey” to imply she was “past her best.” The character went on to become a pantomime staple — a bawdy, eccentric “dame” traditionally played by a man in drag, often depicted running a chaotic Chinese laundry in a fictionalized “Old Peking.”

For modern readers, the fact that a Chinese tea term was transformed into a theatrical punchline can come as a shock. Yet placed within the broader OED record, Twankey remains a clear exception. The vast majority of Chinese tea terms in English have been treated with linguistic and cultural respect.

Take Bohea (Wuyi tea), for instance. As one of the earliest black teas imported into Britain in the early 1700s, OED citations show it was initially regarded as a luxury product. Although its commercial standing later declined — by the mid-19th century it was classified among lower-grade black teas — its literary presence remained stable. From Alexander Pope to William Makepeace Thackeray, Bohea continued to appear in print as an authentic beverage.

Similarly, congou (gongfu tea) was established as a marker of upper-class refinement. In Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s 1777 comedic play “The School for Scandal,” congou appears alongside exotic luxuries such as avadavats (tropical songbirds) and Indian crackers. Victorian dietary writers later formalized this hierarchy. In his 1874 “A Treatise on Food and Dietetics,” F.W. Pavy explicitly ranked major black teas in ascending order of quality: Bohea, oolong, congou, campoi.

This documentary respect extends to souchong and Lapsang souchong. In the 18th century, souchong was among the most expensive “brown teas” (the contemporary term for what is now called black tea), attracting such attention that it was subjected to chemical analysis by the Royal Society. Lapsang souchong, despite its distinctive smoky profile, was embraced by intellectual circles. Samuel Beckett praised the “choicest lapsang souchong,” while Aldous Huxley and Iris Murdoch incorporated it naturally into their writing. The OED also records its organic evolution in everyday speech, recording spelling variations like “lapseng,” “lapsang soochong,” and “lapsang suchong.”

The same holds true for pekoe. As early as 1713, essayist Joseph Addison listed it alongside coffee and chocolate as a fashionable social staple, while East India Company records documented its premium trade value. From the tinfoiled chests of “flowery Pekoe” described by G.A. Sala in 1859 to the “teak-colored pekoe” poured in Annie Proulx’s 1993 novel “The Shipping News,” pekoe has maintained a continuous literary and commercial presence. Gunpowder tea, tightly rolled into pellets, was elegantly translated by early British scholars as “pearl tea.”

Importantly, this documentary trail is not limited to black teas. Hyson, known in Chinese as xichun, was championed by Thomas Jefferson, who preferred “young Hyson” for its strength and flavor. By 1948, The New York Times described young Hyson and pinhead gunpowder as the “aristocrats of green teas.”

Singlo was once a major commercial variety in the 18th century, with East India Company ledgers recording millions of pounds imported annually. Known in Chinese as Songluo, after the Songluo Mountain in Anhui where it originates, it was so highly prized that travelers noted authentic batches had become exceedingly rare, with counterfeit versions flooding the market.

Even the obsolete terms in the OED offer a fascinating philosophical counterpoint. Imperial, for instance, once described by J.M. Walsh in 1892 as “the perfection of tea,” has since fallen out of use. Similarly, bing has vanished from common usage. First documented by the Royal Society in 1702 as “the second growth in April,” it is a dialect romanization of the Chinese character “ming” (meaning “bright”), evoking the clarity of early spring after Qingming. Another example, “Oopack,” a highly valued tea from the central Hubei province that fetched top auction prices in The Times as late as 1855, now survives only as a rare lexical relic.

Today, the translation of Chinese tea culture continues to evolve. While traditional teas such as Longjing (Dragon Well) remain largely untranslated in English, modern milk tea brands are experimenting with hybrid naming strategies. Chagee (drawing on “cha,” the Chinese word for tea, and “gee” (which approximates the sound of the Chinese character ji – a classical Chinese term for female performers) and ChaPanda merge Chinese linguistic cues with global marketing logic.

Meanwhile, a new wave of tea culture is reshaping global consumption. Bubble tea (boba), which originated in Taiwan in the 1980s, has become a global phenomenon. What began as a simple blend of black tea, milk, and chewy tapioca pearls has evolved into a highly customizable, brightly colored drink embedded in global youth culture. Driven by social media aesthetics and its distinctive texture, boba has moved from East Asian diaspora spaces into mainstream cafés worldwide, reshaping expectations of what tea can be.

Similarly, yum cha, the Cantonese tradition of drinking tea with dim sum, remains strong across global cities, functioning as a social anchor in urban dining culture. Beyond this, yin yeung — the Hong Kong-style blend of milk tea and coffee — is also gradually capturing international attention. As this bold, caffeinated fusion finds its way onto menus outside Hong Kong, it signals the ongoing global influence of hybridized regional drinks.

This modern expansion is part of a broader global tea renaissance that also includes the Indian-derived chai, now a staple in Western coffee chains. From the early days of Singlo and Imperial to the modern ubiquity of boba and yin yeung, Chinese tea has left a lasting mark on the English language. The theatrical figure of Widow Twankey remains an outlier, a historical distortion rather than a defining pattern.

Yet tea’s vitality has never been confined to its point of origin. A beverage rooted solely in China would have remained culturally rich but geographically limited; its global life depends on circulation, adaptation, and reinterpretation. Today, as global consumers fall in love with tea, they continue to reshape it into new forms, from South Asia’s spiced chai to Southeast Asia’s milk tea variations and contemporary café experiments in the West.

It is this ongoing exchange and reinvention that sustains tea’s global relevance. Ultimately, its legacy is not only Chinese heritage embedded in language, but a shared cultural system in motion — a cup that grows richer with every new tradition poured into it.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.title: The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018834/The Chinese Chicken Joint That Rejected Fame Now Craves It
World.content:
From “don’t come,” to “the more customers, the better.” These were the refrains made by the owner of a chicken hotpot restaurant in southern China famous for shirking fame and which has recently drawn criticism for perceived hypocrisy due to its rapid expansion.

In April, “Mo’s Chicken Hotpot,” in the southern Guangdong province’s Foshan City, went viral after the recommendation of a popular food vlogger. The eatery drew crowds for its signature medicinal hotpot made from freshly slaughtered chickens — and whose healing properties included causing diarrhea, according to notices in the restaurant.

During the initial vlogger’s visit, the restaurant’s owner, surnamed Mo, insisted that customers should “not come” as he would not be able to handle the popularity. Nevertheless, the restaurant began drawing thousands of customers a day, including celebrities and influencers.

But the restaurant’s expansion to five branches in Guangdong and Shanghai — with another expected to open in the southern city of Shenzhen next year — and frequent online s in the months since have drawn ridicule, domestic media reported this week. Social media users argue the restaurant’s current activities contradict Mo’s previous rejection of fame.

Earlier interviews quoted Mo as saying he had no plans to raise prices or open new outlets, leading some online to question whether his indifferent persona had been a marketing strategy from the beginning.

As of this month, Mo said the restaurant has hired a 20-person livestreaming team and broadcasts twice a day. “We can’t afford not to livestream,” he told domestic media. “The pressure is just too great.”

The eatery’s official account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, now has around 500,000 followers. It posts two to three times a week, mainly skits promoting its signature chicken hotpot alongside health tips. Several videos have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

The restaurant also sells meal kits, Chinese medicine, herbal teas, and local specialties such as salt-baked chicken via its online store.

The rating for Mo’s Chicken Hotpot on review platform Dianping has fallen from a peak of 4.8 out of 5 in April to 3.7, according to domestic media. Negative reviews mention inconsistent food quality, flies and poor hygiene standards in the restaurant, and high prices.

Visitor numbers have also fluctuated. In June, domestic media reported that sales at the original restaurant had fallen from 200 to 400 orders a day to fewer than 20 a day by the end of the month. However, Mo told domestic media in mid-July that the restaurant handles no fewer than 150 orders a day.

In a video interview with domestic media, Mo responded to the criticism, saying, “At first, when we suddenly became so popular, I really didn’t want the attention. We were so busy, it made me want to throw up.”

“Now I actually want the business to be even better,” he added. “When fortune gives you an opportunity like this … and there’s money to be made, why wouldn’t I try to make money? I’d be a fool not to.”

Mo also admitted that despite the restaurant’s expansion and livestreaming business, profits remain limited.

“Traffic comes quickly, and it disappears just as quickly. After a month or two, how do you sustain it? It’s really hard,” adding that if another wave of popularity were to come, he would “honestly close shop and stop.”

Mo also joined the second season of popular domestic cooking competition show “The Divine Dish,” which premiered Wednesday. He was eliminated in the first round.

“The ingredients (he used) were good, but his technique was poor,” one of the show’s judges said of his signature chicken hotpot.

On his Douyin account, Mo responded to his elimination, saying, “I will continue to use the finest ingredients and simplest methods to cook you the familiar chicken hotpot that warms your heart.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.
