World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Residents hope to raise $750,000 to fix small town's aged care problem
World.content:
Joan White and her husband Alan, affectionately known as Stumpy, did everything together.

They were side-by-side for 58 years of marriage, raising three sons and navigating the highs and lows of being primary producers on their Texas property on Queensland's southern border.

The former country mayor said she thinks euthanising 62 head of cattle rather than having them starve to death due to drought in 2015 was the beginning of the end for her husband.

Mr White soon developed dementia, and the couple sold their farm and moved to town in 2018 to be closer to care.

Joan and Stumpy White were married for 58 years and did everything together. (Supplied: Joan White)

"It became really, really horrendous," she said.

Ms White said her husband was sent to Millmerran, 120 kilometres away, to be cared for in an aged care facility after she had a heart attack.

"It is a sad story, but I don't want anybody else to make it their journey," she said.

In the small country town, there is no public transport and barely any traffic, but the number of mobility scooters used in the area highlights a big problem facing the aging community.

A sign outside the post office reads "Texas is a dementia friendly community" and features a picture of Mr and Ms White.

Joan and Stumpy White feature on a sign in the main street of Texas. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

And while Texas has a median age of 53, 15 years higher than the rest of the country, it does not have an aged care facility.

Ms White is the driving force behind a community push to build a facility that could keep older people, including those with dementia, in their hometown.

The Texas Care Foundation Limited is a board of community members pulled together by the gaps in services for older people.

Joan and Alan are not alone

Brian and Annette Mearns have been married almost 60 years and fear being separated when they need aged care. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Aged care is a high priority for many of the town's 800 residents.

Brian Mearns, 83, and his wife Annette Mearns, 84, say they are on a "downhill run" both with serious health problems.

"I tell her she can leave anytime she likes, but I'm coming with her," Mr Mearns jokes.

"He's been telling me that for 60 years," she replies.

But the couple, who are due to celebrate their 60th anniversary in a few months, said the thought of being separated was "absolutely traumatic".

"You're used to someone in bed beside you at night and you're used to talking to someone at the table … and togetherness," Ms Mearns said.

They keep themselves busy tending to a beautiful garden, including 110 fruit trees, but accept there will be a time they will have to leave it behind.

They will likely move closer to family in Dalby, more than 200km away, but are supportive of the push for a local aged care facility.

Cristine Miller says she is worried about the future for her and her husband. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Cristine Miller, 75, and her 80-year-old husband were "taking each day at a time" but said they share the same worries.

"I just hope and pray I can look after Brian forever," she said.

" I tell him we've both got to die at home, but I haven't worked the time out yet. "

Sally-Ann Masters says she coped using humour during the hard years caring for her mother. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Sally-Ann Masters said dementia was her only fear in life after she saw her mother go from being a strong lady "back to being a little girl" when she was living with the condition.

"You grieve them twice. You grieve them while you're nursing them, and you grieve them when they've gone," she said.

Small community, big challenges

Rural GP Colin Owen has lived in the nearby town of Inglewood, 55km away, for 58 years, and has many patients from Texas.

He said in his opinion, home was the best place for people with dementia to be looked after.

But Dr Owen said when someone needs an aged care facility, it was best in the patient's hometown.

Residents in Texas say the idea of being separated to live in aged care is traumatic. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

"This is where they grew up, this is where their family are, this is where they know people and my other belief is that they get looked after better in their own hometown by people who know them," he said.

Securing the site

Despite the challenges, Texas Care Foundation Limited has earmarked a 3.5-hectare property for an aged care home.

While Ms White said it would be a big task, but the group aims to raise $750,000 to secure the site in the next 12 months.

Board member Warwick Trim, the owner of a fuel supplier in town, said he felt it was his responsibility to become involved.

"We need something like this in Texas, not just now, but that will be for years and probably generations to come as well," he said.

"We're all going to get old one day."

When Joan White was awarded a Medal of the Order of Australia, Stumpy was too unwell to attend the official ceremony but they still celebrated together. (Supplied: Joan White)

Mr White said she would not stop until her big dream was a reality, motivated by her husband's memory.

She smiles when remembering Stumpy's final days, when she would climb into his hospital bed, and the nurses would say, "Look at these lovebirds".

"If he could touch my skin and I could rub his hand or rub his leg, he knew I was there," she said.

World.title: Single mum has front-row seat to first home buyer struggles
World.content:
It is a sunny Thursday afternoon in the leafy inner-city Perth suburb of Mount Hawthorn.

Tess McKenna is preparing afternoon tea for her four kids after getting home from a busy day at work.

Tess McKeanna has four children aged under 13. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The 31-year-old gets them settled with some colouring-in at the dining table. Then, she starts scrolling.

Ms McKenna works as a buyer's agent. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"It's really hard, it's a really hard market," she said.

" As a single parent, I feel like right now it's very next to impossible for me. "

There is a limited number of affordable homes available in Perth. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She is on the hunt for an affordable first home in Perth — something well under $1 million, in a good, established area with space for the kids.

But she is not alone in that search; in fact, she is just one of thousands competing in a market described by experts as "messy", "unaffordable" and "very limited".

Familiar with disappointment

Ms McKenna understands Perth property well, because she analyses it for a living.

Working as a buyer's agent — a role increasingly sought by first home buyers to help with their search — she is in tune with the current challenges.

Ms McKenna is well-versed in the challenges faced by first home buyers. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She knows all too well the feeling of scrolling websites, only to be disappointed the next day when listings are marked sold.

She relates to the stress of searching for properties while going from rental to rental as cost of living pressures rise.

"It's very isolating, and there are not many options; you feel like you're going backwards and you're constantly having all this self-doubt thinking that you're failing all the time," she said.

The McKenna family is competing with thousands of others in a tough market. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She has made her current rental feel like home with art on the wall and photos lining the fridge, but the last few years have not been easy.

"A lot of the time I'm left sort of living pay cheque to pay cheque and month by month … and I'm having to dip into any savings that I potentially might have been able to put towards [a] deposit," she said.

"It just seems to get harder."

The buyer's agent first started looking for a property two-and-a-half years ago. Since 2023, she has lived in four rentals.

Advised to shop around

The irony of helping others with the same problem she is facing is not lost on Ms McKenna.

"The Australian dream is to own a home, so when it seems so out of reach for people and so impossible, I definitely can relate," she said.

"The fact that I can help other people do it [find a home] is awesome … I would love to do it for myself."

Tess McKenna helps others to find homes, but would love to achieve that for herself too. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She said houses around the $600,000-mark close to the city have become almost non-existent, likely because Perth's median house price is still stubbornly high after breaking through the $1 million mark in January.

Property analyst Gavin Hegney said he is now advising first home buyers in Perth to hold off and shop around.

Gavin Hegney is a real estate expert, property valuer and advisor. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"If a normal cycle prevails, we should see a settling back in values over the next 12 months … prices are coming off a bit in some areas, and so there's no sense of urgency," he said.

"It creates a little bit of uncertainty for first home buyers wondering whether they should be paying prices of today or whether the price will be cheaper in a year's time."

Perth no longer 'affordable state'

Curtin University property professor Steven Rowley said Perth's property squeeze had been driven by one factor.

Steven Rowley is the director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute’s Curtin Research Centre. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"We've had really strong demand, particularly from investors the last few years and there just isn't the supply there," he said.

"[The] combination of a really struggling rental market plus very strong demand and low supply in the buying market has meant real problems for first home buyers."

Perth's median house price surges through $1 milion mark Domain's latest quarterly house price report has found the cost to buy a home increased by 9.9 per cent in the last quarter of 2025, to a median of $1,087,762.

He said while Perth used to be considered "the affordable state", that is "no longer the case", pointing to substantial growth at the bottom end of the market.

"We've caught up with Melbourne, we're not that far behind Sydney, we've accelerated ahead of Adelaide … because of that demand-supply balance," he said.

He said some "generous government schemes" probably have not helped in terms of inflating prices — namely, the Help to Buy Scheme, the 5 per cent Deposit Scheme and WA's Keystart program.

Property analyst Mr Hegney also believes the federal government's negative gearing tax changes in this year's budget are not necessarily helping.

"We've got two investors walking out [of the market] for every one first home buyer walking in … the problem is not all first home buyers are in a position to be able to buy today," he said.

Laser-focus on supply

WA Housing Minister John Carey said he has a "resolute focus" on getting more supply onto the market.

"As a government, you keep making bold decisions," he said.

"I accept that some of the decisions I'm making, particularly around enabling 50,000 subdivisions, do not resonate [with everyone]."

John Carey says he is determined to bring more property supply to market. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Referencing proposed building code subdivision changes announced last month, Mr Carey said "more medium density" was needed in WA.

"We're not taking [the West Australian] dream away from people, but what we are trying to do is create choice for young couples, first-home buyers who might actually want to buy an apartment that's well-serviced, close to a public train station," he said.

When asked when it would get easier for first home buyers, Mr Carey said he "can't anticipate the future".

"There isn't a single silver bullet, but by god we've got to keep pushing out that housing and introducing new measures, new reforms, cutting red tape — whatever it takes," he said.

Cold comfort

For Ms McKenna, it's cold comfort as she continues her search.

She has not given up hope completely, but the constant scrolling and missing out has worn her down.

"I definitely do feel a bit defeated at times," she said.

Ms McKenna says she still has hope and will secure a place. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"I still hold hope that I will get there and I'm sure I will; I'm quite a determined person.

"At some stage, there has to be some sort of change that'll happen to make it possible."

World.title: Live: Big tech faces higher tax if it does not reach deals with local publishers
World.content:
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino says artificial intelligence companies will remain exempt from the government's News Bargaining Incentive.

The government has made some adjustments to its News Bargaining Incentive draft legislation, increasing the tax rate to 2.5 per cent.

Under the changes, Labor will push to tax the revenue of big tech companies rather than the company's entire revenue stream.

Speaking to ABC's AM program, the assistant treasurer says taxing advertising revenue will target the part of the business that uses news.

"We don't want to discourage those large tech companies from having a growing footprint in Australia," Mulino says. "What we do want though is that part of their business which is using news to be fairly compensating the producers of that news."

Platforms like Microsoft, Snapchat and OpenAI have been excluded from the tax and from coming to agreements with publishers.

Asked if artificial intelligence companies will now fall under the incentive, Mulino says they still remain exempt.

"The prime minister speech delivered a week and a half ago made very clear that he was going to implement a series of processes to look at things like copyright to make sure that creative producers are protected."

World.title: Live: ASX set to tumble despite Wall St rallying on Amazon earnings
World.content:
Wall Street closed the month with AI stocks back in favour, lifting all key indices.

S & P 500: +0.7%

+0.7% Dow: +0.5%

+0.5% Nasdaq: +1.0%

That good fortune appears unlikely to flow through to the ASX this morning with futures markets pointing to a nasty 1% decline when trading closed on Saturday morning (AEST).

Amazon dominated the corporate news flow with a consensus smashing result.

It recorded its strongest cloud revenue growth in more than four years, which reassured investors looking for proof that massive AI spending is paying off.

Amazon shares jumped more than 15%.

It could have been an even bigger session had not Apple — a "Magnificent Seven" company that hasn't been splashing out on AI investment — delivered a downbeat forecast.

The iPhone maker said it was struggling to secure enough components as the AI-driven data-centre boom strains global supply chains.

Apple shares plunged 7%.

European shares slipped marginally, but the global index, the MSCI was up 1.2% on Friday.

US Treasury yields jumped after the three Fed Reserve members who voted to hike rates last week publicly stated their case for why US rates need to rise, sooner rather than later.

Traders are now pricing in a 69% chance that the Fed will raise rates at its September meeting.

The Aussie dollar was marginally lower but still holding just above 70 US cents.

Oil jumped around $US1 a barrel, or more than1%, on news that Iran had forced to several tankers to turn around rather than risk a passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures : +1.2% to $US90.12/barrel

: +1.2% to $US90.12/barrel West Texas Intermediate crude futures: +1.3% to $US84.67/barrel.

For July, Brent gained 24% and WTI rose 21%.

Gold slipped marginally (-1.3%) but still gained 1.1% for over July, its largest monthly gain since February.

Copper was little changed on Friday but gained a solid 3% over the month as limited inventories weighed on traders' minds.



With Reuters

World.title: Lorena Wiebes sprints to second straight win at Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Lorena Wiebes again sprinted to victory in the second stage of the Women’s Tour de France.

The Dutch rider of SD Worx-Protime won the flat 147.9-kilometre stage from Aigle to Geneva, the second on Swiss territory, in 3 hours, 42 minutes, 8 seconds on Sunday.

Wiebes went ahead with some 250 metres to go and claimed her seventh overall victory at the tour.

Wiebes also won the opening stage on Saturday in the same dominant fashion.

Lidl-Trek rider Elisa Balsamo finished second and Marianne Vos of Team Visma-Lease a Bike was third.

Wiebes leads Kim Le Court Pienaar by 14 seconds overall, with the 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering another two seconds back in third.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Monday's 156.5km (97.2-mile) hilly stage starts in Geneva before the riders cross the border to France to finish in Poligny.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women’s Tour, covers 1,175km (730 miles) over nine days.

Amanda Spratt is the leading Australian in the race, in 68th place, 3 minutes and 20 seconds behind Wiebes.

Tadej Pogacar won his fifth men's Tour de France title last weekend.

AP/ABC

World.title: Kellie Sloane needs clear air, but ICAC claims are starving her of oxygen
World.content:
Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane was once a world away from the extraordinary behaviour being alleged in the Independent Commission Against Corruption.

In 2021, when a now-fugitive property developer was allegedly funnelling money to right-wing Liberal powerbrokers and plotting to end the careers of his rivals, Ms Sloane was working alongside a giant, talking giraffe promoting healthy lifestyles for children.

Pretty wholesome stuff.

In 2022, she bid "Healthy Harold" farewell, quitting her job as CEO of Life Education Australia to run for the blue-ribbon Liberal seat of Vaucluse, which she won in 2023.

Kellie Sloane is quick to remind people the allegations predate her time in politics. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

Ms Sloane is quick to remind people that the allegations being heard as part of Operation Rosny predate her time in politics.

Last week, she described the opening day's evidence as "pretty awful" and "intensely uncomfortable listening," but gave the impression her focus was nowhere near the inquiry.

However, by the time Friday rolled around, two of her shadow ministers had been dragged into the saga.

And this week, ICAC's gaze is likely to feel even closer, as the anti-corruption commission hears from one of her most senior parliamentary colleagues.

Tudehope to give evidence

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Former shadow attorney-general Damien Tudehope is due in the witness box on Monday and his evidence is expected to last for one day.

While he has not been accused of wrongdoing, he stepped aside from the frontbench last month in anticipation of his appearance as a witness.

Mr Tudehope had a personal connection with members of the Reformers, the right-wing sub-faction of the Liberal party, which is at the centre of this inquiry.

Damien Tudehope is due in the witness box on Monday, and has not been accused of wrongdoing. (ABC News)

ICAC's been told Mr Tudehope hosted a barbecue for them in 2018 to support the recruitment of like-minded Liberals with socially conservative values.

During that event, a former colleague of Mr Tudehope's, Michael O'Hara, was introduced to the group.

The corruption commission was told Mr O'Hara later decided to support the Reformers financially, despite being a prohibited donor.

Damien Tudehope had a connection with members of the Reformers, a right-wing sub-faction of the Liberal party. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

On Monday, Mr Tudehope is likely to be asked whether he had any knowledge or suspicion of these alleged payments.

Such questions are often fact-finding exercises and are not allegations, but Mr Tudehope's association with the Reformers could make for an uncomfortable day in the witness box.

Ms Sloane describes Mr Tudehope as a "man of integrity" whom she would welcome back into her shadow cabinet when the time is right.

The speed with which he returns to the frontbench will largely depend on his performance on Monday.

Catching curveballs

While Ms Sloane may have hoped Mr Tudehope's early resignation would help neutralise controversy during the first week of ICAC, she wasn't prepared for the evidence concerning shadow industry minister, Eleni Petinos.

Ms Petinos is not accused of wrongdoing, but ICAC is investigating a curious phone call made by fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, who's accused of funding the Reformers and seeking influence in the NSW government.

Eleni Petinos is not accused of wrongdoing. (Facebook: Eleni Petinos MP)

During the 2021 call, which was intercepted by investigators, he boasted that he could get rid of building commissioner David Chandler, because one of his "girls" was going to become the relevant minister.

Two months later, Ms Petinos was appointed fair trading minister.

And by mid 2022, Mr Chandler had left his position following a code of conduct investigation that had been requested by Ms Petinos's office, the inquiry was told.

However, Counsel Assisting Peggy Dwyer was cautious about drawing a link between Nassif's boastful conversation and Mr Chandler's departure as building commissioner.

Peggy Dwyer SC is the counsel assisting the ICAC for Operation Rosny. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Dr Dwyer raised the prospect that his bragging may have been "wishful thinking" that "serendipitously came to pass".

Ms Sloane was keen to emphasise that prospect last week, reminding people that Ms Petinos was "not named as a subject of interest".

She said the inquiry should be allowed to run its course and noted that Ms Petinos was on maternity leave.

It means she won't be attending parliament when it resumes this week, after the winter break.

Kellie Sloane says Ms Petinos has not been named "as a subject of interest". (Facebook: Eleni Petinos MP)

The opposition leader was also forced to defend shadow planning minister Chris Rath, after Nine newspapers reported he may have helped at least one of the Reformers avoid a summons to appear in a 2023 parliamentary inquiry into allegations of branch stacking.

He'd reportedly tipped off an individual about the location of a process server, someone who'd been hired to serve the summons.

Ms Sloane said she'd spoken to Mr Rath and expressed her "disappointment."

Kellie Sloane says she spoke to Chris Rath to express her "disappointment". (Supplied)

"Chris has acknowledged that he made an error of judgement, apologised for it at the time and accepts that he should not have disclosed confidential committee information," she said.

However, she noted her shadow minister was not under investigation by ICAC, nor had he been asked to provide evidence.

Even still, for the third time in a week she'd been forced to answer questions about her colleagues' conduct.

Just seven months out from an election, the timing could hardly be worse.

Labor keeps its glee in check

Throughout August and September, ICAC will likely produce many damaging headlines about alleged corruption involving figures linked to the Liberal party.

On one hand, it's a gift to the Labor government, which seems content to sit back and watch it all unfold every day.

Even before the inquiry began, Ms Sloane and her team were facing an uphill battle to win government.

The Resolve Political Monitor published in Nine newspapers last month put voter support for the Coalition at just 23 per cent.

However, Labor was not the main beneficiary, with the same poll showing support for One Nation has surged to 25 per cent.

Polling suggests support for One Nation has surged. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The eight weeks of public hearings are unlikely to improve the Coalition's standing with voters.

However, Premier Chris Minns has — for the most part — resisted the urge to make political hay out of his opponents' predicament.

On Sunday, he said the allegations raised at ICAC risked casting all politicians in a bad light, at a time when voter frustration with the major parties was on the rise.

Chris Minns says the allegations raised at ICAC risked casting all politicians in a bad light. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

"One Nation's vote has skyrocketed and they've got nothing to do with this ICAC investigation," he said.

"And my concern is that people say, well, I've seen Labor at ICAC and I've seen the Liberal Party at ICAC, I'm going to vote for a third party this time."

ICAC is supposed to give voters confidence that public institutions and politicians are, on the whole, acting in an honest and transparent manner.

It would be a strange irony if, after all these inquiries, voters decided they could no longer trust them at all.

World.title: 52 long weekends a year as council trials four-day work week
World.content:
Employees will get 52 long weekends next year when a four-day working week trial begins at a south-west New South Wales council.

Murrumbidgee Council will be the first local government organisation in the country to implement a four-day work week model in a bid to increase productivity and attract staff.

"The agreement will be for 15 months so that we can have a review in 12 months … and we can determine whether it's going to continue or revert back," council general manager John Scarce said.

"As everybody knows, in rural Australia it is hard to attract staff so you always have to have a competitive edge."

The trial will retain a 38-hour week for people at the council's depot, office, library and in its work crews at Darlington Point, Coleambally and Jerilderie, but compressed into four days.

Most services will be closed on Fridays, though the childcare centre and caravan park will remain open and on-call essential service workers will still be rostered.

John Scarce says implementing a four-day work week could help the organisation attract and retain staff. (Supplied: Murrumbidgee Council)

Mr Scarce said the trial will start in January.

He said the data already collected, particularly around road repair and construction, indicated a positive outcome was likely.

"In a week, we can grade 6 kilometres [of road]; with this compressed to four days, then we expect that 6 kilometres to be done, but there's also probably going to be another half a kilometre of road done because the lost travel time is work time," he said.

It follows staff and community consultations that indicated 75 per cent of staff preferred the compressed work week, while just under 40 per cent of community submissions opposed it.

Over the next six months, Mr Scarce will put together an agreement about what the working week will look like and which performance indicators will be used to measure the trial's success.

Community divided

Darlington Point resident Michael Painting said he was dubious about how it would work, especially outside daylight-saving time.

Michael Painting says he is not sure the council has taken everything into account for the four-day working week. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

"I can't see how they can increase the productivity when there's going to be less daylight hours to work in with the extended hours," he said.

Alan Surl, a former Murrumbidgee Council employee, said while he could see it working, the council had to ensure the change had positive community outcomes.

"If you extend the day, you can be more active, get more done without having to crank up and then wind down and travel to and fro, but again, it sounds quite simple," he said.

" What are the logistics and how is it going to work and does it mean that all the council's assets are just sitting idle for longer? "

Jody Heath, who owns a butcher shop in Darlington Point, supports the new model, based on his own experience.

Jody Heath says the four-day working week has suited his business well. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Three years ago, he cut the shop's working days from five and a half to four days per week and, so far, it has been a success.

"It really works having that one day off a week. It's just more productive for us. We got a lot of early starts and later finishes, but we get a lot more work done," he said.

"We've been in business now for 30 years this year, and with the five and a half days that we were doing, you never got a lot of time for yourself … having the four days there makes up for that bit of time out that you need."

Other businesses in the region have already started four-day working weeks. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Union supports move

The United Services Union, the peak body for council workers in NSW, which supports reduced workdays, has been negotiating with Murrumbidgee Council about the proposal.

"This is the first council nationally to trial shutting the whole council for the day," industrial officer Stuart Geddes said.

" It really is a brilliant test case to see if this notion of shutting the council down for one day is effective and what the benefits potentially are. "

Mr Geddes said while it was uncharted waters for Australia, the model has been a success in overseas markets.

"A lot of the data comes from Scandinavian countries … When countries, particularly in the local government sector, implemented a four-day work week, they saw an improvement of productivity despite longer work hours," he said.

Mr Scarce said while he anticipates some teething issues with the community, he was optimistic about the outcome of the trial for workers.

"For the staff, I think it will be quite an easy transition, and we're hoping it will also be a recruitment attraction as well," he said.

World.title: Cut-price cars, pay rises and trips by foster care charity execs face scrutiny
World.content:
A New South Wales charity responsible for finding foster homes for children spent more than $40,000 of taxpayer money to send its chief executive on a "sabbatical" to the US and Europe.

That same year, it awarded the individual a $120,000 pay rise, allegedly without "discussion or formal approval", boosting their salary by two-thirds.

Taxpayer money was also allegedly misused on Airbnb stays, rugby league sponsorships, parties, alcohol and more.

The ABC is not naming the organisation accused in a confidential forensic audit of misusing taxpayer funds for legal reasons.

The charity had received tens of millions of dollars under state government Permanent Support Program (PSP) contracts, to help more than 100 children under 18 years old find foster homes, mostly in Greater Sydney.

It is not the only organisation holding PSP contracts that is suspected of fraudulently using taxpayer funds.

The ABC understands five others are being targeted by the Department of Communities and Justice (DCJ).

Three of the organisations have to meet new conditions to keep their PSP contracts.

Three others are not having their contracts renewed and will no longer be allowed to find foster homes for children and teenagers.

The ABC is not naming the five other providers for legal reasons.

Overseas trips, cars and events a concern

The Department of Communities and Justice is targeting a number of organisations that find foster homes for children and young people. (Pixabay, truthseeker08)

A "high volume of complaints" against the chief executive, "financial impropriety, and a perceived lack of board oversight", were some of the reasons why the DCJ ordered a forensic audit into one foster care organisation in Greater Sydney.

The confidential forensic audit covered operations from October 1, 2022, to June 30, 2025, when more than 99 per cent of the charity's funding came from taxpayers, exceeding $34 million.

Independent firm BDO Services said $1.6 million had not been recorded because the organisation under-reported the interest it made from funds, overcharged or double charged services, and had not documented some of the assets it sold.

In addition to uncovering unaccounted-for money, the auditors flagged several expenses as "potentially non-compliant", because they had no clear link to the work it was contracted to carry out.

Travel was a "key concern" with more than $98,000 flagged.

This included almost $41,500 spent on a sabbatical to the US and Europe for its chief executive, and about $8,600 for a trip to New Zealand for the chief executive, the deputy chief executive, and chair of the board.

A smaller share of money is finding its way to the children and young people in need. (Pexels)

Another concern was a pay increase secured by the chief executive, as their salary of $181,761 jumped to $300,574 in the financial year ending in 2024, an increase of 65 per cent.

"Based on the Board minutes reviewed, we did not identify discussion or formal approval relating to the performance or remuneration of the CEO," the audit read.

" On the material available, it is unclear when, by whom, or through which governance process the annual pay increases were approved. "

Other transactions flagged by the forensic audit included:

Five cars sold to staff, family and friends at up to 55.3 per cent below the market rate

$226,971.72 for advertising and promotion, including the sponsorship of five football teams and events, mostly in regions the charity did not service

$22,876.16 on catering, make-up services, office amenities and entertainment

$14,978.10 on coaching lessons for the CEO and the Board

$6,709.09 on a security system and door camera installed at the CEO's residential address

$10,123.84 on food and alcohol at restaurants and hotels, both in Australia and overseas

'Genuinely shocked'

Ms Washington says the status quo is unacceptable. (ABC News: Emily Jane Smith )

The cost of finding foster homes for children and young people soared by 239 per cent during a six-year period to 2024, according to state government figures, increasing from $322 million to $1.1 billion.

Executive and corporate manager fees tripled, from $38 million to $117 million.

Meanwhile, a smaller share of money found its way to the children and young people in need, dropping from 43 per cent to 30 per cent.

"I was genuinely shocked to find that the system that was created was allowing funding to flow away from vulnerable children and towards the financial interests of individuals and providers," NSW Government Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington said.

"One of the very first reports to land on my desk was about young children not even having the winter school uniform they needed to stay warm at school, despite the provider receiving millions of dollars in funding to provide services to those kids."

Years of reform ahead

The NSW government said one of the issues with the current foster care system was the "weak accountability for delivery of services".

NSW unveils sweeping foster care reforms for vulnerable children While some child protection services will continue to be outsourced, the NSW government will play a larger role in the sector, including through the recruitment of foster carers.

It is changing the out-of-home-care strategy in stages until 2030.

"A large part of our reforms is ensuring that we are introducing stronger measures around accountability and transparency," Ms Washington said.

"Contracts will require information to be provided to us that wasn't required before, in terms of where and how they are spending their money."

Part of the reform process is phasing out the PSP contracts held by providers.

Shadow Families and Communities Minister Natasha Maclaren-Jones said the government should focus more on early prevention programs to lower the number of kids needing foster care.

"At the end of the day, it's about ensuring that the standards we have in place are workable and that children are being protected," she said.

"And of course, taxpayers' funds are being used appropriately."

World.title: Two killed as firefighting helicopters collide in Greece
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires Two killed as firefighting helicopters collide in Greece Elena Becatoros and Thomas Adamson August 3, 2026 — 7:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Athens: Two Greek firefighting helicopters collided in midair as they were battling a wind-driven wildfire west of Athens, sending one aircraft crashing to the ground. Two crew members, a Greek and a Danish national, died in the crash. The collision on Sunday (Greek time) laid bare the danger at the most volatile front of Europe’s wildfire emergency. Strong winds drove flames deeper into the region of the Greek capital and forced fresh evacuations, France guarded a still-burning scar four times the size of Paris, while Spain’s major fires stopped advancing. Loading Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed “sorrow for the tragic accident” and extended condolences to the families of the firefighters killed in the crash.



“The loss of the Greek coordinator and the Danish pilot at the time they were attempting the major fire in Porto Gremeno fills us all with grief,” Mitsotakis said in a statement. The aircraft were Bell helicopters operating over the Psatha area west of Athens, each with a two-person crew. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires during the country’s hot, dry summers. Wreckage of the helicopter lies on a road near Psatha. Hellenic Red Cross/Facebook The Guardian reported that the helicopters involved had been leased from Australia’s McDermott Aviation and were part of a fleet of 15. Video posted online and reported in Greek media appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames.



The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not yet verified the authenticity of the footage. The two crew members who were recovered alive were a Greek and a British national. A firefighter stands as flames rising during a wildfire near Porto Germeno, northwest of Athens, on Sunday. AP Photo/Michael Varaklas The flames had spread rapidly, threatening communities and an industrial district as violent gusts prevented firefighting aircraft from collecting water from the sea. The blaze carried a grim resonance in a region where the 2018 Mati wildfire killed 104 people, Europe’s deadliest blaze this century. Farther west, containment brought no end to the emergency. France’s largest wildfire remained held within its perimeter after forcing 224,000 people to flee in what may have been the country’s largest civilian evacuation outside wartime.



Hot spots still burned within a 420-square-kilometre scar, thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde megafire and a second, still-uncontained blaze in Provence. Together, fires in France and Spain have driven about a third of a million people from homes and vacation sites, emptied communities at the height of the European summer and stretched emergency services across simultaneous disasters. Firefighters work at the site where firefighting helicopters crashed on Sunday. EPA The mass evacuations in France and Spain are the latest measure of a wildfire threat growing across Europe. The continent entered 2026 after its worst fire year on record, with more than 10,000 square kilometres burned in 2025. Over the past four decades, wildfires have been linked to nearly 800 deaths across much of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency.



Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent. It has warmed more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Human-caused climate change made the extreme fire-weather conditions behind this year’s French blazes at least twice as likely, scientists at World Weather Attribution found in a rapid analysis conducted while the fires were still burning. A firefighting helicopter drops water over a smoke-filled forest during a wildfire near Porto Germeno. AP Photo/Michael Varaklas In Greece, nearly 500 firefighters and 23 aircraft were deployed, but gale-force winds drove flames through dry forest and crippled the response, preventing some aircraft from reaching the sea to collect water. Authorities ordered the evacuation of Kandili, Agia Skepi and Toutouli as smoke rose over the mountains. Crews were particularly concerned about Porto Germeno, a seaside community on the Gulf of Corinth.



The fire began on Friday near Agios Vasileios before sweeping toward Porto Germeno and into the forested mountains west of Athens. Firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea Friday and another 12 Saturday – often the last escape route when fire and smoke cut the few roads from coastal communities. Related Article Exclusive

Bushfires ‘It looked like an atomic bomb’: The Aussie pilots flying into a French firestorm Elsewhere in Greece, flames threatened homes on Kefalonia, forcing evacuations from inland communities as aircraft made water drops over the Ionian island. Firefighters battled another blaze near Nea Tenedos on the peninsula of Halkidiki. Earlier this week, two firefighters died fighting a fire on Crete, while a third was killed on the Peloponnese. In south-western France, the Gironde megafire remained held within its perimeter on Sunday but continued to burn after scorching 420 square kilometres of forest in 10 days.



“The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped. The region remained under France’s highest red forest-fire alert. Dry conditions, soaring temperatures around Bordeaux and afternoon winds threatened to rekindle the flames. A volunteer tries to extinguish small flames northwest of Athens. AP Photo/Michael Varaklas In Le Porge, local officials said about 150 homes were destroyed. Mechanic Matthieu Plessis returned Saturday to the ruins of a house that had been in his family for seven generations. “There are places I don’t even recognise anymore,” he said. “You don’t even know what was here anymore, or who lived where.”



Firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation. Related Article Bushfires Emergency warnings as US west battles wildfires, extreme heat In south-eastern France, nearly 1500 firefighters battled a separate blaze in the Var department that tore through about 18 square kilometres in little more than a day. The Gros Bessillon fire was stabilised Sunday after its perimeter held overnight, but it remained uncontained. Some 2500 people were evacuated as flames threatened nearby communities. It was the fourth major fire to strike central Var since July 19. A smaller blaze near Brignoles in the week forced actor George Clooney and his family, along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control.



Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said France’s fires were generally under control but warned that conditions remained volatile. He appointed a national coordinator to oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. Related Article Bushfires George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage More than 1170 square kilometres have burned across France this year. Spain’s major fires – which have killed at least 13 people, produced the country’s largest recorded wildfire and prompted a national emergency – were no longer advancing on Sunday. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called for a national pact to confront wildfires, warning that climate change is making them increasingly destructive.
