World.title: Coercion, control and high demands: How cults squash their members’ identities
World.content:
A 15-month parliamentary inquiry has defined what a “high-control” organisation is and proposed that their leaders be subject to criminal charges. How it might work is another question.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Laura McConnell was kicked out of her family and the religious cult they raised her in, she went to Centrelink so she could feed herself, a counsellor to work through her issues, and a doctor for a check-up. None of them understood what she was telling them. Laura McConnell, who was kicked out of the Two-by-Twos cult as a teenager. “They just didn’t have the vocabulary,” McConnell says. She was a teenager, so Centrelink wanted a form signed by a parent or guardian – which was impossible. The GP said, “All the women in your religion are depressed – I don’t know what to do for you.” The counsellor gave McConnell the number of a priest, but her group relied on lay preachers, so she “grew up thinking that, to speak to a priest is to speak to the devil”. “I just shut down and didn’t talk to a counsellor for years because I thought that’s where I’d be sent … I found myself in a world I didn’t know anything about, with no language to describe what had happened to me.” All this happened 27 years ago, but McConnell said she helped people leaving the group today who still struggled with the same problems.



Children’s ‘entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it’. Crossing the line: Coercion and harm in high‑control groups McConnell was born and raised in an ultra-strict Christian sect known as Two-by-Twos – but ignorance about the practices of such “high-control groups” is almost universal. Last week, a Victorian parliamentary committee tried to find a language to combat that ignorance. It defined the features of groups sometimes known as cults, and recommended better training for police and child protection workers. It also recommended the Law Reform Commission formulate a new criminal offence for “group-based coercion” to prosecute the leaders of such groups. Patrick McIvor, a former member of a high-control organisation and a counsellor and policy consultant, said “the development of shared language that we haven’t had before” was the committee’s most significant finding. Patrick McIvor, former member of City Builders church and now a counsellor and policy consultant. “People have talked about this experience of not being able to know or name what they’ve been through, especially kids who have grown up in this environment,” McIvor said. “They have felt they’ve had to try to translate themselves into existing categories or terms that people understand.”



It’s unclear how many people are part of high-control groups, but the committee chair, Labor MP Ella George, said her 15-month inquiry had received more than 600 submissions and responses to questions from Victorians, and “to me that speaks to the size of the issue”. George said she had found the evidence she’d heard “heartbreaking and devastating”. Related Article Victorian Parliament Laws failing to protect cult survivors, inquiry finds Her report says the beliefs of these groups are almost immaterial – they can be “religious, commercial enterprise, therapeutic or wellness communities, or any other type of group structure”. What makes them a problem are their practices. The committee found the coercive control these groups exercise over their members – whether they are born into them or are recruited – suppresses their capacity to act, think or live independently. The groups demand ideological or religious purity, they surveil and monitor their members’ activities and patrol their thoughts. They also foster an “us versus them” mindset towards the broader community. The threat of public humiliation or excommunication fosters fear and keeps people under the thumb. Cumulatively, it means members rely on the group for their identity, self-worth, morality, and decision-making – while questioning and critical thinking are punished.



The committee found these practices caused life-long psychological damage. People live in a state of threat, anxiety and hypervigilance, often even well after they have left the group. The erosion of individual autonomy and self‑trust means people often struggle to form or maintain their identity. Related Article Explainer

Psychology Why do people join cults? And how do they get out of them? Children, such as McConnell, who were born into such groups were even more vulnerable than those who were recruited. “Their entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it,” the committee found. Children schooled at home or by the group are worse off because of severely constrained access to “safe adults” outside the group. Healthy groups, by contrast, were transparent and gave their members choice and the freedom to question or refuse, and the ability to leave the group without fear of punishment, the report found. “People also have the right to be free from religion,” McIvor said. Cassie Davies, who was born into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, said the church’s practices had suppressed her identity, and, as a woman, had “boxed me in” to a framework of what was acceptable and not acceptable.



“The suppression of any sort of sexual exploration, the complete taboo of the subject, all of that is completely emotionally abusive of children,” she added. Cassie Davies, who is happily out of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church. Establishing who to blame, though, was complex, Davies said. “Who’s the perpetrator? My mum is – but that’s because she believes that’s right, and that’s how her identity has been formed.” Davies did not give evidence to the Victorian parliamentary inquiry. A Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman said the church had not been approached by the committee, and “its report and findings have nothing at all to do with our church”. Asked about coercive practices, the spokesman said “none of this describes life in our church. This report is not about us.” Related Article Exclusive

Investigations God, Christ, man, woman: The ‘divine order’ that defines life for Exclusive Brethren women Among the committee’s recommendations are that the charities regulator, ACNC, abolish the category of “basic religious charity”, under which a number of high-control organisations are exempt from key governance and reporting obligations. The committee said its proposed new criminal offence would be similar to coercive control offences for family violence that have been introduced in some jurisdictions and promised in Victoria, but different in crucial ways.

World.title: ‘He’s unbelievably sexist’: Brit TV star tackles his toughest role yet
World.content:
CultureMusicalsStage shows ‘He’s unbelievably sexist’: Brit TV star tackles his toughest role yet Kerrie O'Brien August 3, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite having won some of Britain and America’s highest theatre awards, and performing opposite Helen Mirren and Dustin Hoffman, Nathaniel Parker has never sung on stage. That’s all about to change: the English actor best-known to Australian audiences for his roles in the BBC’s The Inspector Lynley Mysteries and Merlin is set to make his musical theatre debut in My Fair Lady in Sydney next month. Nathaniel Parker will star as Professor Henry Higgins alongside Australian soprano Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady, which opens in September. Simon Schluter “I’m like a kid in a comedy store. This is a whole new game,” he says. “This is like, I don’t know, it’s like a promotion towards the end of my career.” Playing Eliza Dolittle is Melbourne-based Claire Lyon, no stranger to musical theatre. Best known for playing Christine in The Phantom of the Opera, the soprano says it’s the role of a lifetime. She spends 85 per cent of the show on stage and must master not only a Cockney accent but that of a plummy English toff as well. Luckily, her mum and grandparents are from north London, so something of the accent is in her DNA.



My Fair Lady tells the story of a flower seller on the streets of London being “discovered” by professor of phonetics Henry Higgins, who makes a bet with a friend that he can transform her from a poor commoner into a duchess. Julie Andrews and Rex Harrison in the original stage production of ‘My Fair Lady’. Over the years, the show has been criticised for being misogynistic; back home in England when Parker talked about playing Higgins, several people described the character as exactly that. But the 64-year-old disagrees. “I think that’s the wrong word,” he says. “He’s sexist, unbelievably sexist. The most sexist man I’ve ever played – and I played Henry VIII for two years [in the stage adaptations of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall books]. But he doesn’t hate women. He doesn’t hate his mother, he doesn’t hate Mrs Pearce. He just doesn’t understand the first thing about them, so he’s kept them at a distance.” That said, Parker admits he is “still figuring out the way to say those awfully sexist lines” that come up. “I can feel myself being punched by various friends of mine,” he says. “I think the reason he gets that extreme is because he doesn’t understand the turmoil inside that this woman has caused.”



Lyon argues that the musical, which is based on George Bernard Shaw’s play Pygmalion, written in 1913 at the height of the Suffragette movement, was created and is set in a very different era and should be honoured as an historical work of art, not altered to suit contemporary norms. When she and Parker spoke with Dame Julie Andrews (who at 20 played Eliza in the original Broadway version) via Zoom last week, they discussed its origins. “Things have been tweaked for sure, but I think of Eliza as an incredibly strong young woman. She’s a fighter. She speaks her mind,” Lyon says. “She stands up to a man who is in a different class to her, who’s her senior, and she holds her own. She fights back, and wins him over in the end.” Australian stage royalty Reg Livermore and Robyn Nevin also appear in the much-loved musical, as Alfred P. Doolittle and Mrs Higgins respectively, with Tony Llewellyn-Jones as Colonel Hugh Pickering. Anne Wood plays Mrs Pearce, David Whitney is Karpathy, and Freddy Hellier makes his main stage musical theatre debut as Freddy Eynsford-Hill.



For Parker and Lyon, My Fair Lady is one of the best musicals ever written. It nails all the key components; the writing, the songs and the choreography, not to mention the costumes, are glorious, says Lyon. It’s a feast for the ears, a feast for the eyes and great for the soul, she adds. Classic numbers include Wouldn’t It Be Loverly, The Rain in Spain, I Could Have Danced All Night and Higgins’ infamous Why Can’t a Woman Be More Like a Man? Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle. When the Lerner and Loewe production premiered on Broadway in 1956 starring Andrews as Eliza and Rex Harrison as Higgins, it was an instant hit, winning six Tony Awards. Audrey Hepburn starred in the lead role in the 1964 film version, with Harrison again as the professor; ghost singer Marni Nixon sang Hepburn’s songs. Now celebrating its 70th anniversary, the show is directed by Karen Johnson Mortimer; it is presented by Opera Australia and John Frost.



Parker quips that none of his songs are well-known because Harrison spoke rather than sang them in his portrayals. The British veteran of stage and screen no doubt hopes that will change when Australian audiences see him make his musical debut, the first time in decades he’s sung outside his dressing room. My Fair Lady is at the Sydney Opera House from September and Arts Centre Melbourne from November. Details: opera.org.au

World.title: ASX set to slip; Amazon soars, Apple sinks on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip; Amazon soars, Apple sinks on Wall Street Stan Choe August 3, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose to finish a wild July for Wall Street as Amazon leaped, Apple sank and rising oil prices worsened worries about inflation staying high. The S&P 500 climbed 0.7 per cent after veering between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones added 276 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1 per cent after briefly losing all of an early 1.3 per cent jump. Wall Street closed a losing month with gains on Friday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to start the week lower, with futures on Saturday pointing to a loss of 85 points, or 1 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.55¢. August reporting season kicks into gear this week, with News Corp and AMP among those due up. It’s a fitting finish to July for the US stock market, which lurched up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and worries grew about whether Big Tech’s massive investments in artificial-intelligence technology will translate into profits and whether chipmaker stocks soared too high in the euphoria around AI.



Friday’s gains sent the S&P 500 to its first winning week in three, but the main measure of the US stock market nevertheless finished the month with a tiny loss. Amazon led the market with a leap of 15.3 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its profit more than tripled from a year earlier, thanks in part to an acceleration of growth in its cloud computing business. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Healthscope meets landlords to head off private equity break-up threat Analysts said that could be a signal Amazon’s huge AI investments are paying off, and Amazon increased its forecast for how much it will spend on investments this year. The reaction was similar to what Microsoft got a day before, when its stock soared to its best day in nearly 18 years on signals that its AI investments may also be yielding higher profits.



Chip companies selling the processors and computer memory that such “hyperscalers” are scrambling to buy swung sharply again on Friday. Micron Technology, for example, went from an early jump of 6.4 per cent to a loss of 6.5 per cent before finishing with a fall of 5.9 per cent. More firmly on the losing end of Wall Street was Apple, which dropped 7.4 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than expected. Its forecast for revenue growth in the current quarter fell short of expectations, which executives pinned on a supply crunch in components getting vacuumed up in the AI boom. All told, the S&P 500 rose 52.09 points to 7,489.72. The Dow Jones added 276.97 to 52,485.03, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 251.68 to 25,373.85. The gains came despite another rise in oil prices as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again from the Middle East. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1.2 per cent to settle at $US87.93 after careening between $US72 and $US102 earlier in July.



Higher oil prices have pushed the cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.11 across the United States, up from $US3.85 a month ago, according to AAA. More expensive oil also puts upward pressure on prices for virtually every product that rides on a ship, plane or truck before getting to a customer. The worries about inflation sent yields in the bond market even higher. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.71 per cent from 4.68 per cent late Thursday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran sent oil prices shooting higher. That’s a notable move for the yield, which moves higher when investors’ expectations for inflation, economic growth and other factors in upcoming years are rising. The leap for the 10-year yield has already sent the average long-term US mortgage rate to its highest level in a year. Longer-term yields jumped on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve’s chairman, Kevin Warsh, promised again to get inflation back down to 2 per cent but refused to say how he plans to get it there. The Fed voted again to keep its main interest rate steady on Wednesday, even though inflation remains well above 2 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Whistleblowers The dismantling of KPMG is about to begin Colin Kruger Senior business reporter Hikes to rates by the Fed could restrain inflation, but they could also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates instead of higher. Warsh has told financial markets that he does not want to give hints about what the Fed will do with interest rates, saying he wants to get direct, “unfiltered” messages from them rather than echoes back of what the Fed has suggested. But “without clarifying why action was or wasn’t taken already, it’s hard to see how statements about being committed to hitting its inflation target aren’t just a bluff,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. “The Fed is facing a growing credibility problem,” economists at Bank of America wrote in a report. Unless data comes in showing less pressure on inflation in the interim, “it is imperative for the Fed to pass the September test by hiking rates and delivering an internally consistent narrative.”



In stock markets abroad, the swings were even wilder for chip stocks. Seoul’s Kospi index soared 17.9 per cent for its best day in history. The index is dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and both surged at least 26.8 per cent on Friday. The Kospi, though, still lost 22 per cent in July despite Friday’s historic move. That’s after it more than doubled in the first six months of the year. World.title: I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of
World.content:
InspirationBali I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of Nina Karnikowski August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two weeks before leaving for Ubud, I was already hyperventilating about Bali’s crowds. As someone who spends much of their life chasing quietude, just the thought of the over-development and the Instagrammable chaos made me twitch. Cottages at Kul Kul Farm. Nina Karnikowski So when a friend told me about Sibang – describing it as Ubud’s calmer cousin and the way it might have been 30 years ago – I was in. Now, waiting for said friend on a dirt road corner with just an ancient temple to my left and jungle to my right, I’m glad I’ve come. That Sibang (which actually encompasses two villages, Sibang Kaja and Sibang Gede) has stayed under the radar is no accident. “Locals have told us about a curse that was placed on the village many years ago, by an angry giant who threatened that it would one day be swallowed by ants,” my friend says. “It’s said the villagers fled because of this, and the jungle took over.” The story lingered for decades, leaving Sibang quiet and largely overlooked – until Canadian John Hardy arrived to build Green School Bali.



Green School’s bamboo campus, which offers eco-focused education to about 500 local and international students from kindergarten to year 12, put the village on the map when it opened in 2008. My friend, who’s living in Sibang, so her son can attend the school, walks me down the street flanking the campus. Aside from local homes and a couple of sleepy cafes, a sustainability-focused concept store named Muka, and a slick year-old villa stay called Mahajiva, there is, happily, not much here. 



Each April, Kul Kul runs a 10-day bamboo-building course, teaching about a material that restores land, grows rapidly, and sequesters carbon. Student-built curving structures, five of which are newly open to guests, are dotted between beds of lettuce, tomato, chilli and eggplant. Much of this produce lands on plates at Taani, Kul Kul’s new restaurant where I slurp the best soto (a warming turmeric-spiced soup) I’ve ever had in Indonesia. Inside a cottage at Kul Kul Farm. Next afternoon I walk to Astungkara Way, a regenerative rice-farming collective. Twenty minutes from Kul Kul Farm, the road dissolves into paddies alive with birdsong and the loamy scent of turned earth. Here, travellers learn how rice is grown the natural way. This means ducks instead of pesticides, compost instead of chemicals, and respect for the Subak system, a co-operative irrigation network that has sustained Bali’s farmers for centuries. “Look around,” says manager Oka Dewanti, spreading her arms wide to the rice paddies rolling out around us. “This is what Ubud or Canggu was 30 years ago.” She speaks of the heartbreak of watching development swallow farmland, the urgency of bringing youth back to agriculture, and how travellers can support the kind of Bali they want to see. To that end, alongside hands-on farming courses, Astungkara Way leads multi-day walking journeys that begin in the thick of traffic and development, and slowly carry travellers back to the Bali that once was. Strolling back to Kul Kul in the indigo evening light, past boys fishing in irrigation canals and women carrying baskets of offerings towards local temples, I worry about what Sibang might lose as more travellers arrive. Change is already gathering at its edges. But if places like Kul Kul Farm and Astungkara Way set the tone for what’s to come, maybe this village has a fighting chance to remain the kind of Bali travellers dream about, rather than the kind we flee.

World.title: Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
NationalWALocal government Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know Hannah Murphy August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian councils could soon get the green light to force roaming cats indoors — but right now, a pet’s freedom depends entirely on which council it lives in. Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley announced plans to change the law to allow local councils to introduce cat containment laws in February. WA’s cats could soon be forced to stay on their own properties. Nick Moir Under the current law, councils need to get permission from a parliamentary committee to introduce changes to their local regulations. More than 20 councils have tried to make their own laws about keeping cats inside in the past, but only three have been successful - all in regional WA.



As a result, the cat laws in each local government differ greatly. Ahead of the planned law change, we asked every Perth metropolitan council what their state of play is when it comes to outdoor cats. Here’s what they told us: The Town of Claremont was the only local council who refused to comment on their current cat laws, and whether it had ever tried to get them changed previously.



Councils said cats were currently banned from upwards of 300 Perth reserves, parks and protected bushland area across the metropolitan area. Nearly all councils have limits on the number of cats people can own, and a select few have trapping programs conducted by rangers for “nuisance” cats. The changes to the 2011 Cat Act are only partway through the parliamentary process, but under its powers, local councils could order owners to: restrict cats to their owners’ premises;

prohibit cats from all public areas;

place conditions on when a cat may be permitted in a public area;

introduce cat curfews; and

require cats to be under the effective control of their owners or contained if leaving their owners’ property. However, Cat Haven chief executive Roz Robinson said it would be interesting to see how any changes would actually worked in practice. “It is interesting times with the review of the cat act coming up and it is interesting to note that whilst many councils are talking about cat containment being part of the cat laws, so many local governments do not enforce the current act,” she said.



“For example, I have it in writing from one western suburbs’ council, when faced with an enquiry from one of their residences about a stray cat, they simply refer them onto us.” Roz Robinson is the chief executive officer of Perth’s Cat Haven. Robinson said the not-for-profit organisation was extremely supportive of cat containment laws, saying it not only improves cat welfare but would ease pressure on the service. “With over 50 per cent of our intake coming in as strays, if we had proper containment laws, it would result in a reduction in these numbers,” she said. However, Robinson also argued any change with the Cat Act needed to focus heavily on the benefits of de-sexing household cats.



“Over 80 per cent of these strays – most friendly re-homable cats – are un-desexed. Un-desexed cats wander – they become strays in their need to mate. “You don’t have to be a mathematician to work out cats are prolific breeders and what numbers would look like without de-sexing. Related Article Exclusive

Biodiversity The staggering death toll of roaming pet cats finally revealed “For years we have been trying to de-sex our way out of the cat problem, but with little appetite from others to assist, we are literally fighting a losing battle.” She said there had to be continual state government funding towards spaying cats, as well as supporting the Cat Haven to deal with stray animals. Currently, she said the government provides just less than two per cent of the charity’s operating costs.



“What changes do we see after the review? It really depends if all stakeholders are serious about improving cat welfare or is it just another review being ticked off,” Robinson said. “Our intake numbers are increasing annually – 8 per cent while the population is only growing two per cent – our site is not fit for purpose, and can only be described as dilapidated. There is no funding forthcoming to improve the site. “We are an open admission shelter, we never say no to any cat and truly believe every cat does matter and want to give them all a second chance. But something has to give.”

World.title: Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying
World.content:
Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying Remember these simple tips and ingredients when grocery shopping and meal-prepping to boost your dietary fibre intake without overthinking it. Susie Burrell August 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Health trends may come and go faster than you can say “TikTok made me do it”, but current darling, dietary fibre, is the real deal. From a renewed focus on supporting digestive health and immune function with gut health superfoods, to fibremaxxing, there is plenty of noise that all comes back to one simple concept: eat more fibre. Here are some easy ways to do that every day without even trying. Use multgrain bread for your sandwiches like Neil Perry’s tuna number. William Meppem Upgrade your carbs Whether it’s cereal for breakfast, or a sandwich or wrap for lunch, the key to optimising your daily intake of dietary fibre is to ensure your daily staples have a wholegrain or wholemeal base. Often, we find ourselves picking up foods on the go, and in most cases, the carbs on offer are white, and as such not offering nearly as much fibre as we need. Bread and wraps



Swap white, sourdough, or plain wraps for high-fibre wholemeal, multigrain, rye, or seed-packed options. As a reference, your daily bread or wraps should be adding at least 3-5g of dietary fibre per serve and while sourdough may sound healthier, generally the options at cafes and bakeries are made with white flour. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Breakfast staples Choose multigrain or high-bran cereals over refined varieties, and toss oats or bran straight into smoothies. When checking breakfast cereal or granola packets, keep in mind that the higher percentage of wholegrains the breakfast cereal offers, the higher the natural dietary fibre content will be. Natural sources of dietary fibre from wholegrains, seeds, fruits and nuts are better options nutritionally than more processed dietary fibre like chicory root and insulin which are often added to bars, cereals and breads to increase the fibre content. Opt for brown rice over white, like in Katrina Meynink’s chickpea, brown rice and greens salad. Katrina Meynink



Pasta and rice There is a growing range of wholemeal, wholegrain and legume pasta options which are all significantly higher in fibre than regular white pasta. In the case of rice, seek out brown or black varieties where possible, or one of the growing ranges of mixed grain and rice quick-cook options that can offer as much as 5-8g of dietary fibre per serve, compared to less than 1g for regular white rice. Can you guess the hidden veg in Jill Dupleix’s spaghetti bolognese? Sneak vegies into every meal With fewer than one in 10 Aussies getting the recommended five serves of vegetables a day, and even less the 7-10 serves to support the goal of optimal health and longevity, there are plenty of reasons including boosting our intake of dietary fibre that come from increasing veggie intake across all of our meals.



Grate and blend Adding a mix of grated zucchini and carrots, or spinach or silverbeet, into scrambled eggs, pasta sauce bases like bolognese, porridge, or smoothies not only significantly increases nutrient intake, but fibre intake as well. Frozen spinach and kale can also be cost-effective options that slip easily into a number of meals without negatively impacting the flavour. Keep the skins on Whether you are mashing vegetables, adding them to smoothies or grating them into dishes, you get extra dietary fibre from vegetables when you leave the skin on. The same goes for fruits, and if you are especially keen, the skins on nutrient-packed kiwifruit and bananas are edible, too. Related Article Canned, pouched and fresh: A dietitian’s guide to the best (and worst) supermarket chicken soups



Know the easy add-ins Budget-friendly and fibre-rich frozen peas can be added to a wide range of mixed dishes including pasta, risotto and stir-fries. Baby cucumbers and carrots are an easy side to enjoy with your favourite sandwich or wrap, while a starter of pre-made vegetable-rich soups add extra nutrients and dietary fibre to any main meal. Make your own baked beans, like Adam Liaw’s, and get a big fibre boose. William Meppem Learn to love legumes If there is one food Aussies should be eating more of, if only for the cost-effective nature of such a nutrient-rich food, it is legumes. There are so many varieties that can easily be worked into many meals, whilst adding loads of protein and dietary fibre.



Swap in with mince Whether you are making spaghetti bolognese, chilli con carne or a sang choy bao, throw in a can of your favourite beans to make any amount of mince go a lot further. Embrace baked beans Ever-versatile baked beans can be added to any hot breakfast, enjoyed with crackers or even as a light meal, adding a massive 6-8 grams of dietary fibre per serve. If you prefer lower sugar options, it is also easy to make your own using a cannellini or white beans. Eat more edamame



Soy beans are especially nutrient rich, and an easy addition to all of your favourite Asian dishes whether they are enjoyed as a side dish with sushi, added to salads or even as a dried, protein-packed snack. Sprinkle chia seeds and nuts onto your cereal. iStock Sprinkle in seeds and nuts Not only are seeds and nuts extremely nutrient rich — offering nutrients including zinc, selenium, magnesium and plant-based omega-3s — but they are also rich in dietary fibre. Breakfast boosters



Stir a tablespoon of chia, flaxseed or pepitas into any mix of cereal, oats, yoghurt or smoothies for a protein, fibre and good fat hit. Or opt for one of the growing ranges of breakfast toppers or nut spreads which offer a mix of nuts and seeds, and as such a mix of nutrients. Related Article Sprinkle these tiny seeds on just about anything for a mighty nutrition punch Your favourite salads A little crunch goes a long way in a salad, and a few roasted nuts or a sprinkle of seeds adds texture and flavour to any salad. Even better, try roasting your favourite nuts or seeds with a little honey or maple syrup for an even tastier salad topper. A go-to snack

World.title: Two killed as firefighting helicopters collide in Greece
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires Two killed as firefighting helicopters collide in Greece Elena Becatoros and Thomas Adamson August 3, 2026 — 7:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Athens: Two Greek firefighting helicopters collided in midair as they were battling a wind-driven wildfire west of Athens, sending one aircraft crashing to the ground. Two crew members, a Greek and a Danish national, died in the crash. The collision on Sunday (Greek time) laid bare the danger at the most volatile front of Europe’s wildfire emergency. Strong winds drove flames deeper into the region of the Greek capital and forced fresh evacuations, France guarded a still-burning scar four times the size of Paris, while Spain’s major fires stopped advancing. Loading Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed “sorrow for the tragic accident” and extended condolences to the families of the firefighters killed in the crash.



“The loss of the Greek coordinator and the Danish pilot at the time they were attempting the major fire in Porto Gremeno fills us all with grief,” Mitsotakis said in a statement. The aircraft were Bell helicopters operating over the Psatha area west of Athens, each with a two-person crew. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires during the country’s hot, dry summers. Wreckage of the helicopter lies on a road near Psatha. Hellenic Red Cross/Facebook The Guardian reported that the helicopters involved had been leased from Australia’s McDermott Aviation and were part of a fleet of 15. Video posted online and reported in Greek media appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames.



The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not yet verified the authenticity of the footage. The two crew members who were recovered alive were a Greek and a British national. A firefighter stands as flames rising during a wildfire near Porto Germeno, northwest of Athens, on Sunday. AP Photo/Michael Varaklas The flames had spread rapidly, threatening communities and an industrial district as violent gusts prevented firefighting aircraft from collecting water from the sea. The blaze carried a grim resonance in a region where the 2018 Mati wildfire killed 104 people, Europe’s deadliest blaze this century. Farther west, containment brought no end to the emergency. France’s largest wildfire remained held within its perimeter after forcing 224,000 people to flee in what may have been the country’s largest civilian evacuation outside wartime.



Hot spots still burned within a 420-square-kilometre scar, thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde megafire and a second, still-uncontained blaze in Provence. Together, fires in France and Spain have driven about a third of a million people from homes and vacation sites, emptied communities at the height of the European summer and stretched emergency services across simultaneous disasters. Firefighters work at the site where firefighting helicopters crashed on Sunday. EPA The mass evacuations in France and Spain are the latest measure of a wildfire threat growing across Europe. The continent entered 2026 after its worst fire year on record, with more than 10,000 square kilometres burned in 2025. Over the past four decades, wildfires have been linked to nearly 800 deaths across much of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency.



Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent. It has warmed more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Human-caused climate change made the extreme fire-weather conditions behind this year’s French blazes at least twice as likely, scientists at World Weather Attribution found in a rapid analysis conducted while the fires were still burning. A firefighting helicopter drops water over a smoke-filled forest during a wildfire near Porto Germeno. AP Photo/Michael Varaklas In Greece, nearly 500 firefighters and 23 aircraft were deployed, but gale-force winds drove flames through dry forest and crippled the response, preventing some aircraft from reaching the sea to collect water. Authorities ordered the evacuation of Kandili, Agia Skepi and Toutouli as smoke rose over the mountains. Crews were particularly concerned about Porto Germeno, a seaside community on the Gulf of Corinth.



The fire began on Friday near Agios Vasileios before sweeping toward Porto Germeno and into the forested mountains west of Athens. Firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea Friday and another 12 Saturday – often the last escape route when fire and smoke cut the few roads from coastal communities. Related Article Exclusive

Bushfires ‘It looked like an atomic bomb’: The Aussie pilots flying into a French firestorm Elsewhere in Greece, flames threatened homes on Kefalonia, forcing evacuations from inland communities as aircraft made water drops over the Ionian island. Firefighters battled another blaze near Nea Tenedos on the peninsula of Halkidiki. Earlier this week, two firefighters died fighting a fire on Crete, while a third was killed on the Peloponnese. In south-western France, the Gironde megafire remained held within its perimeter on Sunday but continued to burn after scorching 420 square kilometres of forest in 10 days.



“The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped. The region remained under France’s highest red forest-fire alert. Dry conditions, soaring temperatures around Bordeaux and afternoon winds threatened to rekindle the flames. A volunteer tries to extinguish small flames northwest of Athens. AP Photo/Michael Varaklas In Le Porge, local officials said about 150 homes were destroyed. Mechanic Matthieu Plessis returned Saturday to the ruins of a house that had been in his family for seven generations. “There are places I don’t even recognise anymore,” he said. “You don’t even know what was here anymore, or who lived where.”



Firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation. Related Article Bushfires Emergency warnings as US west battles wildfires, extreme heat In south-eastern France, nearly 1500 firefighters battled a separate blaze in the Var department that tore through about 18 square kilometres in little more than a day. The Gros Bessillon fire was stabilised Sunday after its perimeter held overnight, but it remained uncontained. Some 2500 people were evacuated as flames threatened nearby communities. It was the fourth major fire to strike central Var since July 19. A smaller blaze near Brignoles in the week forced actor George Clooney and his family, along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control.



Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said France’s fires were generally under control but warned that conditions remained volatile. He appointed a national coordinator to oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. Related Article Bushfires George and Amal Clooney flee luxury French home as wildfires rage More than 1170 square kilometres have burned across France this year. Spain’s major fires – which have killed at least 13 people, produced the country’s largest recorded wildfire and prompted a national emergency – were no longer advancing on Sunday. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called for a national pact to confront wildfires, warning that climate change is making them increasingly destructive.

World.title: Coercion, control and high demands: How cults squash their members’ identities
World.content:
A 15-month parliamentary inquiry has defined what a “high-control” organisation is and proposed that their leaders be subject to criminal charges. How it might work is another question.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Laura McConnell was kicked out of her family and the religious cult they raised her in, she went to Centrelink so she could feed herself, a counsellor to work through her issues, and a doctor for a check-up. None of them understood what she was telling them. Laura McConnell, who was kicked out of the Two-by-Twos cult as a teenager. “They just didn’t have the vocabulary,” McConnell says. She was a teenager, so Centrelink wanted a form signed by a parent or guardian – which was impossible. The GP said, “All the women in your religion are depressed – I don’t know what to do for you.” The counsellor gave McConnell the number of a priest, but her group relied on lay preachers, so she “grew up thinking that, to speak to a priest is to speak to the devil”. “I just shut down and didn’t talk to a counsellor for years because I thought that’s where I’d be sent … I found myself in a world I didn’t know anything about, with no language to describe what had happened to me.” All this happened 27 years ago, but McConnell said she helped people leaving the group today who still struggled with the same problems.



Children’s ‘entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it’. Crossing the line: Coercion and harm in high‑control groups McConnell was born and raised in an ultra-strict Christian sect known as Two-by-Twos – but ignorance about the practices of such “high-control groups” is almost universal. Last week, a Victorian parliamentary committee tried to find a language to combat that ignorance. It defined the features of groups sometimes known as cults, and recommended better training for police and child protection workers. It also recommended the Law Reform Commission formulate a new criminal offence for “group-based coercion” to prosecute the leaders of such groups. Patrick McIvor, a former member of a high-control organisation and a counsellor and policy consultant, said “the development of shared language that we haven’t had before” was the committee’s most significant finding. Patrick McIvor, former member of City Builders church and now a counsellor and policy consultant. “People have talked about this experience of not being able to know or name what they’ve been through, especially kids who have grown up in this environment,” McIvor said. “They have felt they’ve had to try to translate themselves into existing categories or terms that people understand.”



It’s unclear how many people are part of high-control groups, but the committee chair, Labor MP Ella George, said her 15-month inquiry had received more than 600 submissions and responses to questions from Victorians, and “to me that speaks to the size of the issue”. George said she had found the evidence she’d heard “heartbreaking and devastating”. Related Article Victorian Parliament Laws failing to protect cult survivors, inquiry finds Her report says the beliefs of these groups are almost immaterial – they can be “religious, commercial enterprise, therapeutic or wellness communities, or any other type of group structure”. What makes them a problem are their practices. The committee found the coercive control these groups exercise over their members – whether they are born into them or are recruited – suppresses their capacity to act, think or live independently. The groups demand ideological or religious purity, they surveil and monitor their members’ activities and patrol their thoughts. They also foster an “us versus them” mindset towards the broader community. The threat of public humiliation or excommunication fosters fear and keeps people under the thumb. Cumulatively, it means members rely on the group for their identity, self-worth, morality, and decision-making – while questioning and critical thinking are punished.



The committee found these practices caused life-long psychological damage. People live in a state of threat, anxiety and hypervigilance, often even well after they have left the group. The erosion of individual autonomy and self‑trust means people often struggle to form or maintain their identity. Related Article Explainer

Psychology Why do people join cults? And how do they get out of them? Children, such as McConnell, who were born into such groups were even more vulnerable than those who were recruited. “Their entire sense of self, relationships, and worldview are constructed by the group before they have the capacity to question it,” the committee found. Children schooled at home or by the group are worse off because of severely constrained access to “safe adults” outside the group. Healthy groups, by contrast, were transparent and gave their members choice and the freedom to question or refuse, and the ability to leave the group without fear of punishment, the report found. “People also have the right to be free from religion,” McIvor said. Cassie Davies, who was born into the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, said the church’s practices had suppressed her identity, and, as a woman, had “boxed me in” to a framework of what was acceptable and not acceptable.



“The suppression of any sort of sexual exploration, the complete taboo of the subject, all of that is completely emotionally abusive of children,” she added. Cassie Davies, who is happily out of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church. Establishing who to blame, though, was complex, Davies said. “Who’s the perpetrator? My mum is – but that’s because she believes that’s right, and that’s how her identity has been formed.” Davies did not give evidence to the Victorian parliamentary inquiry. A Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman said the church had not been approached by the committee, and “its report and findings have nothing at all to do with our church”. Asked about coercive practices, the spokesman said “none of this describes life in our church. This report is not about us.” Related Article Exclusive

Investigations God, Christ, man, woman: The ‘divine order’ that defines life for Exclusive Brethren women Among the committee’s recommendations are that the charities regulator, ACNC, abolish the category of “basic religious charity”, under which a number of high-control organisations are exempt from key governance and reporting obligations. The committee said its proposed new criminal offence would be similar to coercive control offences for family violence that have been introduced in some jurisdictions and promised in Victoria, but different in crucial ways.

World.title: ‘He’s unbelievably sexist’: Brit TV star tackles his toughest role yet
World.content:
CultureMusicalsStage shows ‘He’s unbelievably sexist’: Brit TV star tackles his toughest role yet Kerrie O'Brien August 3, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite having won some of Britain and America’s highest theatre awards, and performing opposite Helen Mirren and Dustin Hoffman, Nathaniel Parker has never sung on stage. That’s all about to change: the English actor best-known to Australian audiences for his roles in the BBC’s The Inspector Lynley Mysteries and Merlin is set to make his musical theatre debut in My Fair Lady in Sydney next month. Nathaniel Parker will star as Professor Henry Higgins alongside Australian soprano Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady, which opens in September. Simon Schluter “I’m like a kid in a comedy store. This is a whole new game,” he says. “This is like, I don’t know, it’s like a promotion towards the end of my career.” Playing Eliza Dolittle is Melbourne-based Claire Lyon, no stranger to musical theatre. Best known for playing Christine in The Phantom of the Opera, the soprano says it’s the role of a lifetime. She spends 85 per cent of the show on stage and must master not only a Cockney accent but that of a plummy English toff as well. Luckily, her mum and grandparents are from north London, so something of the accent is in her DNA.



My Fair Lady tells the story of a flower seller on the streets of London being “discovered” by professor of phonetics Henry Higgins, who makes a bet with a friend that he can transform her from a poor commoner into a duchess. Julie Andrews and Rex Harrison in the original stage production of ‘My Fair Lady’. Over the years, the show has been criticised for being misogynistic; back home in England when Parker talked about playing Higgins, several people described the character as exactly that. But the 64-year-old disagrees. “I think that’s the wrong word,” he says. “He’s sexist, unbelievably sexist. The most sexist man I’ve ever played – and I played Henry VIII for two years [in the stage adaptations of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall books]. But he doesn’t hate women. He doesn’t hate his mother, he doesn’t hate Mrs Pearce. He just doesn’t understand the first thing about them, so he’s kept them at a distance.” That said, Parker admits he is “still figuring out the way to say those awfully sexist lines” that come up. “I can feel myself being punched by various friends of mine,” he says. “I think the reason he gets that extreme is because he doesn’t understand the turmoil inside that this woman has caused.”



Lyon argues that the musical, which is based on George Bernard Shaw’s play Pygmalion, written in 1913 at the height of the Suffragette movement, was created and is set in a very different era and should be honoured as an historical work of art, not altered to suit contemporary norms. When she and Parker spoke with Dame Julie Andrews (who at 20 played Eliza in the original Broadway version) via Zoom last week, they discussed its origins. “Things have been tweaked for sure, but I think of Eliza as an incredibly strong young woman. She’s a fighter. She speaks her mind,” Lyon says. “She stands up to a man who is in a different class to her, who’s her senior, and she holds her own. She fights back, and wins him over in the end.” Australian stage royalty Reg Livermore and Robyn Nevin also appear in the much-loved musical, as Alfred P. Doolittle and Mrs Higgins respectively, with Tony Llewellyn-Jones as Colonel Hugh Pickering. Anne Wood plays Mrs Pearce, David Whitney is Karpathy, and Freddy Hellier makes his main stage musical theatre debut as Freddy Eynsford-Hill.



For Parker and Lyon, My Fair Lady is one of the best musicals ever written. It nails all the key components; the writing, the songs and the choreography, not to mention the costumes, are glorious, says Lyon. It’s a feast for the ears, a feast for the eyes and great for the soul, she adds. Classic numbers include Wouldn’t It Be Loverly, The Rain in Spain, I Could Have Danced All Night and Higgins’ infamous Why Can’t a Woman Be More Like a Man? Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle. When the Lerner and Loewe production premiered on Broadway in 1956 starring Andrews as Eliza and Rex Harrison as Higgins, it was an instant hit, winning six Tony Awards. Audrey Hepburn starred in the lead role in the 1964 film version, with Harrison again as the professor; ghost singer Marni Nixon sang Hepburn’s songs. Now celebrating its 70th anniversary, the show is directed by Karen Johnson Mortimer; it is presented by Opera Australia and John Frost.



Parker quips that none of his songs are well-known because Harrison spoke rather than sang them in his portrayals. The British veteran of stage and screen no doubt hopes that will change when Australian audiences see him make his musical debut, the first time in decades he’s sung outside his dressing room. My Fair Lady is at the Sydney Opera House from September and Arts Centre Melbourne from November. Details: opera.org.au

World.title: ASX set to slip; Amazon soars, Apple sinks on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip; Amazon soars, Apple sinks on Wall Street Stan Choe August 3, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose to finish a wild July for Wall Street as Amazon leaped, Apple sank and rising oil prices worsened worries about inflation staying high. The S&P 500 climbed 0.7 per cent after veering between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones added 276 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1 per cent after briefly losing all of an early 1.3 per cent jump. Wall Street closed a losing month with gains on Friday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to start the week lower, with futures on Saturday pointing to a loss of 85 points, or 1 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.55¢. August reporting season kicks into gear this week, with News Corp and AMP among those due up. It’s a fitting finish to July for the US stock market, which lurched up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and worries grew about whether Big Tech’s massive investments in artificial-intelligence technology will translate into profits and whether chipmaker stocks soared too high in the euphoria around AI.



Friday’s gains sent the S&P 500 to its first winning week in three, but the main measure of the US stock market nevertheless finished the month with a tiny loss. Amazon led the market with a leap of 15.3 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its profit more than tripled from a year earlier, thanks in part to an acceleration of growth in its cloud computing business. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Healthscope meets landlords to head off private equity break-up threat Analysts said that could be a signal Amazon’s huge AI investments are paying off, and Amazon increased its forecast for how much it will spend on investments this year. The reaction was similar to what Microsoft got a day before, when its stock soared to its best day in nearly 18 years on signals that its AI investments may also be yielding higher profits.



Chip companies selling the processors and computer memory that such “hyperscalers” are scrambling to buy swung sharply again on Friday. Micron Technology, for example, went from an early jump of 6.4 per cent to a loss of 6.5 per cent before finishing with a fall of 5.9 per cent. More firmly on the losing end of Wall Street was Apple, which dropped 7.4 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than expected. Its forecast for revenue growth in the current quarter fell short of expectations, which executives pinned on a supply crunch in components getting vacuumed up in the AI boom. All told, the S&P 500 rose 52.09 points to 7,489.72. The Dow Jones added 276.97 to 52,485.03, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 251.68 to 25,373.85. The gains came despite another rise in oil prices as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again from the Middle East. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1.2 per cent to settle at $US87.93 after careening between $US72 and $US102 earlier in July.



Higher oil prices have pushed the cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly $US4.11 across the United States, up from $US3.85 a month ago, according to AAA. More expensive oil also puts upward pressure on prices for virtually every product that rides on a ship, plane or truck before getting to a customer. The worries about inflation sent yields in the bond market even higher. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.71 per cent from 4.68 per cent late Thursday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran sent oil prices shooting higher. That’s a notable move for the yield, which moves higher when investors’ expectations for inflation, economic growth and other factors in upcoming years are rising. The leap for the 10-year yield has already sent the average long-term US mortgage rate to its highest level in a year. Longer-term yields jumped on Wednesday after the Federal Reserve’s chairman, Kevin Warsh, promised again to get inflation back down to 2 per cent but refused to say how he plans to get it there. The Fed voted again to keep its main interest rate steady on Wednesday, even though inflation remains well above 2 per cent.



Related Article Opinion

Whistleblowers The dismantling of KPMG is about to begin Colin Kruger Senior business reporter Hikes to rates by the Fed could restrain inflation, but they could also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has lobbied for lower interest rates instead of higher. Warsh has told financial markets that he does not want to give hints about what the Fed will do with interest rates, saying he wants to get direct, “unfiltered” messages from them rather than echoes back of what the Fed has suggested. But “without clarifying why action was or wasn’t taken already, it’s hard to see how statements about being committed to hitting its inflation target aren’t just a bluff,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. “The Fed is facing a growing credibility problem,” economists at Bank of America wrote in a report. Unless data comes in showing less pressure on inflation in the interim, “it is imperative for the Fed to pass the September test by hiking rates and delivering an internally consistent narrative.”



In stock markets abroad, the swings were even wilder for chip stocks. Seoul’s Kospi index soared 17.9 per cent for its best day in history. The index is dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and both surged at least 26.8 per cent on Friday. The Kospi, though, still lost 22 per cent in July despite Friday’s historic move. That’s after it more than doubled in the first six months of the year.
