World.title: I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of
World.content:
InspirationBali I discovered an overlooked part of Bali most visitors dream of Nina Karnikowski August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two weeks before leaving for Ubud, I was already hyperventilating about Bali’s crowds. As someone who spends much of their life chasing quietude, just the thought of the over-development and the Instagrammable chaos made me twitch. Cottages at Kul Kul Farm. Nina Karnikowski So when a friend told me about Sibang – describing it as Ubud’s calmer cousin and the way it might have been 30 years ago – I was in. Now, waiting for said friend on a dirt road corner with just an ancient temple to my left and jungle to my right, I’m glad I’ve come. That Sibang (which actually encompasses two villages, Sibang Kaja and Sibang Gede) has stayed under the radar is no accident. “Locals have told us about a curse that was placed on the village many years ago, by an angry giant who threatened that it would one day be swallowed by ants,” my friend says. “It’s said the villagers fled because of this, and the jungle took over.” The story lingered for decades, leaving Sibang quiet and largely overlooked – until Canadian John Hardy arrived to build Green School Bali.



Green School’s bamboo campus, which offers eco-focused education to about 500 local and international students from kindergarten to year 12, put the village on the map when it opened in 2008. My friend, who’s living in Sibang, so her son can attend the school, walks me down the street flanking the campus. Aside from local homes and a couple of sleepy cafes, a sustainability-focused concept store named Muka, and a slick year-old villa stay called Mahajiva, there is, happily, not much here. 



Each April, Kul Kul runs a 10-day bamboo-building course, teaching about a material that restores land, grows rapidly, and sequesters carbon. Student-built curving structures, five of which are newly open to guests, are dotted between beds of lettuce, tomato, chilli and eggplant. Much of this produce lands on plates at Taani, Kul Kul’s new restaurant where I slurp the best soto (a warming turmeric-spiced soup) I’ve ever had in Indonesia. Inside a cottage at Kul Kul Farm. Next afternoon I walk to Astungkara Way, a regenerative rice-farming collective. Twenty minutes from Kul Kul Farm, the road dissolves into paddies alive with birdsong and the loamy scent of turned earth. Here, travellers learn how rice is grown the natural way. This means ducks instead of pesticides, compost instead of chemicals, and respect for the Subak system, a co-operative irrigation network that has sustained Bali’s farmers for centuries. “Look around,” says manager Oka Dewanti, spreading her arms wide to the rice paddies rolling out around us. “This is what Ubud or Canggu was 30 years ago.” She speaks of the heartbreak of watching development swallow farmland, the urgency of bringing youth back to agriculture, and how travellers can support the kind of Bali they want to see. To that end, alongside hands-on farming courses, Astungkara Way leads multi-day walking journeys that begin in the thick of traffic and development, and slowly carry travellers back to the Bali that once was. Strolling back to Kul Kul in the indigo evening light, past boys fishing in irrigation canals and women carrying baskets of offerings towards local temples, I worry about what Sibang might lose as more travellers arrive. Change is already gathering at its edges. But if places like Kul Kul Farm and Astungkara Way set the tone for what’s to come, maybe this village has a fighting chance to remain the kind of Bali travellers dream about, rather than the kind we flee.

World.title: Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
NationalWALocal government Lockdowns are looming for Perth’s roaming cats. Here’s what you need to know Hannah Murphy August 3, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian councils could soon get the green light to force roaming cats indoors — but right now, a pet’s freedom depends entirely on which council it lives in. Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley announced plans to change the law to allow local councils to introduce cat containment laws in February. WA’s cats could soon be forced to stay on their own properties. Nick Moir Under the current law, councils need to get permission from a parliamentary committee to introduce changes to their local regulations. More than 20 councils have tried to make their own laws about keeping cats inside in the past, but only three have been successful - all in regional WA.



As a result, the cat laws in each local government differ greatly. Ahead of the planned law change, we asked every Perth metropolitan council what their state of play is when it comes to outdoor cats. Here’s what they told us: The Town of Claremont was the only local council who refused to comment on their current cat laws, and whether it had ever tried to get them changed previously.



Councils said cats were currently banned from upwards of 300 Perth reserves, parks and protected bushland area across the metropolitan area. Nearly all councils have limits on the number of cats people can own, and a select few have trapping programs conducted by rangers for “nuisance” cats. The changes to the 2011 Cat Act are only partway through the parliamentary process, but under its powers, local councils could order owners to: restrict cats to their owners’ premises;

prohibit cats from all public areas;

place conditions on when a cat may be permitted in a public area;

introduce cat curfews; and

require cats to be under the effective control of their owners or contained if leaving their owners’ property. However, Cat Haven chief executive Roz Robinson said it would be interesting to see how any changes would actually worked in practice. “It is interesting times with the review of the cat act coming up and it is interesting to note that whilst many councils are talking about cat containment being part of the cat laws, so many local governments do not enforce the current act,” she said.



“For example, I have it in writing from one western suburbs’ council, when faced with an enquiry from one of their residences about a stray cat, they simply refer them onto us.” Roz Robinson is the chief executive officer of Perth’s Cat Haven. Robinson said the not-for-profit organisation was extremely supportive of cat containment laws, saying it not only improves cat welfare but would ease pressure on the service. “With over 50 per cent of our intake coming in as strays, if we had proper containment laws, it would result in a reduction in these numbers,” she said. However, Robinson also argued any change with the Cat Act needed to focus heavily on the benefits of de-sexing household cats.



“Over 80 per cent of these strays – most friendly re-homable cats – are un-desexed. Un-desexed cats wander – they become strays in their need to mate. “You don’t have to be a mathematician to work out cats are prolific breeders and what numbers would look like without de-sexing. Related Article Exclusive

Biodiversity The staggering death toll of roaming pet cats finally revealed “For years we have been trying to de-sex our way out of the cat problem, but with little appetite from others to assist, we are literally fighting a losing battle.” She said there had to be continual state government funding towards spaying cats, as well as supporting the Cat Haven to deal with stray animals. Currently, she said the government provides just less than two per cent of the charity’s operating costs.



“What changes do we see after the review? It really depends if all stakeholders are serious about improving cat welfare or is it just another review being ticked off,” Robinson said. “Our intake numbers are increasing annually – 8 per cent while the population is only growing two per cent – our site is not fit for purpose, and can only be described as dilapidated. There is no funding forthcoming to improve the site. “We are an open admission shelter, we never say no to any cat and truly believe every cat does matter and want to give them all a second chance. But something has to give.”

World.title: Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying
World.content:
Tips & adviceDietitian’s guide Easy ways to eat more fibre every day without even trying Remember these simple tips and ingredients when grocery shopping and meal-prepping to boost your dietary fibre intake without overthinking it. Susie Burrell August 3, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Health trends may come and go faster than you can say “TikTok made me do it”, but current darling, dietary fibre, is the real deal. From a renewed focus on supporting digestive health and immune function with gut health superfoods, to fibremaxxing, there is plenty of noise that all comes back to one simple concept: eat more fibre. Here are some easy ways to do that every day without even trying. Use multgrain bread for your sandwiches like Neil Perry’s tuna number. William Meppem Upgrade your carbs Whether it’s cereal for breakfast, or a sandwich or wrap for lunch, the key to optimising your daily intake of dietary fibre is to ensure your daily staples have a wholegrain or wholemeal base. Often, we find ourselves picking up foods on the go, and in most cases, the carbs on offer are white, and as such not offering nearly as much fibre as we need. Bread and wraps



Swap white, sourdough, or plain wraps for high-fibre wholemeal, multigrain, rye, or seed-packed options. As a reference, your daily bread or wraps should be adding at least 3-5g of dietary fibre per serve and while sourdough may sound healthier, generally the options at cafes and bakeries are made with white flour. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Breakfast staples Choose multigrain or high-bran cereals over refined varieties, and toss oats or bran straight into smoothies. When checking breakfast cereal or granola packets, keep in mind that the higher percentage of wholegrains the breakfast cereal offers, the higher the natural dietary fibre content will be. Natural sources of dietary fibre from wholegrains, seeds, fruits and nuts are better options nutritionally than more processed dietary fibre like chicory root and insulin which are often added to bars, cereals and breads to increase the fibre content. Opt for brown rice over white, like in Katrina Meynink’s chickpea, brown rice and greens salad. Katrina Meynink



Pasta and rice There is a growing range of wholemeal, wholegrain and legume pasta options which are all significantly higher in fibre than regular white pasta. In the case of rice, seek out brown or black varieties where possible, or one of the growing ranges of mixed grain and rice quick-cook options that can offer as much as 5-8g of dietary fibre per serve, compared to less than 1g for regular white rice. Can you guess the hidden veg in Jill Dupleix’s spaghetti bolognese? Sneak vegies into every meal With fewer than one in 10 Aussies getting the recommended five serves of vegetables a day, and even less the 7-10 serves to support the goal of optimal health and longevity, there are plenty of reasons including boosting our intake of dietary fibre that come from increasing veggie intake across all of our meals.



Grate and blend Adding a mix of grated zucchini and carrots, or spinach or silverbeet, into scrambled eggs, pasta sauce bases like bolognese, porridge, or smoothies not only significantly increases nutrient intake, but fibre intake as well. Frozen spinach and kale can also be cost-effective options that slip easily into a number of meals without negatively impacting the flavour. Keep the skins on Whether you are mashing vegetables, adding them to smoothies or grating them into dishes, you get extra dietary fibre from vegetables when you leave the skin on. The same goes for fruits, and if you are especially keen, the skins on nutrient-packed kiwifruit and bananas are edible, too. Related Article Canned, pouched and fresh: A dietitian’s guide to the best (and worst) supermarket chicken soups



Know the easy add-ins Budget-friendly and fibre-rich frozen peas can be added to a wide range of mixed dishes including pasta, risotto and stir-fries. Baby cucumbers and carrots are an easy side to enjoy with your favourite sandwich or wrap, while a starter of pre-made vegetable-rich soups add extra nutrients and dietary fibre to any main meal. Make your own baked beans, like Adam Liaw’s, and get a big fibre boose. William Meppem Learn to love legumes If there is one food Aussies should be eating more of, if only for the cost-effective nature of such a nutrient-rich food, it is legumes. There are so many varieties that can easily be worked into many meals, whilst adding loads of protein and dietary fibre.



Swap in with mince Whether you are making spaghetti bolognese, chilli con carne or a sang choy bao, throw in a can of your favourite beans to make any amount of mince go a lot further. Embrace baked beans Ever-versatile baked beans can be added to any hot breakfast, enjoyed with crackers or even as a light meal, adding a massive 6-8 grams of dietary fibre per serve. If you prefer lower sugar options, it is also easy to make your own using a cannellini or white beans. Eat more edamame



Soy beans are especially nutrient rich, and an easy addition to all of your favourite Asian dishes whether they are enjoyed as a side dish with sushi, added to salads or even as a dried, protein-packed snack. Sprinkle chia seeds and nuts onto your cereal. iStock Sprinkle in seeds and nuts Not only are seeds and nuts extremely nutrient rich — offering nutrients including zinc, selenium, magnesium and plant-based omega-3s — but they are also rich in dietary fibre. Breakfast boosters



Stir a tablespoon of chia, flaxseed or pepitas into any mix of cereal, oats, yoghurt or smoothies for a protein, fibre and good fat hit. Or opt for one of the growing ranges of breakfast toppers or nut spreads which offer a mix of nuts and seeds, and as such a mix of nutrients. Related Article Sprinkle these tiny seeds on just about anything for a mighty nutrition punch Your favourite salads A little crunch goes a long way in a salad, and a few roasted nuts or a sprinkle of seeds adds texture and flavour to any salad. Even better, try roasting your favourite nuts or seeds with a little honey or maple syrup for an even tastier salad topper. A go-to snack

World.title: Luxon plans chat with Peters about 'racist' remarks 'at some point', says they've both 'been on the road'
World.content:
Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 9m

The prime minister is yet to pick up the phone to Winston Peters after his tirade towards a Chinese-born MP in Parliament last week, saying he will talk to the foreign minister "at some point".

New Zealand First's leader responded to heckling in the House on Wednesday by attacking the Greens' Lawrence Xu-nan, telling him to go back to his own country.

Christopher Luxon on Monday told Morning Report the comments were racist, but he had not yet spoken with Peters about it.

"This is him talking in his New Zealand First capacity," Luxon said.

Multiple international media outlets have published Peters' comments, referring to him as New Zealand's foreign minister.

Luxon said he had made his position clear in previous comments to the media.

"I will talk to him at some point, I'm sure, about it. But the point is I've been on the road, he's been on the road," he said.

"I have a strong view about it. It is racist and offensive. That's it."

Luxon said he was calling out Peters' game-playing.

"It is deliberate attention seeking to push buttons to get the attention on himself... rather than issues that matter to Kiwis."

Luxon was asked whether he would rule out forming another coalition with NZ First.

"There's a lot of hypotheticals - at the moment, I don't want to work with anyone," he said.

"My ideal situation is 20 National ministers in Cabinet would be the very best outcome for New Zealand."

But Luxon said National had proven it could find common ground with coalition partners, ACT and NZ First, despite disagreeing with them on some things.

World.title: Auckland axe attacker quietly deported to China
World.content:
A man who launched a frenzied attack on guests at three Auckland restaurants has been deported.

Government briefings show how the man was allowed to leave New Zealand's specialist mental health clinic, a year after a judge ruled he should be detained there.

Fanrong Meng wielded a wood-chopping axe and metal pole when he attacked customers at neighbouring eateries in Albany in June 2023, three months after he arrived in Auckland.

The courts ruled the 25-year-old was insane at the time of the offending - suffering hallucinations and delusions - and was not criminally liable for his actions.

Three people were hospitalised, and one needed emergency surgery to his skull. The attacks only ended when his sixth victim managed to overpower him - despite being hit so hard his head hit the bowl of food he was eating. He managed to hold onto the axe and Meng until police arrived.

His victims and restaurant staff told RNZ how they had been left traumatised by the late-night rampage.

A psychiatric report in court said Meng had a lengthy history of mental illness, and had been previously diagnosed with obsessive compulsive disorder and schizophrenia in China.

His detention as a 'special patient' under mental health laws at the Mason Clinic initially prevented him from being deported.

In the 'no surprises' notes to ministers, released to RNZ, officials set out the steps needed to have him deported.

They show a Special Patient Review Panel decided to downgrade Meng's 'special patient' status in September 2024, paving the way for his deportation.

In February last year, government agencies met to discuss the case, officials noting that 'due to the number of unresolved issues, the individual's deportation will not be imminent.'

They included a health minister needing to sign off on Meng's new patient status, MFAT confirming that the treatment of people with mental illness in China met human rights standards and the logistics of holding him in custody after he left the clinic while awaiting deportation.

But after the agency meeting it took less than six weeks to deport him, and officials say he was met off the plane in China by health officials in March last year.

"Immigration Compliance worked on this complex case for 12 months with the Ministry of Health and other agencies," said officials in the final ministerial notes. "As arranged, the Chinese government health officials met the client on his arrival in Shanghai."

Under the judge's original ruling, Meng could have been detained for seven years in a secure psychiatric facility, half the length of the maximum sentence for the most serious charge he faced of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

His lawyer Michael Kan said the young man should not be subject to a special patient order, so that he could return to China, live with his parents and receive treatment.

But the judge agreed with prosecutors that Meng posed a significant and ongoing risk to others.

'Degree of trust' in visa application

Meng, a carpenter assistant, reportedly said the cost of medication prompted him to stop taking anti-psychotics before moving to New Zealand.

He arrived in Auckland in March 2023 on an accredited employer visa, but lost his job only weeks before the June attack because his employer did not have enough work available.

He had been suffering from delusional beliefs about being attacked himself.

His victims and staff at the affected restaurants questioned how Meng came to be granted a three-year work visa, given his health condition.

RNZ asked Immigration New Zealand (INZ) what medical tests visa applicants underwent, and whether INZ assessors would have seen medicals documents from Meng's own doctors.

In a statement, INZ acting deputy chief operating officer Peter Elms said it empathised with Meng's victims.

"The case of Fanrong Meng has been deeply traumatic for everyone involved," he said. "As Mr Meng applied for a temporary work visa that was valid for more than 12 months, he was required to undergo an immigration medical examination and provide a chest X-ray as part of his visa application. Applicants in these circumstances cannot simply self-certify that they are healthy."

Medical examinations are completed by INZ-approved 'panel' physicians based in New Zealand and overseas.

"The immigration medical examination includes questions about an applicant's medical history, along with a physical examination and blood and urine tests," he said.

"Mr Meng underwent the required immigration medical examination in November 2022. Based on the information available through that process, INZ's Health Assessment Team assessed him as having an acceptable standard of health. The medical assessment did not identify any pre-existing psychiatric condition."

Elms said INZ medical assessors do not see applicants in person, instead reviewing information they receive. "This includes the assessment completed by panel physicians, as well as any specialist reports or test results provided with an application. INZ did not receive any medical documentation from Mr Meng's doctors in China."

Applicants were warned if they provide false or misleading health information they can face a visa decline or deportation.

"There is a degree of trust involved in the immigration system, and while not every piece of information supplied by every applicant can be independently verified, all applicants are required to declare that the information they provide is true, complete and correct.

"It is also important to note that psychiatric conditions can be difficult to identify through a general immigration medical examination. Where an applicant does not disclose a pre-existing psychiatric condition, a panel physician may have no basis to identify that condition through the standard assessment process."

INZ said requiring specialist psychiatric assessments for all visa applicants would add significant cost and administrative burden, as serious undisclosed psychiatric conditions would only occur in a 'very small proportion' of applications.

World.title: Hoyts Cinema's IMAX plans for New Zealand
World.content:
Big cinema chain operators like Hoyts have tended to rely on sure-fire, big-name blockbusters and superhero movies to drive ticket sales at cinemas across New Zealand and Australia.

This year - to some extent - has been no exception, with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey set to overtake Toy Story 5 as the biggest movie of the year in New Zealand, according to Hoyts Group chief executive Damien Keogh.

Box office sales this year would be the best since Covid, Keogh believes.

But something unusual has also happened at the box office this year - blockbusters are not the only story driving up sales.

Two horror films, Backrooms and Obsession, made by younger independent filmmakers who cut their teeth on YouTube have also had a big impact.

It was something Keogh admitted caught the industry by surprise.

"There were a couple of, I guess, movies that weren't really on our radar. One called Obsession, which has done over $3 million at the New Zealand box office, and another one called Backrooms. So, basically by someone who built a following on YouTube. That Gen Z audience is discovering content online and then when there is a cinema version of it, they're turning up to the cinema to watch it."

A scene from Backrooms. A24/AP

It was a trend Keogh hoped would continue, as younger generations looked for more social connection.

"This younger generation, who is probably locked in their bedroom looking at their phones for an inordinate amount of time, not surprisingly, are craving a bit of social interaction and the cinema provides that immersive experience with the big screen, it is a social environment with people of their own age."

The Hoyts Group - which has been operating cinemas for more than 100 years - runs about 62 theatres across Australia and New Zealand, with about 500 screens and 57,000 seats across its network.

It is the number one cinema chain in Australia. In New Zealand it currently sits behind Event Cinemas in the number two spot.

But Hoyts is planning to increase its investment in New Zealand as it looks to improve its cinema experience and range of offerings here, including IMAX with Laser.

IMAX with Laser is a special film projection technology that aims to provide an enhanced visual and audio experience for movie-goers on extra-large screens.

It is having a moment, with The Odyssey filmed with IMAX cameras to make the most of that bigger-screen experience.

Christopher Nolan brings Homer's epic to life from behind the IMAX camera. Supplied: Universal Pictures

Event Cinemas currently operates the only two IMAX theatres in New Zealand, in Wellington and Auckland.

But Hoyts recently partnered with the US owner of IMAX to roll out four IMAX with Laser cinemas in Australia and is planning to bring IMAX to its offering in New Zealand, although Keogh was not yet ready to say where.

Keogh said directors like Nolan and big studios were investing in IMAX technology and consumers wanted to see the movies in IMAX if they could.

"Without going into specifics, we certainly will have an IMAX presence in New Zealand within the next 12 months."

But it is not just IMAX technology. Hoyts is also planning to add 12 new ScreenX auditoriums to its network across Australia and New Zealand.

ScreenX is another new technology that provides 270-degree experience for viewers by using projectors on side walls as well as the main screen.

Along with the new technology offerings, Hoyts will also upgrade existing cinema complexes in Riccarton in Christchurch, Te Awa in Hamilton and Sylvia Park in Auckland.

"The ones we're targeting, there's Sylvia Park in Auckland, which currently is the third biggest cinema in the country. We think once we renovate, it's got a chance to get to number one."

The last few years have not been easy for the cinema business, with Covid-19, a writers' strike and the rise of TV streaming platforms like Netflix hitting demand.

However, Keogh believed the sector was finding its footing again.

"I guess we're kind of the best way to describe it is we're getting back to a normal release pattern that we did have pre-Covid. And when the movies are there, the customers are there."

He was also optimistic that whatever happened with the cost-of-living crisis and the wider economy, people would keep coming to the movies.

World.title: Declining birth rate is more complex than a 'baby bonus' can fix, academic says
World.content:
Paul Spoonley discusses NZ First’s new parent payment policy Morning Report Download MP3 4m

New Zealand's declining population is "much more complex than simply providing a baby bonus".

That's the opinion of Massey University's professor Paul Spoonley.

It comes after New Zealand First leader Winston Peters announced it would pay people to have babies if it was elected into government.

At a public meeting at the weekend, Peters said New Zealand was facing a "population precipice" and the rate of New Zealand citizens having children had fallen dramatically.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters. RNZ/Giles Dexter

"We need more Kiwis having more children, and one way to do that is to substantially lower the main barrier most are facing, that is the cost," he said.

The party's Kiwi Kids Grant would seek to arrest that fall, by paying parents $5000 a year for the first three years, and for up to three children.

That meant parents, as long as one was a New Zealand citizen, would receive up to $45,000.

Peters said the tax-free payment would be administered through Inland Revenue.

Speaking to Morning Report on Monday, Spoonley - who is an expert in demographics and social change - said New Zealand's declining birth rate did need to be discussed and he applauded New Zealand First for raising it.

"I want to acknowledge New Zealand First. At least they've recognised there is a demographic issue and that the cost of childcare, of having children is an issue."

Massey University's professor Paul Spoonley. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

He said the current birth rate was about 25 percent below where it needed to be and in the past 10 years, there had been a "very sharp" gradient down.

Spoonley said New Zealand's number of births per woman was currently 1.53 and he estimated it was likely to get down to 1.2-1.3 - as experienced across most of Europe.

He said international evidence had proven that such an incentive might produce a "short-term blip" but it does nothing to stem the decline.

Sweden, for example, offered 480 days of paid leave - with 90 of those available to grandparents to help, Spoonley said.

It was "extremely generous" and also came with free check-ups, child health clinics, extra insurance, tax-free cash for each child until they turn 16 and low-cost pre-school.

It was a "very comprehensive package" to encourage people to have more children.

Spoonley said it caused a short-term blip but Sweden's fertility rate was almost the exact same as New Zealand's.

"Even that generosity doesn't change people's behaviour."

Spoonley said the discussion that needed to be had was about how many migrants were wanted to come to New Zealand to counter balance the decline in fertility.

He said immigration was one of the "few policy levers you have" to increase the population or keep it growing.

"It's great that New Zealand First have raised it (declining birth rate), I think it's an important issue, the cost of having children in New Zealand is an important issue.

World.title: Squishy dumpling toy banned overseas can still be ordered in New Zealand
World.content:
* This story has been updated to clarify The Warehouse toys meet safety requirements.



Consumer NZ is warning that gaps in Aotearoa's product safety system are leaving shoppers exposed, after finding a toy banned in the UK can still be bought here through online marketplaces.

A number of Squeezy Dumplings - a popular toy shaped like a soft dumpling - were recalled in the UK in June after testing found benzene in the outer layer.

Benzene can irritate the skin and, where exposure is significant, cause a burning feeling throughout the digestive tract.

While Consumer NZ said this recalled toy cannot be bought in stores like The Warehouse or Kmart, it can be ordered from Aliexpress.

Stores such as The Warehouse and Kmart do, however, sell similar products. The Warehouse said its toys were original versions, not imitations, and met statutory safety requirements.

Head of research and advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said the availability of potentially dangerous toys through online marketplaces exposed a weakness in how product safety is managed in New Zealand.

"Shoppers shouldn't have to wonder whether a toy is safe. Yet for many products sold online, there has been no independent testing before they reach New Zealand homes."

She said New Zealand product safety laws had not been significantly updated in decades, while in-store and online marketplaces had changed dramatically.

New Zealand has a product safety standard for children's toys enforced by the Commerce Commission.

However, Rasmussen said the system was far from watertight and there remained a risk that unsafe products cross into the country every day.

"That system only works if manufacturers are doing the right thing and problems are identified quickly," Rasmussen said.

"Unfortunately, that's not always the case."

Earlier this month, research by Auckland University of Technology confirmed asbestos was present in some children's play sand sold in New Zealand and that airborne fibres could be released during normal play.

Rasmussen said the safety regime currently used by New Zealand and Australian regulators was heavily reliant on risk assessments commissioned by product suppliers themselves, rather than independently verified testing.

"Whether it's asbestos in play sand or benzene in a toy, these cases demonstrate why we cannot rely solely on manufacturers' own safety claims."

World.title: Concern as number of laws rushed through parliament surges
World.content:
Andrew Geddis discusses government’s use of urgency Morning Report Download MP3 6m

* This article has been updated to clarify that the number of laws passed under urgency is more than any year according to immediately available data going back to 2008.

The coalition government has passed more legislation in one term under urgency than any other Parliament since records dating back to 2008, raising concerns public scrutiny of proposed laws is diminishing.

Parliamentary Library data provided to RNZ showed 17.4 percent of all bills sent for Royal Assent in the first 940 days of this Parliament - to 2 July this year - passed through all stages of lawmaking all at once, skipping the select committee stage and its public feedback process.

This is part of an increasing trend over multiple parliaments. Over the same period, the Labour government passed 15.5 percent of bills in this way.

Former Labour Prime Minister and Attorney-General Sir Geoffrey Palmer said the coalition government's use of urgency wasn't about coping with large volumes of legislation.

He said it was more about "avoid[ing] the scrutiny of select committees" - something the government rejected.

Parliamentary Library data showed that while the total number of bill stages passed under urgency jumped in the first 940 days of this Parliament, the number of bills passed into law remained steady at just under 200 over the past few terms.

The previous Labour government passed several laws in this way, including the bill enabling the Covid-19 traffic light system and workforce vaccination mandates.

Palmer said governments of all stripes had used urgency, but not on this scale.

"Its use has been normalised by degrees until it has become an instrument of convenience rather than of necessity," he said.

"I do think the desire to get things done quickly is driving some of this.

"Impatience is a very bad thing for lawmaking, because you'll get it wrong, and it has to be done in a solemn and serious way."

Palmer said overworked and under-resourced select committees were a related issue. For example, the government received hundreds of thousands of submissions for the Treaty Principles Bill.

"They only give you about five minutes, but try to hear most people. It's become overwhelming."

Chris Finlayson, who was Attorney-General in the John Key government, said the data pointed to a need for Parliament to consider extending House sitting hours, given the complexity and volume of legislation.

"I don't necessarily see it as a sort of a partisan issue against this government, but perhaps a wider question.

"The real area of concern is if legislation goes through all its stages without some kind of committee work being done, because that enables the public to have their say about the bill.

"Often, and I think for example… the New Zealand Law Society invariably makes very valuable comments on legislation."

Government: Urgency used when necessary

Shadow Leader of the House Kieran McAnulty said National criticised Labour's use of urgency during the pandemic, but then quickly surpassed those figures once in government.

"They [the government] have used urgency to pass laws that will negatively impact many people. In many cases, these Bills are passed in the dead of night, with no consultation with the public," he said.

"Labour's use of urgency to get through more than a couple of stages of a bill at any one time wasn't at all frequent."

McAnulty said discomfort with the high use of urgency is reflected in submissions to Parliament's Standing Orders Committee.

Before November's election, the cross-party group will consider the rules for the next Parliament.

"We will take our concerns that much of the use of urgency by this government has been to avoid scrutiny to [the] Standing Orders Committee, but no amount of extending sitting hours will address the harm this government has caused."

Leader of the House Louise Upston said the "vast majority" of bills being considered under urgency had gone through a select committee process.

"Therefore, the only effect of urgency is to allow stages to happen back-to-back, and extend the hours the House can sit."

She said of the bills that had skipped the select committee, only 10 were not Budget-related legislation, or were passed in the first 100 days of government, some to repeal laws enacted under Labour.

"All of these bills had necessary reasons to be enacted as soon as possible. Five of these Bills were supported by Labour at [the] third reading.

"This government has never used urgency for the purpose of skipping scrutiny. Much of the urgency that we use is just to get overtime, to get extra hours, and that is to progress the legislation that the government and the parties in the Coalition campaigned on in the election that we won."

RNZ also approached Chris Bishop - who has been the Leader of the House for most of this Parliamentary term - for comment. His office said Upston would be the most appropriate spokesperson.

Should the rules change?

Parliament's rules require a minister to move a motion in the House to enter urgency, which is passed through a simple majority. When doing so, the minister must give "some particularity of the circumstances that warrant the claim for urgency".

Standing Orders do not define what those circumstances are or allow MPs to debate those reasons, something Geoffrey Palmer told the Standing Orders Committee a submission he wanted to see changed.

He said four-year terms, while putting more safeguards in place, could also be considered.

During the Key government, there was a drop in the level of urgency used between the three years after 2008, and the same period after 2011.

This coincided with Standing Orders amendments allowing pre-arranged extended House sittings on Wednesday or Thursday mornings.

It followed criticism of the Key government's use of urgency after the 2008 election and the Clark government's rapid lawmaking during its final year in power.

Chris Finlayson said the House could consider sitting more often on Friday mornings or abolishing dinner breaks since MPs are not present for all debates anyway.

For constituent MPs who needed to be in their electorates on Fridays, he said they should be allowed to go home.

RNZ asked Finlayson and Palmer to assess MPs' willingness to enact changes for the next Parliament, given political parties tended to justify their own use of urgency while in government, then criticise the other side while in Opposition.

"Everyone said it's the other person's fault. That's just part of politics," Finlayson said.

He was keen to present alternatives, and "less interested in attributing blame".

Palmer said there were instances where urgency was necessary, including when mistakes needed to be corrected quickly.

"The difficulty is that you don't want to make urgency a standard method of making legislation. But it's rather become that in New Zealand in recent years."

Asked about his own government's use of urgency, Palmer said: "There was quite a bit because there was a terrific amount when Muldoon left office.

"There was a terrific mess, and it had to be fixed up with a lot of legislation… There are proper occasions for urgency.

World.content:
All the medals have been handed out and the Glasgow Commonwealth Games draws to a close with the ceremony at OVO Hydro.

Traditionally, this has been a chance for athletes to let their hair down and party, after the tension of competition, but this has been anything but a traditional Games.

World.title: Diamonds win bronze medal with an eye to greater things for netball
World.content:
There's a sentiment in team sports at multi-sport events like the Commonwealth Games that you lose silver and win bronze.

The bronze medallists get to climb on the podium having won their last match, while second place is coming off a heartbreaking loss, having let gold slip through their grasp.

For the Diamonds, bronze at the 2026 Commonwealth Games is a complicated celebration.

Less than 20 hours after Jamaica ripped their hearts out in the semifinal, the Aussie netballers were back on court at 9am in Glasgow for the first centre pass of their first-ever bronze-medal match.

Diamonds fumble Australia's most anticipated gold medal The Diamonds will miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica in front of a crowd baying for Australia's downfall.

It was hard to bounce back from the loss but they did so against England, winning 65-80.

"We had such a quick time to process what happened, I think a lot of us still feel quite numb," defender Jo Weston said.

"Then you go out and have a game like we did, we're so proud and we know all of Australia have been behind us, so it's been a real rollercoaster of emotions in a very short time frame. But I think the overwhelming feeling is pride and a lot of love for each other.

"It's immensely challenging for us having that mental fortitude to come back out. We have very high expectations of ourselves and we want to do our country proud.

The Diamonds rediscovered their flow to keep their medal-winning streak alive. (AP: Andrew Milligan/PA)

"They always say Diamonds are made under pressure and I think that really showed in us today. Although it's not the colour we were after we're really proud about it."

Coach Stacey Marinkovich said the night between the games was about leaving space for team members to "be vulnerable".

There was no point pretending they weren't gutted, that the loss was anything other than gut-wrenching, but once they left the meeting room it was about moving forward.

"It was very emotional last night, it was still probably lingering today a little bit, so to be able to mentally switch in showed our culture isn't words on a wall," she said.

There were complicated emotions for Australia's bronze medallists. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"That took a lot of grit to be able to go out there and get that result."

Adding another layer of emotion for these stewards of the game, constantly fighting for eyeballs and recognition, is the more objective flip-side of the loss.

That is those celebrations of the Sunshine Girls after the semifinal.

For the first five Commonwealth Games, only Australia and New Zealand won gold and silver. In 2018, England stunned the Diamonds on their home patch for the Gold Coast title. Four years ago Jamaica beat the Aussies in their group match and made their first final. And in Glasgow, they went even better to take the Diamonds down in a knockout match to fight New Zealand for gold.

"International netball is the best it's ever been, which is so good for the sport, it's what we want to see," Weston said.

Four countries is not an enormous range of winners or even contenders, but in every event around the world there are dominant forces.

It wasn't the colour they wanted or expected, but a medal's a medal. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

With six years to the Brisbane Olympics and a push for the sport's inclusion, the Diamonds' bronze may have been the best thing for game.

"It's great for the sport because we always want the game to grow. Gone are the days where it's just one or two nations really dominating," Kiera Austin said.

"It's disappointing for us to have not gotten to that point ... but Jamaica were far too good on the day and that's great going into Brisbane hopefully getting netball into the Olympics.

"It's a sport we absolutely love, a sport we think deserves a great platform on the international stage and if it means a greater competition, then winning that gold medal whenever we get the chance to again is going to be all that much sweeter."

World.title: Australia's Rhiannan Iffland becomes greatest cliff diver of all time
World.content:
Australia's Rhiannan Iffland has officially become the greatest cliff diver of all time after winning the penultimate event of the season in Mostar, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 34-year-old from Newcastle arrived at the historic bridge knowing that victory on Saturday local time from the 21m platform would seal her 10th World Series title in a row and 48th victory of her career.

An estimated 23,000 fans turned out across three days of competition to see Iffland tally 363.20 points, finishing ahead of Canada's Molly Carlson (361.60) and Australian Xantheia Pennisi (345.80) to again lift the King Kahekili Trophy.

Pennisi's 10th career podium came thanks to a personal best total score, while Stella Forsyth (276.15), the third Australian participating, came 10th in the 12-woman field.

Rhiannan Iffland is now a commanding 27 points ahead of her nearest rival in the standings. (Getty Images: Dean Treml)

"I'm super stoked, and I guess it's time to process and then celebrate," said Iffland, who entered the final round just 1.6 points ahead of Carlson in sweltering conditions.

"I knew deep down in my heart that it wasn't going to be an easy one today. I knew Molly wasn't going to leave without putting up a good fight."

Iffland's triumph — her 48th in 59 stops — moved her to 77 points after four of the five stops on tour, an unassailable 27 clear of Carlson, with compatriot Pennisi (35) fifth.

The win — thanks to a stunning inward three somersaults half twist tuck dive into the Neretva River — also moved Iffland ahead of Englishman Gary Hunt on the all-time wins list.

It is the third time she has wrapped up the title with a stop to spare.

Romania's Constantin Popovici (right) joined Australia's Rhiannon Iffland in celebrations after winning the men's event in Mostar. (Getty Images: Romina Amato)

"Forty-eight out of 50-something starts, it's nuts," the five-time high diving world champion added.

"But I guess the recipe really comes down to passion, and drive and hard work. There is no secret recipe to being so consistent. Practice, practice, practice, and it paid off for me."

The men's event was won by Romania's Constantin Popovici, who edged out Britain's Aidan Heslop and James Lichenstein of the United States.

Heslop leads the standings on 68 points, followed by Lichtenstein (57) and Popovici (55).

Divers now have an extended two-month break before the final event of the 2026 calendar takes place in Polignano a Mare, Italy — the home of European cliff diving — from September 27.

World.title: 'Rubbish' costs Rabbitohs as Hynes chases NRL record, Eels beat Tigers
World.content:
South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has said "rubbish" from his team continues to cost them chances to win games, as the Rabbitohs were beaten by the Cronulla Sharks.

The Rabbitohs started Sunday's top-eight battle brightly, scoring first and then playing against 12 men when Cronulla's Teig Wilton was sin-binned for a high shot on Jack Wighton.

But the Sharks would bounce back with 18 unanswered points before half-time, before kicking on in the second half for a 32-16 win.

Souths were their own worst enemy at times, missing more than 50 tackles as well as conceding six penalties and three six-again restarts.

The loss leaves the Rabbitohs seventh on the NRL ladder with 10 wins and nine losses, just one win ahead of 10th place Manly in the tight race for the top-eight.

After Sunday's 16-point loss to Cronulla, Bennett told reporters Souths' repeated errors were costing them the chance of competing with the best team in the league.

"Our Achilles heel is when we don't execute and then we pay a bit of a price for it," Bennett said.

"We can run deep (in the premiership) any day of the week if we can just get over the rubbish that gets in our game.

"If we can get that right, we can hold our own with most teams in the competition."

Meanwhile, Sharks halfback Nicho Hynes set a new club record by successfully kicking his 32nd consecutive goal.

Entering the day with a streak of 26, Hynes was perfect from his six attempts on Sunday to extend his run and close within three of the all-time record.

Canterbury Bulldogs great Hazem El Masri holds the record when he converted 35 consecutive goals in 2003.

In the final match on Sunday, Parramatta broke the hearts of Wests Tigers fans with a late try to Isaiah Iongi, snatching a 16-13 win.

The Eels led 12-0 at half-time before suffering a shocking second half, camped in their own end thanks to repeated errors, while two defence lapses allowed the Tigers to level the score.

Tigers halfback Adam Doueihi, who returned to the side after refusing to play last week, scored the try to level the scores, and kicked the Tigers ahead with a 72nd-minute field goal.

But a late try to Iongi in the 76th minute sealed an unconvincing win for the blue and gold.

World.title: Glorious athletics campaign ends in an empty stadium near midnight
World.content:
The final moment of celebration in Australia's glorious athletics campaign at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games was hilariously understated.

Approaching midnight, Lachlan Kennedy, Calab Law, Josh Azzopardi, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius finally walked onto the podium to receive their gold medals for the men's 4x100-metre relay.

The crowd had long since filed out of Scotstoun Stadium when the medal ceremony, which was supposed to happen two and a half hours earlier, kicked off.

The track and field that had hosted seven golds, five silvers and five bronze medals for Australia on a jam-packed day, had been leaf-blown, cleaned and stripped of most of its Games paraphernalia.

The stadium was empty when the medal ceremony took place. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Only a handful of volunteers, family, stadium crew, media members and team support staff remained to applaud the historic relay winners, Australia's first since 1974.

A protest by the initially disqualified Canadian team had finally succeeded, reinstating the Olympic champions to the silver medal spot and cutting short Ghanaian celebrations of bronze deep in the bowels of the Glasgow Warriors' rugby club home ground.

In a credit to organisers, the pyrotechnics still fired, the flags were still raised by military personnel in full regalia, and the anthem still played over the stadium PA.

Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi, Calab Law, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius eventually got their moment. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Advance Australia Fair was sung even more drone-fully than usual without the safety of a crowd to hide the nasal tones of the Aussie accent, before the small gathering shuffled off the track.

It was a bizarrely low-key moment for one of the crowning achievements of this breakout meet for Team Australia, equalling the most medals won by the track and field team at a Commonwealth Games on foreign soil.

Of the 12 gold medals, 11 silver, and 11 bronzes, none sums up what the team has and can become more than this relay triumph.

Administrators, cheerleaders and athletes alike have been spruiking this new golden generation for Australian Athletics, which has pumped countless hours and very countable dollars into the nation's relays program in recent years.

Team Australia athletes pose for a photo after the women's and men's 4x100 metres relay finals on day nine of the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

In the past four years, Commonwealth Games Australia invested $11.6 million into the Green2Gold2Great program.

That covered a wide range of athletes, with $500,000 dedicated to relays specifically.

In that time, Australia's teams have found some phenomenal success across a number of events.

In 2025, there were green and gold teams in all six events at the World Athletics Relays for the first time ever and the mixed 4x400m team won silver.

At this year's World Relays, the men's 4x400m picked up an Australian record and bronze.

Calab Law handed over to final runner Rohan Browning with Australia in first place. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

So well drilled are these teams that when it came time for the heats on the final morning of the athletics program, both the men's and women's teams could rest individual 100m medallists Kennedy and Torrie Lewis.

Azzopardi put aside his bitter disappointment at only being brought to Glasgow as a relay runner to contribute to the cause, describing the heats as "a training run".

That is a far cry from the team that missed out in Birmingham because Browning took a tumble in the heats.

They missed the 2024 Olympic final despite running faster heat times than the top three in the opposite heat, mucked up the final change in last year's world championships final, and missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second at World Relays in May.

This gold medal puts the world on notice, and there is still more room to grow.

Lachlan Kennedy, Joshua Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning celebrate victory in the men's 4x100m relay final at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It is a credit to the system and their confidence in it that they didn't rush Glasgow 100m finalist Eddie Nketia into the team, even for the heats, opting instead for quick-start specialist Ius to lead off.

Kennedy replaced him for the final, playing his role to perfection, handing off cleanly to Azzopardi deep in the box, before Law and Browning came home in 38.07.

"We knew what we had in us, we're training well, we compete domestically all year against each other, [so] we're pretty used to each other. I think it's a big part of why we're so successful. Train together all year, camps all year," Kennedy said.

Kennedy said there is no first and second squad in their team, but 1A and 1B, described as "green and gold" by Browning, who flagged the looming arrivals of Gout Gout and Nketia once they have more time to train with the team that now carries a golden aura.

"I hope there are kids at home tonight watching this who aspire to grow up and be part of this team," Browning said.

"Not just aspire to the baggy green or the Wallabies or the Australian AFL team, aspire to be part of the Australian relay team."

We have already seen glimpses of it, with former Cronulla Sharks under-17 player Zavier Peacock opting for the track and finishing second behind Gout at this year's junior Australian titles.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

And veteran Kurtis Marschall was spurred on by their performance.

The back-to-back-to-back Commonwealth Games pole vault champion started his competition first and finished last on a frigid summer's night in Glasgow, getting the chance to watch his teammates pick up medals as he made his way up to a Games record of 5.85m, claiming the last Aussie gold of the program.

"The system is working. The boys' relay tonight was just phenomenal. They inspired me to get over the line," he said.

"We just want to keep pushing this sport along more and more and more. It's the best sport in the world and deserves more eyes, so we're just doing our part."

The whole stadium was watching his crowning moment and while no-one saw "the boys" get theirs, they weren't there to see the work it took to get there either.

World.title: Eagles star in tears after loss, Crows into top four after downing Dons
World.content:
Melbourne captain Max Gawn was inspirational in his team's nine-point win over Gold Coast. (Getty Images)

Melbourne has cemented its top six status ahead of next weekend's clash with ladder leaders Fremantle, defeating Gold Coast by nine points at Carrara Stadium.

In a contest featuring several lead changes, the Demons did just enough in the fourth quarter to claim an 18.6 (114) to 16.9 (105) victory.

After a four-goal display against Geelong last week, Harrison Petty kicked three majors including a crucial after-the-siren effort at the end of the third quarter, while Jacob van Rooyen also kicked three for the visitors.

Melbourne captain Max Gawn was huge for the Demons, notching 25 disposals, 10 marks, 33 hit-outs and nine clearances.

After last weekend's loss to the Cats, Demons coach Steven King was thrilled by his team's ability to find a way to victory ahead of the clash with the Dockers.

"We've already played them once earlier this year, and we got taught a lesson," King said.

"This time we'll be at the MCG and we love playing there but I'm sure they'll come over as a full dress rehearsal for what's in front of them as a footy club.

"It's a privilege to play in big games that count, and we're lucky we grabbed our opportunity today and can still be relevant in this competition for what's ahead."

Jed Walter kicked three for the Suns, all in the first half, as Gold Coast was unable to prevent slumping to its 10th straight defeat in what was Christian Petracca's first match against his former club.

Petracca, whose impact at the Suns had been under the spotlight throughout the week following an on-field argument with young gun Leo Lombard in the loss to Carlton, had minimal impact on the contest with 16 disposals and two clearances.

Instead it was John Noble (34 disposals, seven tackles, 10 marks) and Matt Rowell (30 disposals, nine tackles, eight clearances) who led the way for the Suns, with coach Damien Hardwick lamenting a similar display to previous defeats.

"It's just frustrating because a lot of those things are absolutely within our control, and it's the stuff that we need to eradicate," Hardwick said.

Gold Coast slumped to its 10th straight loss, a feat unthinkable at the start of the season. (Getty Images)

"I've got to coach harder and tougher because otherwise we don't move forward.

"So we've learned a lot of lessons like that this year, unfortunately, but not getting the result we're after."

Both teams had injury worries with Sam Collins (ribs) and Blake Howes (wrist) sent to hospital for X-rays after coming off in separate incidents.

Melbourne set the template for their accuracy in front of goal early, kicking five straight in the opening term to hold a three-point lead at the first break.

Bailey Humphrey's goal after the siren at the end of the second quarter, despite a question mark over whether he ran off the line of the mark as he came into kick, had the hosts in front heading into the main break.

And the Suns extended that lead to three goals during a high-scoring third term, kicking four goals alone from free kicks.

The Demons, however, kicked two goals in the last 30 seconds including another after-the-siren major to Petty to snatch a one-point lead heading into the final quarter.

Howes' nasty looking fall early in the last term didn't deter the Demons, who kicked four goals to three to secure the points.

While the Demons host the Dockers next weekend, the Suns will aim to snap their losing run in Canberra against GWS.

World.title: After javelin gold, Aussie star heads straight back to hospital work
World.content:
Sydney doctor Mackenzie Little has finally become a golden girl with the javelin as she led one last parade of Commonwealth Games field event medallists in the green and gold.

The remarkable 29-year-old Little, a doctor at Northern Beaches Hospital, can barely even call herself a part-time athlete these days, such is her busy medical life, but she still proved too good for her opponents as she finally lifted a major international title.

She nailed victory with her first throw and then revealed she will be jetting straight back to work on Tuesday as an ear, nose and throat registrar.

On a night when pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall completed Australia's golden track-and-field program by soaring to a Games-record 5.85 metres and a third-straight title, Little's achievement felt even more astonishing.

"I'm so I'm relieved and excited — this is so fantastic. Nailing the first throw is maybe something to do with how my training's been a bit quality over quantity in the last couple of years," she said.

"I wish I could say, you know, that I'm really, really training my butt off, but I'm just having to fit things in around my job. I'm having to make the most of sometimes challenging situations, not having all the time in the world.

"I perform surgeries and see outpatients in clinics and take care of patients who are in the ward sick in hospital. Then in the evenings, I'll get to training, but I've had to change my training locations this year to stay within 30 minutes of the hospital. When you're on call, you need to — overnight and in the evenings — be within 30 minutes of the hospital in case of emergencies.

"I'm gonna go and fly home straight away and get back to work."

On a tricky night for throwers in the Scotstoun Stadium on the last evening of track and field competition, Little believed her technique of throwing low and hard to cut through the wind helped her to a season best 61.88m with an opener that no-one else threatened.

New Zealand silver medallist Tori Moorby hurled 60.08m in the third round to grab the silver, while Kenya's Irene Jepkemboi took the bronze.

Kurtis Marschall reacts after securing his third Commonwealth Games gold medal in the pole vault. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Marschall, winner at both the Gold Coast and Birmingham Commonwealth Games, finished the night in style by becoming only the third Australian ever to win three titles in a row in the same event, and ending with a leap that surpassed his hero Steve Hooker's 5.80m in Melbourne 20 years ago.

Entering the competition late, the hot favourite from Adelaide held his nerve to defeat South African silver medallist Kyle Rademeyer and England's bronze winner Owen Heard (both 5.70m).

It was the latest big achievement for the 29-year-old, who earlier in the season handed a once-in-a-blue-moon defeat to the sport's modern-day legend, Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis.

"I just wanted to solidify myself in the record books, like I already did with the gold medal, but I definitely wanted to jump that 5.85 and take it off Steve," Marschall said.

Brooke Buschkuehl in action and on her way to bronze in the long jump. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Melbourne's Brooke Buschkuehl, the indefatigable 33-year-old mum, also made it a hat-trick of medals, but again missed out on the one she really wanted as she added a bronze in the long jump to go with her two silvers from Gold Coast and Birmingham.

Promising Wollongong teenager Delta Amidzovski, the 19-year-old world junior long jump champion, finished fourth, just five centimetres off a podium place.

World.title: Quick hits: Sprinter's surprise, a bored prince and a stunning upset
World.content:
An Australian sprinter receives a surprise visit, Jamaica celebrates in style after beating the Diamonds and Prince George looks bored at the cycling.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Surprise guests shock Aussie sprinter

Chloe Mannix-Power (right) had some fans she was not expecting to see in the stands. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Chloe Mannix-Power somewhat controversially missed out on an individual 100-metre berth at these Games, but hit the track for the first time in the women's 4x100m heats.

In the moments after she and teammates Ebony Lane, Monique Hanlon and Georgia Harris made it through to the women's 4x100m final, Mannix-Power looked up into the stands and received quite a shock.

"I thought [my parents] were at home watching on the lounge, but no they're up in the top of the grandstand cheering me on," she said.

"My parents love a surprise moment, they've done it before, so to be honest I kind of had a little feeling they would be up there, but they never tell me they're here until the end of the race."

Mannix-Power later helped Australia finish fourth in the final.

2. Prince George bored?

Prince William, Princess Catherine and their three children took in a few of the sports on day nine.

Prince George, however, seemed as though he wanted to be anywhere else when they visited the velodrome.

Prince George watches on at the velodrome. (AP: Andrew Milligan)

Earlier, the royals watched on as the Diamonds lost 46-45 to Jamaica in a major upset in the netball semifinals.

The Prince and Princess of Wales took to Instagram to thank the athletes for putting on a show.

The Prince and Princess of Wales and their family watching the netball at the Hydro in Glasgow. (Getty Images)

"Incredible atmosphere at the Commonwealth Games today," a post from their official Instagram account read.

"Watching world-class talent compete and seeing the power of sport to bring people together is truly special.

"Thank you to everyone involved for such a wonderful day."

3. 'Absolute scenes'

Jamaica celebrates its win over the Diamonds. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Not only did the Royals take in Jamaica's shock victory, but they also witnessed some of the wildest celebrations seen at the Commonwealth Games.

After Sophie Dwyer missed the shot that would have sent the semifinal to extra time, the entire Jamaican squad celebrated like they never had before.

We lost count of how many social media videos featured the caption: "Absolute scenes."

Loading Instagram content

For the Jamaicans, this was personal.

They were still hurting from their loss to the Diamonds in the 2022 Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham.

"We're carrying a bit of vengeance from the last Commonwealth Games," Jamaica captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey said.

"We've graduated from bronze medals. We didn't want bronze this year."

Jamaica faces New Zealand in the final, while the Diamonds meet England in the bronze medal play-off.

4. Montag admits to being 'selfish'

Elizabeth McMillen led Jemima Montag for most of the race, but did not win gold. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

It was an Australian sweep of the medals in the women's 10,000m race walk, but the fight for the gold medal between teammates was a fierce one.

Australian Elizabeth McMillen and Jemima Montag broke clear from the pack early and led for the entire race.

McMillen was at the front, with Montag her shadow just behind.

Montag's strategy was to use McMillen as protection from the wind, a tactic which worked to perfection.

McMillen's lead for the better part of 23 laps of the 25-lap race, before Montag ducked out from behind her and put on the burners in a decisive attack to claim gold.

It was a move she had no regrets over.

"In a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," Montag said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

McMillen was not particularly happy, but understood.

"What can you do? That's racing for you," McMillen said.

"I did look back a few times thinking, 'Are you going to help out here?', but no. I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

5. Indian boxer explains celebration

Arundhati Choudhary celebrates in her unique way. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

India boxer Arundhati Choudhary is a beacon of positivity inside and outside the ring.

Choudhary, who won gold in the women's 70-kilogram category in Glasgow, takes inspiration from a Hindu deity, Lord Rama.

This is why she opts for a bow and arrow celebration.

"In India we have Lord Rama, who killed negativity with his bow," Choudhary explained.

"Last year I was suffering from surgery and my family was also suffering from many problems.

"So I just throw the bow and arrow and shoot all the negativity out."

Tech.title: Fender’s CEO seems to think your bandmates are just analog AI
Tech.content:
Cole’s philosophy is that AI in music is nothing new. “I think AI has existed in music as long as there’s been recorded music,” he says. While the biggest barrier to playing guitar is the time it takes to learn the instrument, it’s the second barrier, writing songs, where he believes AI plays a part.

“I actually believe cover music has been sort of analog AI for a long time,” says Cole. Those that don’t yet have the skills to write their own songs can play the songs written by their favourite artists instead. “I listened a lot to REM, U2, The Smiths and The Cure, and at some point I got sick of just listening to them. I wanted to play it, so I learned to play guitar.”

Those taking their first steps into writing, according to Cole, can also lean on a second analogue form of AI: their band mates. You might just have a chorus or a riff to start with but then the drummer or bassist can add to it, and a song is born. AI can also play this role. “I actually think that we are in the brink of freeing up people to move beyond the same old covers and to really get into working like they do with their bands,” says Cole.

Tech.title: Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

When Microsoft announced its latest round of Xbox price bumps in June, it only gave US pricing. Now we know the pricing increases for the EU and UK, and they’re dramatic. Depending on the model, Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170. The 1TB Xbox Series X with a disc drive is going up by over 30 percent from £499.99 / €599.99 to £669.99 / €799.99. The 512GB Xbox Series S is getting a price increase of over 43 percent, jumping from £299.99 / €349.99 to £429.99 / €499.99.

While other consoles have received price bumps as RAM and storage prices skyrocket due to demand from the AI industry, none have been quite as dramatic as Microsoft’s. This is the third round of price increases since May of 2025, with the highest-end model now costing $300 more than its launch price of $499.99 in 2020. The 2TB model is also being retired in the face of the storage crunch. Here’s the full list of price changes:

Tech.title: Skylight’s smart calendars are up to $90 off during its back-to-school sale
Tech.content:
The start of a new school year can feel hectic, as parents juggle their kids’ classes, extracurriculars and sports on top of work, appointments, and other responsibilities. It’s easy for things to slip through the cracks, but Skylight’s shared smart calendars can help keep everyone on track, and from August 2nd through August 9th they’re up to $90 off.

The sale includes the 10-inch Skylight Calendar for $119.99 ($50 off), the 15-inch Skylight Calendar 2 for $259.99 ($20 off), and the 27-inch Skylight Calendar Max for $479.99 ($90 off). The 10-inch model takes up the least amount of space, though the newer, larger 15-inch Calendar 2 features faster performance, a brighter display, and swappable magnetic frames. The 27-inch Calendar Max, meanwhile, offers the sharpest and largest screen and must be mounted to the wall (the other models can stand on a table or be mounted), making it the easiest option for large families to view from across the room.

Regardless of which model you choose, every Skylight Calendar includes the same set of organizational features. Each member of your household can have their own color-coded profile, and each can sync events from Google, Outlook, Apple, Cozi, or Yahoo calendars. You can also create shared lists for groceries, chores, and other to-dos that everyone can access from the calendar or the companion mobile app, and even send your grocery list to Instacart with a couple of taps. Built-in weather forecasts also can help you plan around upcoming events, and you can also share calendar access with family members and trusted contacts.

You get even more perks if you subscribe to the $79 per year Plus Plan (the first month of the service is free to try). Skylight uses AI to automatically turn emails, photos, flyers, and spreadsheets into calendar entries. It also adds meal planning, tools for assigning and rewarding completed chores, and a mode that displays your photos like a digital picture frame.

Tech.title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES, replaces the HP Victus 15, a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming.

The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026’s latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it’s also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff.

I’d call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon, the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 — a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you’re going to find it.
