Tech.title: There Are 2 Eclipses This August. Here’s How to See Them
Tech.content:
The 2026 astronomical calendar features only four eclipses. But August is a bounty of riches, with two set to occur.

They include a full solar eclipse on August 12 and a partial lunar eclipse on August 27 and 28. Catch one—or both—of these eclipses if you can: They’ll be the last ones of 2026, as the other two have already taken place.

We’ve got all the details on what to expect, the path of each August eclipse, and how to watch the celestial happenings.

Solar Eclipse on August 12

The first eclipse of the month will be a total solar eclipse. This occurs when the moon passes between Earth and the sun. The August solar eclipse will be visible in the northern hemisphere.

Path: The moon’s shadow will travel from west to east, beginning in the Arctic. Parts of Alaska will be treated to a partial view of the eclipse, as well as other northerly locations including Canada, Iceland, and parts of the North Atlantic. Some locations in Europe and the eastern US will also get a glimpse of the eclipse.

Only a few areas on land will get to see totality, though. Sparsely populated stretches of eastern Greenland will see the sun completely obscured, as will the far western edge of Iceland. Spain is the most populated region in the path of totality. It’s the first time the Iberian Peninsula will be treated to a full solar eclipse in more than a century.

How to view it: For one, not with your naked eye! For areas in the path of totality, the eclipse will reach its peak in the late afternoon. That’s an idea and dramatic time for viewing, when the sun is low on the horizon. Again, just not with your naked eye!

Animation: courtesy of NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio

Times vary slightly by city, but in almost all of Spain the eclipse will occur at sunset, with totality around 8:30 pm Central European Time. From start to finish, the eclipse will last about an hour; totality is expected to last about two minutes.

Lunar Eclipse on August 27–28

The second eclipse of the month will be a partial lunar eclipse, which occurs when the Earth comes between the sun and the moon. A portion of the lunar surface will remain lit while the rest of the disk darkens or takes on a reddish hue.

Path: Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse does not follow a narrow path across the Earth. The partial lunar eclipse will be visible simultaneously across a vast region of the planet. However, the eclipse will be best viewed across the Americas, primarily in eastern and central Canada, the US, and Mexico, as well as throughout Central America, the Caribbean, and South America.

While the eclipse is partial, up to 96 percent of the lunar disk will be in the Earth’s shadow, making for a dramatic view.

Tech.title: Is It Possible to Make Smart Glasses That Aren’t Creepy?
Tech.content:
Face computers are on the upswing, as companies, massive and tiny, are all vying for nuggets in the smart-glasses gold rush.

That also means the industry is garnering its fair share of criticism, mostly focusing on the fact that creeps can abuse camera-equipped smart glasses to capture photos and videos of people without their knowledge or consent.

The prime target for such criticism is the biggest company in the space, Meta. The company’s smart glasses can capture images, audio, and video of whatever and whoever the wearer is looking at. That alone is enough to alarm anyone concerned about protecting their privacy. Meta’s smart glasses do have an indicator light to warn bystanders when they’re being recorded, though some Meta users have figured out how to bypass those safety features and disable the lights. More recently, the company has added anti-tamper features that disable the glasses if a user has meddled with them.

Other concerns about the glasses have continued to mount. Earlier this year, Meta programmed a feature that, if enabled, would add face-recognition technology to its smart glasses. After a WIRED report exposed this feature, Meta then deleted the code from its app. Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth verified the existence of the feature, called Name Tag, on The Atlantic’s podcast The Most Interesting Thing in AI.

(At an event in June, Meta also said it's considering adding camera-free smart glasses to its lineup.)

Tech.title: Europeans Are About to Find Out How Entrenched AI Is in Their Daily Lives
Tech.content:
s, music recommendations, calendar management apps, and complaint hotlines—if they use AI, Europeans will need to be told.

Starting on Sunday, citizens of the European Union must be informed when they are interacting with an AI system or viewing content generated or altered by the technology. These new transparency regulations come as part of the bloc’s Artificial Intelligence Act, which goes into effect August 2. The act is intended to reduce deception and manipulation, and help people make informed choices within the wider aim of fostering trustworthy AI in Europe.

“If a provider’s really compliant with the transparency obligations, it will become very visible how much AI is used,” Frederiek Fernhout, a technology lawyer at Stibbe, tells WIRED. “Especially in marketing.”

Ads or corporate social media posts using deepfakes will be slapped with a label stating they are AI-generated. Chatbots and hotlines handling complaints and other issues will have to state clearly if they are AI-based. Call centers using machine learning to monitor caller emotions and detect frustration will need to declare they are doing so at the start of the call.

Even among businesses, any commercial use of the technology, including scheduling appointments, handling correspondence, or negotiating contracts, will have to be declared. If companies don’t comply, they will face fines of up to €15 million ($17 million) or 3 percent of worldwide annual turnover—whichever is higher.

Model developers will also be subject to the new law, and will be monitored by the European Commission’s recently established AI Office. That includes companies beyond the obvious examples of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind. Thibau Duquin, a technology and data lawyer at Stibbe, pointed to firms like Spotify, which uses AI-powered recommendations, or Adobe for its AI editing features in Photoshop.

Tech.title: YouTube Star AboFlah Made Streaming His Life. He Wants His Kids to Live Offline
Tech.content:
AboFlah keeps looking directly into the camera. He can’t help it—the YouTuber has collected 50 million subscribers and has spent most of his life streaming. For most people, a camera lens is intimidating and cold. For AboFlah, known as Hassan Suleiman in the few hours he spends offline, it is more comforting to look into it than to ignore it.

We have our conversation in the studio of 8Flamez, the company he cofounded alongside Eyad Siyam and Saad Sarwar to manage creators and build infrastructure for the creator economy. It’s a massive, white-walled space scattered with props, furniture, and recording equipment, ready to film at any moment. He arrives on time but slightly annoyed at having missed an appointment earlier in the day. He’s not one to miss an appointment; or even an email, as I later find out. His inbox has a measly 17 unread emails.

Online, he is frequently compared to IShowSpeed and KSI, both of whom he has collaborated with. But his defining moment goes beyond any clickbait; his charity livestream, where he spent 12 days locked in a glass box in Dubai, raised $11 million for refugees and broke two world records for the longest livestream video and the most viewers for a livestream charity donation event.

Seated on a beanbag on the floor of his studio, he talks the way he streams: fast and unfiltered, in long unbroken runs that he occasionally interrupts to apologize for. He does this before, during, and after our conversation.

At 50 million subscribers and with a company, a cartoon character on the way, and a target of 100 million subscribers ahead of him, he is thinking about what comes next.

He speaks in Arabic, his speech threaded with the expressions of faith—Alhamdulillah, Inshallah, Bi’ithnillah—that punctuate many of his answers, and which I’ve kept intact.

Tech.title: Amazon Will Give Tariff Refunds to Some Customers
Tech.content:
Months after the US Supreme Court struck down certain tariff-related import charges, some Amazon customers could soon see money returned to their accounts. The online retail giant announced on Thursday that it will issue refunds to eligible customers who paid tariff-related import charges, although the timing and amounts have not been disclosed.

Amazon Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky said on an earnings call that the company had received $600 million from the US government following the Supreme Court’s February decision that President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs on imports were illegal.

From February to April 2025, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on many countries exporting goods to the US, using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act as justification. As of mid-December, more than 301,000 U.S. importers had paid $175 billion to the US government in tariff penalties. The federal government is now issuing refunds to those importers.

Under the tariff system, the US importer — not the international exporter — pays the fees to the US government.

Olsavsky said that the $600 million payment from the government was the “majority of refunds we expect to receive.”

Which customers will get refunds?

Amazon did not disclose details about the refund process for customers — who will get them, how much they will get or when. Olsavsky said there were “a limited set of circumstances” where customers had to pay tariff charges on their items.

“When we receive those refunds, we will proactively contact affected customers and automatically issue refunds to them,” he said.

Olsavsky said most Amazon customers didn’t have to pay import charges and that the company “largely absorbed” the higher prices of products affected by the tariffs. He said the company was able to avoid many tariff charges by building up its inventory before the charges hit.

An Amazon representative said the company had no further comment beyond Olsavsky’s remarks on the earnings call.

Other large merchants have also received refunds from the US government. Walmart said it would use the refunds to lower product prices, while Costco said it would compensate customers in some form, perhaps not necessarily with payments.

Bernstein analyst Zhihan Ma told Barron’s that consumers should not expect to get big paychecks in the mail from retailers. She said companies will pay some of their refund money to suppliers, and that Walmart and Costco would most likely “pass on value to their customers/members” through lower prices.

Tech.title: DuckDuckGo’s Anti-AI Sunglasses Won’t Spy On Anyone
Tech.content:
Sunglasses used to exist simply to block the sun from your eyes — and to make you look cool, like Tom Cruise in Risky Business or Top Gun. But in recent years, those innocent little shades transformed into a tech product, with Meta and other companies creating camera- and audio-enabled smart glasses. And that’s created controversy, because people can be recorded without their consent.

Enter DuckDuckGo, the privacy-focused internet search engine and web browser company. The company has partnered with eyewear company Knockaround and is now selling what it calls “anti-surveillance” sunglasses, a simple yet chic style that’s just like the sunglasses we all knew before the AI surge. They protect your eyes and don’t spy on anyone.

Yes, you can buy analog sunglasses in a million other places, including your local drugstore. But DuckDuckGo is out to make a point: AI glasses don’t respect your privacy, and the best way to protest them is not to buy them. The DuckDuckGo sunglasses even have a sassy name: Normal F* ****** Sunglasses.

No camera. No AI. Just Normal Sunglasses.



From DuckDuckGo x @Knockaround.



(Yes, these are actually real. Get a pair here: https://t.co/97UNAZMDCZ) pic.twitter.com/TUu5C81ls2 — DuckDuckGo (@DuckDuckGo) July 30, 2026

“We see the new wave of AI glasses as yet another privacy-invasive technology from Big Tech, so we created a satirical campaign around them and released Normal F****** Sunglasses,” a DuckDuckGo representative said. “Why? Because ultimately, the only truly privacy-respecting glasses are ones without cameras, mics, or AI listening in on you and others you come into contact with.”

The representative noted that DuckDuckGo CEO Gabriel Weinberg has publicly said that “AI surveillance should be banned while there is still time.”

The matte black sunglasses come in Knockaround’s Paso Robles frame design, look a lot like classic Ray-Ban Wayfarers with a small DuckDuckGo logo, and offer polarized lenses and UV400 protection. The playful website copy declares that they include zero cameras, guarantee zero notifications, offer a seamless offline mode and infinite charge life. They sell for $35 a pair.

Humor publication The Onion published a sly post about the DuckDuckGo sunglasses, sharing comical quotes from made-up consumers. “0/10, useless for perverts,” says one fictional person. Says another, “Guess I’ll have to violate people’s privacy the old-fashioned way: From the bushes.”

The representative told us that “a significant percentage of the inventory has sold, though it’s still too early to release sales data.”

Tech.title: Inside the Luxury Robotaxi Uber, Lucid and Nuro Are Testing
Tech.content:
Self-driving vehicles have become a common sight in the San Francisco Bay Area, and there are more companies looking to deploy their autonomous vehicles to public riders in the coming months.

Earlier this year, ride-hailing giant Uber, electric vehicle maker Lucid Motors and autonomous vehicle company Nuro unveiled the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, the result of a three-way partnership announced last year. I got an early look at what the companies have deemed the “industry’s most luxurious robotaxi” at CES in January, but the vehicle was parked inside a conference hall.

Last week, Nuro invited me to swing by its headquarters in Mountain View, California, to take a ride in one of its engineering prototype vehicles — with a safety driver onboard — as the companies aim for a public launch later this year.

Nuro is conducting tests on public roads with safety operators behind the wheel in the San Francisco Bay Area and in Houston. The company is also using closed-course testing and simulations to prepare its self-driving technology for a public rollout. Lucid is manufacturing the robotaxis at its factory in Arizona. Once the service becomes available, riders will be able to hail an autonomous ride in the Uber app.

“The beauty of this partnership is that it allows each company to do what it does best,” Nuro COO Andrew Chapin told me. “Uber brings the marketplace logistics, the demand and the overall in-app experience. We bring this safe AI driver, and Lucid brings a really awesome vehicle. “

The Lucid Gravity robotaxi will join the ranks of other AV companies, including Waymo and Zoox, which was just granted federal regulatory approval to begin charging for rides in its steering-wheel-less vehicles. One element that sets the Lucid Gravity AV apart is that it can fit up to six passengers, topping the four-passenger capacity of Waymo and Zoox’s offerings.

Here’s a look inside the roomy robotaxi prototype from Uber, Lucid and Nuro.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The sensor suite equipped with cameras, lidar and radar is pretty subtle on the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, at least compared with the more prominent sensor suite on Waymo’s Jaguar I-Pace vehicles.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

There’s plenty of leg room, whether you’re sitting in the front or the back. The interior colors may differ in the final version of the vehicle, but I quite like the color contrast between the tan seats and the black surroundings.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

A look at where the safety operator sits as the test vehicles navigate roads.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

There’s a nice panoramic roof to elevate the rider experience.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

This isn’t the final version of what riders will see aboard the Lucid Gravity robotaxi, but it’s meant to show how the car navigates around other vehicles.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Temperature controls allow riders to adjust the air in the cabin.

Notice how the safety operator’s hands are hovering next to the steering wheel, ready to take over if needed. They remained positioned that way for the duration of our nearly 20-minute ride.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Some Lucid Gravity robotaxis will seat up to six people, while others will seat up to four. Both options will have space for luggage, so you could take the vehicle to or from the airport without worrying about where to put your things.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

A closer look at the sensor suit atop the vehicle.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Uber, Lucid and Nuro’s robotaxi partnership is slated to kick off in the San Francisco Bay Area later this year and in Houston in mid-2027.

Tech.title: Living Underwater in 2026: New Ocean Habitat Just Dropped
Tech.content:
A new subsea habitat for humans just dropped (literally), all the way to the ocean floor. The habitat is called Vanguard, and it’s designed by a company named Deep. This habitat houses up to four people for stays of a week or more without surfacing.

DEEP

Living under pressure at depth for extended periods is already widely used in something called “saturation diving,” where divers’ bodies become fully saturated with the gas mix they’re breathing and remain under pressure between dives, eliminating the need for repeated ascents to equalize. These time-consuming ascents often involve safety stops that can take longer than the dive itself, especially at great depths.

The habitat includes a living area with four beds, a food prep station and a meal table with an ocean view. Next to that is a bathroom-and-workstation combo, and beyond that is the dive center, which includes a moon pool for entering and exiting the water.

DEEP

Vanguard is a small-scale proof of concept for a much bigger vision. Deep plans to build the equivalent of the International Space Station for the ocean: A place where humans can live, study and work long-term in an inhospitable environment.

The mechanism for this large-scale ocean living is called Sentinel: a larger, modular undersea habitat with individual sleeping quarters for added comfort during long stays.

But Sentinel is still a ways away. For now, the Deep team is gearing up to welcome the first aquanauts to Vanguard and embark on a series of studies in ocean life, reef restoration, human subsea habitation and much more. Vanguard may even prove useful for helping astronauts train for life in space. To put a slight twist on a popular phrase: the sea’s the limit.
